passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 周本纪：五十九年，秦取韩阳城负黍，西周恐，倍秦，与诸侯约从，将天下锐师出伊阙攻秦，令秦无得通阳城。秦昭王怒，使将军摎攻西周。西周君饹秦，顿首受罪，尽献其邑三十六，口三万。秦受其献，归其君於周。 周君、王赧卒，周民遂东亡。秦取九鼎宝器，而迁西周公於惮狐。 秦本纪：五十一年，将军摎攻韩，取阳城、负黍，斩首四万。攻赵，取二十余县，首虏九万。西周君背秦，与诸侯约从，将天下锐兵出伊阙攻秦，令秦毋得通阳城。于是秦使将军摎攻西周。西周君走来自归，顿首受罪，尽献其邑三十六城，口三万。秦王受献，归其君于周。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Zhou: In the fifty-ninth year, Qin took Yangcheng and Fushu from Han. Western Zhou took fright, turned against Qin, and swore the Vertical Alliance with the Lords, intending to lead the crack troops of all under Heaven out through Yique to attack Qin, so that Qin should have no way through to Yangcheng. King Zhao of Qin was angered and sent General Jiu to attack Western Zhou. The Lord of Western Zhou fled to Qin, knocked his head to the ground and acknowledged his guilt, and surrendered all his settlements, thirty-six of them, with thirty thousand persons. Qin accepted what he surrendered and sent its lord back to Zhou. The Lord of Zhou and King Nan died, and the people of Zhou thereupon fled east. Qin took the Nine Tripods and the precious vessels, and moved the Duke of Western Zhou to Danhu. Basic Annals of Qin: In the fifty-first year, General Jiu attacked Han, took Yangcheng and Fushu, and took forty thousand heads. He attacked Zhao, took more than twenty Counties, and took ninety thousand heads and captives. The Lord of Western Zhou turned his back on Qin and swore the Vertical Alliance with the Lords, intending to lead the crack soldiers of all under Heaven out through Yique to attack Qin, so that Qin should have no way through to Yangcheng. Qin thereupon sent General Jiu to attack Western Zhou. The Lord of Western Zhou came running to submit of his own accord, knocked his head to the ground and acknowledged his guilt, and surrendered all his settlements, thirty-six Fortresses, with thirty thousand persons. The King of Qin accepted what he surrendered and sent its lord back to Zhou.
passages.no: The fifty-ninth and last year of King Nan of Zhou, 256 BC. The Basic Annals of Qin, below, record the same events under the fifty-first year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin; the two counts name the same year. The edition reads 饹, equivalent to 奔, "fled to". 周君、王赧卒: two persons, following the punctuation of the edition. The Lord of Zhou here is the Lord of Western Zhou who had surrendered to Qin, Duke Wu 西周武公 (so Song Zhong in the Jijie; the Suoyin: 此时武公与王赧皆卒，故连言也). The Duke of Western Zhou moved to Danhu in the next sentence is therefore his successor, Duke Wen 文公 (Suoyin: 盖武公之太子文公也，武公卒而立，为秦所迁). 惮狐: the edition writes the first character with 单 over 心 (憚); the commentaries place it in the Liang County of the time, near modern Ruzhou, Henan. 邑三十六城: 城 rendered Fortress. 周: the remnant of the Western Zhou domain to which its lord was sent back. The Basic Annals for 256 BC, the year in which Qin extinguished Western Zhou: the entry of the Basic Annals of Zhou under the fifty-ninth year of King Nan, and the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the fifty-first year of King Zhaoxiang, which record the same events from the two sides.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 周：赧王卒。 魏：韓、魏、楚救趙新中，秦兵罷。 韓：秦擊我陽城。救趙新中。 楚：救趙新中。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Zhou: King Nan died. Wei: Han, Wei and Chu went to the relief of Zhao at Xinzhong; the Qin troops withdrew. Han: Qin attacked our Yangcheng. Went to the relief of Zhao at Xinzhong. Chu: Went to the relief of Zhao at Xinzhong.
passages.no: The four lines are the entries of the Table of the Six States (六国年表) for this year, one line to a state: Zhou, Wei, Han and Chu; the states without an entry for the year are not given. 我: the Table speaks from the standpoint of the state whose column it is, so "our Yangcheng" is Han's Yangcheng. The Basic Annals, above, record that Qin took Yangcheng and Fushu from Han in this year. The subject of the following clause, and of the Chu line, is likewise the state of the column. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year. The Table runs the states in parallel columns, one line to a state; only the states with an entry for the year appear.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 楚世家：六年，秦围邯郸，赵告急楚，楚遣将军景阳救赵。七年，至新中。秦兵去。 赵世家：十年，燕攻昌壮，五月拔之。赵将乐乘、庆舍攻秦信梁军，破之。太子死。而秦攻西周，拔之。徒父祺出。 韩世家：十七年，秦拔我阳城、负黍。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Chu: In the sixth year, Qin besieged Handan; Zhao sent word of its peril to Chu, and Chu sent General Jing Yang to the relief of Zhao. In the seventh year, he reached Xinzhong. The Qin troops departed. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the tenth year, Yan attacked Changzhuang and took it in May. The Zhao generals Yue Cheng and Qing She attacked the Qin army under Xinliang and routed it. The Heir Apparent died. And Qin attacked Western Zhou and took it. Tufu Qi went out. Hereditary House of Han: In the seventeenth year, Qin took our Yangcheng and Fushu.
passages.no: The sixth and seventh years of King Kaolie of Chu, 257 and 256 BC; the entry is given from the sixth year because the relief that ends in this year begins there. The tenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 256 BC. The Heir Apparent of Zhao, whose name the history does not record (Suoyin). Xu Guang, noting that King Nan of Zhou died this year, asks whether 太子 may stand for 天子, the Son of Heaven. 出: the Zhengyi takes this as leading troops out beyond the border — Zhao, seeing Qin take Western Zhou, sent Tufu Qi out with an army. The seventeenth year of King Huanhui of Han, 256 BC. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the houses of Chu, Zhao and Han, each under its own count of years.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 魏公子列传：魏公子无忌者，魏昭王子少子而魏安釐王异母弟也。昭王薨，安釐王即位，封公子为信陵君。是时范睢亡魏相秦，以怨魏齐故，秦兵围大梁，破魏华阳下军，走芒卯。魏王及公子患之。 公子为人仁而下士，士无贤不肖皆谦而礼交之，不敢以其富贵骄士。士以此方数千里争往归之，致食客三千人。当是时，诸侯以公子贤，多客，不敢加兵谋魏十馀年。 公子与魏王博，而北境传举烽，言“赵寇至，且入界”。魏王释博，欲召大臣谋。公子止王曰：“赵王田猎耳，非为寇也。”复博如故。王恐，心不在博。居顷，复从北方来传言曰：“赵王猎耳，非为寇也。”魏王大惊，曰：“公子何以知之？”公子曰：“臣之客有能深得赵王阴事者，赵王所为，客辄以报臣，臣以此知之。”是後魏王畏公子之贤能，不敢任公子以国政。 魏有隐士曰侯嬴，年七十，家贫，为大梁夷门监者。公子闻之，往请，欲厚遗之。不肯受，曰：“臣脩身絜行数十年，终不以监门困故而受公子财。”公子於是乃置酒大会宾客。坐定，公子从车骑，虚左，自迎夷门侯生。侯生摄敝衣冠，直上载公子上坐，不让，欲以观公子。公子执辔愈恭。侯生又谓公子曰：“臣有客在市屠中，原枉车骑过之。”公子引车入巿，侯生下见其客朱亥，俾倪故久立，与其客语，微察公子。公子颜色愈和。当是时，魏将相宗室宾客满堂，待公子举酒。巿人皆观公子执辔。从骑皆窃骂侯生。侯生视公子色终不变，乃谢客就车。至家，公子引侯生坐上坐，遍赞宾客，宾客皆惊。酒酣，公子起，为寿侯生前。侯生因谓公子曰：“今日嬴之为公子亦足矣。嬴乃夷门抱关者也，而公子亲枉车骑，自迎嬴於众人广坐之中，不宜有所过，今公子故过之。然嬴欲就公子之名，故久立公子车骑巿中，过客以观公子，公子愈恭。巿人皆以嬴为小人，而以公子为长者能下士也。”於是罢酒，侯生遂为上客。 侯生谓公子曰：“臣所过屠者硃亥，此子贤者，世莫能知，故隐屠间耳。”公子往数请之，硃亥故不复谢，公子怪之。 魏安釐王二十年，秦昭王已破赵长平军，又进兵围邯郸。公子姊为赵惠文王弟平原君夫人，数遗魏王及公子书，请救於魏。魏王使将军晋鄙将十万众救赵。秦王使使者告魏王曰：“吾攻赵旦暮且下，而诸侯敢救者，已拔赵，必移兵先击之。”魏王恐，使人止晋鄙，留军壁鄴，名为救赵，实持两端以观望。平原君使者冠盖相属於魏，让魏公子曰：“胜所以自附为婚姻者，以公子之高义，为能急人之困。今邯郸旦暮降秦而魏救不至，安在公子能急人之困也！且公子纵轻胜，弃之降秦，独不怜公子姊邪？”公子患之，数请魏王，及宾客辩士说王万端。魏王畏秦，终不听公子。公子自度终不能得之於王，计不独生而令赵亡，乃请宾客，约车骑百馀乘，欲以客往赴秦军，与赵俱死。 行过夷门，见侯生，具告所以欲死秦军状。辞决而行，侯生曰：“公子勉之矣，老臣不能从。”公子行数里，心不快，曰：“吾所以待侯生者备矣，天下莫不闻，今吾且死而侯生曾无一言半辞送我，我岂有所失哉？”复引车还，问侯生。侯生笑曰：“臣固知公子之还也。”曰：“公子喜士，名闻天下。今有难，无他端而欲赴秦军，譬若以肉投馁虎，何功之有哉？尚安事客？然公子遇臣厚，公子往而臣不送，以是知公子恨之复返也。”公子再拜，因问。侯生乃屏人间语，曰：“嬴闻晋鄙之兵符常在王卧内，而如姬最幸，出入王卧内，力能窃之。嬴闻如姬父为人所杀，如姬资之三年，自王以下欲求报其父仇，莫能得。如姬为公子泣，公子使客斩其仇头，敬进如姬。如姬之欲为公子死，无所辞，顾未有路耳。公子诚一开口请如姬，如姬必许诺，则得虎符夺晋鄙军，北救赵而西卻秦，此五霸之伐也。”公子从其计，请如姬。如姬果盗晋鄙兵符与公子。 公子行，侯生曰：“将在外，主令有所不受，以便国家。公子即合符，而晋鄙不授公子兵而复请之，事必危矣。臣客屠者硃亥可与俱，此人力士。晋鄙听，大善；不听，可使击之。”於是公子泣。侯生曰：“公子畏死邪？何泣也？”公子曰：“晋鄙嚄唶宿将，往恐不听，必当杀之，是以泣耳，岂畏死哉？”於是公子请硃亥。硃亥笑曰：“臣乃市井鼓刀屠者，而公子亲数存之，所以不报谢者，以为小礼无所用。今公子有急，此乃臣效命之秋也。”遂与公子俱。公子过谢侯生。侯生曰：“臣宜从，老不能。请数公子行日，以至晋鄙军之日，北乡自刭，以送公子。”公子遂行。 至鄴，矫魏王令代晋鄙。晋鄙合符，疑之，举手视公子曰：“今吾拥十万之众，屯於境上，国之重任，今单车来代之，何如哉？”欲无听。硃亥袖四十斤铁椎，椎杀晋鄙，公子遂将晋鄙军。勒兵下令军中曰：“父子俱在军中，父归；兄弟俱在军中，兄归；独子无兄弟，归养。”得选兵八万人，进兵击秦军。秦军解去，遂救邯郸，存赵。赵王及平原君自迎公子於界，平原君负籣矢为公子先引。赵王再拜曰：“自古贤人未有及公子者也。”当此之时，平原君不敢自比於人。公子与侯生决，至军，侯生果北乡自刭。 魏王怒公子之盗其兵符，矫杀晋鄙，公子亦自知也。已卻秦存赵，使将将其军归魏，而公子独与客留赵。赵孝成王德公子之矫夺晋鄙兵而存赵，乃与平原君计，以五城封公子。公子闻之，意骄矜而有自功之色。客有说公子曰：“物有不可忘，或有不可不忘。夫人有德於公子，公子不可忘也；公子有德於人，原公子忘之也。且矫魏王令，夺晋鄙兵以救赵，於赵则有功矣，於魏则未为忠臣也。公子乃自骄而功之，窃为公子不取也。”於是公子立自责，似若无所容者。赵王埽除自迎，执主人之礼，引公子就西阶。公子侧行辞让，从东阶上。自言罪过，以负於魏，无功於赵。赵王侍酒至暮，口不忍献五城，以公子退让也。公子竟留赵。赵王以鄗为公子汤沐邑，魏亦复以信陵奉公子。公子留赵。 公子闻赵有处士毛公藏於博徒，薛公藏於卖浆家，公子欲见两人，两人自匿不肯见公子。公子闻所在，乃间步往从此两人游，甚欢。平原君闻之，谓其夫人曰：“始吾闻夫人弟公子天下无双，今吾闻之，乃妄从博徒卖浆者游，公子妄人耳。”夫人以告公子。公子乃谢夫人去，曰：“始吾闻平原君贤，故负魏王而救赵，以称平原君。平原君之游，徒豪举耳，不求士也。无忌自在大梁时，常闻此两人贤，至赵，恐不得见。以无忌从之游，尚恐其不我欲也，今平原君乃以为羞，其不足从游。”乃装为去。夫人具以语平原君。平原君乃免冠谢，固留公子。平原君门下闻之，半去平原君归公子，天下士复往归公子，公子倾平原君客。 公子留赵十年不归。秦闻公子在赵，日夜出兵东伐魏。魏王患之，使使往请公子。公子恐其怒之，乃诫门下：“有敢为魏王使通者，死。”宾客皆背魏之赵，莫敢劝公子归。毛公、薛公两人往见公子曰：“公子所以重於赵，名闻诸侯者，徒以有魏也。今秦攻魏，魏急而公子不恤，使秦破大梁而夷先王之宗庙，公子当何面目立天下乎？”语未及卒，公子立变色，告车趣驾归救魏。 魏王见公子，相与泣，而以上将军印授公子，公子遂将。魏安釐王三十年，公子使使遍告诸侯。诸侯闻公子将，各遣将将兵救魏。公子率五国之兵破秦军於河外，走蒙骜。遂乘胜逐秦军至函谷关，抑秦兵，秦兵不敢出。当是时，公子威振天下，诸侯之客进兵法，公子皆名之，故世俗称魏公子兵法。 秦王患之，乃行金万斤於魏，求晋鄙客，令毁公子於魏王曰：“公子亡在外十年矣，今为魏将，诸侯将皆属，诸侯徒闻魏公子，不闻魏王。公子亦欲因此时定南面而王，诸侯畏公子之威，方欲共立之。”秦数使反间，伪贺公子得立为魏王未也。魏王日闻其毁，不能不信，後果使人代公子将。公子自知再以毁废，乃谢病不朝，与宾客为长夜饮，饮醇酒，多近妇女。日夜为乐饮者四岁，竟病酒而卒。其岁，魏安釐王亦薨。 秦闻公子死，使蒙骜攻魏，拔二十城，初置东郡。其後秦稍蚕食魏，十八岁而虏魏王，屠大梁。 高祖始微少时，数闻公子贤。及即天子位，每过大梁，常祠公子。高祖十二年，从击黥布还，为公子置守冢五家，世世岁以四时奉祠公子。 太史公曰：吾过大梁之墟，求问其所谓夷门。夷门者，城之东门也。天下诸公子亦有喜士者矣，然信陵君之接岩穴隐者，不耻下交，有以也。名冠诸侯，不虚耳。高祖每过之而令民奉祠不绝也。 范雎蔡泽列传：後数日，入朝，言於秦昭王曰：“客新有从山东来者曰蔡泽，其人辩士，明於三王之事，五伯之业，世俗之变，足以寄秦国之政。臣之见人甚众，莫及，臣不如也。臣敢以闻。”秦昭王召见，与语，大说之，拜为客卿。应侯因谢病请归相印。昭王彊起应侯，应侯遂称病笃。范雎免相，昭王新说蔡泽计画，遂拜为秦相，东收周室。 蔡泽相秦数月，人或恶之，惧诛，乃谢病归相印，号为纲成君。居秦十馀年，事昭王、孝文王、庄襄王。卒事始皇帝，为秦使於燕，三年而燕使太子丹入质於秦。 廉颇蔺相如列传：明年，秦兵遂围邯郸，岁馀，几不得脱。赖楚、魏诸侯来救，乃得解邯郸之围。赵王亦以括母先言，竟不诛也。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of the Prince of Wei: Wuji, Prince of Wei, was the youngest son of King Zhao of Wei and the half-brother of King Anxi of Wei. When King Zhao died and King Anxi came to the throne, he enfeoffed the Prince as Lord Xinling. At this time Fan Ju had fled from Wei and become Chancellor of Qin, and because of his grudge against Wei Qi the Qin troops besieged Daliang, defeated the Wei army below Huayang, and put Mang Mao to flight. The King of Wei and the Prince were troubled by this. The Prince was by nature humane and humbled himself before gentlemen; whether a gentleman was worthy or unworthy, he met him with modesty and courtesy, and never dared to lord it over gentlemen on account of his wealth and rank. For this reason gentlemen from thousands of li around vied to go over to him, until he had three thousand retainers. At that time the Lords, because the Prince was worthy and had many retainers, dared not raise troops or plot against Wei for more than ten years. The Prince was playing at bo with the King of Wei when from the northern border beacons were passed along, with word that "Zhao raiders have come and are about to cross the border". The King of Wei put down the game and wished to summon the great ministers to take counsel. The Prince stopped the King: "The King of Zhao is only out hunting; it is no raid." And he went on with the game as before. The King was afraid, and his mind was not on the game. After a while word came again from the north: "The King of Zhao was only hunting; it was no raid." The King of Wei was greatly startled and said: "How did the Prince know it?" The Prince said: "Among your servant's retainers is one who can get at the King of Zhao's secret doings; whatever the King of Zhao does, the retainer at once reports to your servant, and that is how I knew it." After this the King of Wei stood in fear of the Prince's worth and ability, and dared not entrust the Prince with the government of the state. In Wei there was a recluse called Hou Ying, seventy years old and poor, who was the keeper of the Yi Gate of Daliang. The Prince heard of him, went to call on him, and wished to make him a rich gift. He would not accept it, saying: "For some tens of years your servant has cultivated his person and kept his conduct clean; I will not, because of the hardship of keeping a gate, accept the Prince's wealth." The Prince thereupon set out wine and called a great gathering of his guests. When they were seated, the Prince went out with his carriage and horsemen, leaving the left-hand seat empty, to fetch Master Hou of the Yi Gate in person. Master Hou gathered up his worn robe and cap, went straight up and took the upper seat in the Prince's carriage without demurring, meaning to observe the Prince. The Prince held the reins with ever greater respect. Master Hou then said to the Prince: "I have a friend among the butchers of the market; I would have you trouble your carriage and horsemen to go round by him." The Prince drove the carriage into the market. Master Hou got down to see his friend Zhu Hai, and, glancing sidelong, stood there on purpose a long while, talking with his friend and covertly watching the Prince. The Prince's expression grew ever milder. At that moment the generals, ministers, royal kinsmen and guests of Wei filled the hall, waiting for the Prince to raise the wine. The people of the market all watched the Prince holding the reins, and the attendant horsemen all cursed Master Hou under their breath. When Master Hou saw that the Prince's expression never changed, he took leave of his friend and got into the carriage. On reaching the house the Prince led Master Hou to the upper seat and presented him to the guests one by one, and the guests were all astonished. When the wine was flowing the Prince rose and drank Master Hou's health before him. Master Hou then said to the Prince: "What Ying has done for the Prince today is enough. Ying is a mere keeper of the bar at the Yi Gate, yet the Prince in person troubled his carriage and horsemen to fetch Ying himself, before a great company of men. It was not fitting to go out of the way for anyone, yet today the Prince went out of his way on purpose. Still, Ying wished to make the Prince's reputation complete, and so he kept the Prince's carriage and horsemen standing a long while in the market, calling on a friend in order to observe the Prince; and the Prince grew ever more respectful. The people of the market all take Ying for a petty man, and the Prince for an elder who can humble himself before gentlemen." With that the drinking ended, and Master Hou became the chief guest. Master Hou said to the Prince: "The butcher Zhu Hai, on whom I called, is a worthy man whom the world has not been able to recognise, and so he hides himself among the butchers." The Prince went several times to call on him, but Zhu Hai purposely never returned the courtesy, and the Prince thought it strange. In the twentieth year of King Anxi of Wei, King Zhao of Qin, having already destroyed the Zhao army at Changping, advanced his troops again and besieged Handan. The Prince's elder sister was the wife of Lord Pingyuan, the younger brother of King Huiwen of Zhao, and she sent letter after letter to the King of Wei and the Prince asking for relief from Wei. The King of Wei sent General Jin Bi at the head of a hundred thousand men to relieve Zhao. The King of Qin sent an envoy to tell the King of Wei: "I am attacking Zhao, and it will fall any day; should any of the Lords dare to relieve it, once I have taken Zhao I shall certainly move my troops and strike him first." The King of Wei was afraid and sent men to halt Jin Bi, who kept his army encamped at Ye, relieving Zhao in name but in fact holding to both sides and watching how things went. Lord Pingyuan's envoys came to Wei one after another, cap after canopy, and he reproached the Prince of Wei: "The reason Sheng attached himself to you by marriage was that the Prince's lofty sense of right could hasten to a man in his extremity. Now Handan may surrender to Qin any day and Wei's relief does not come — where is the Prince's hastening to a man in his extremity! And even if the Prince thinks nothing of Sheng and abandons him to surrender to Qin, has he no pity for his own sister?" The Prince was troubled; he pleaded with the King of Wei again and again, and his guests and disputants argued with the King in ten thousand ways. The King of Wei feared Qin and in the end would not listen to the Prince. The Prince judged that in the end he would never obtain it from the King, and resolved not to live on alone while Zhao perished; so he called on his guests, mustered a hundred-odd carriages and horsemen, and meant to go with his guests and fling himself on the Qin army, to die together with Zhao. On his way he passed the Yi Gate and saw Master Hou, and told him in full how he meant to die against the Qin army. He took his leave and set off, and Master Hou said: "May the Prince do his utmost; your old servant cannot follow." The Prince had gone several li when he grew uneasy at heart and said: "The way I have treated Master Hou was complete, and none under Heaven has not heard of it; now I am going to my death and Master Hou has not a word or half a phrase to send me off with — have I failed in something?" He turned the carriage back and questioned Master Hou. Master Hou laughed and said: "I knew, of course, that the Prince would come back." He said: "The Prince delights in gentlemen, and his name is heard throughout all under Heaven. Now there is trouble, and with no other plan you mean to fling yourself on the Qin army; that is like throwing meat to a starving tiger — what good can it do? And what use then are your retainers? Yet the Prince has treated me generously, and when the Prince went and I did not see him off, I knew by that that the Prince would resent it and come back." The Prince bowed twice and asked his counsel. Master Hou then sent the others away and spoke with him privately: "Ying has heard that the tally for Jin Bi's army is always kept in the King's bedchamber, and that Lady Ru is the most favoured and goes in and out of the King's bedchamber; it is in her power to steal it. Ying has heard that Lady Ru's father was killed by someone, and that Lady Ru nursed the grievance three years; from the King downward they sought to avenge her father, and none could. Lady Ru wept before the Prince, and the Prince had a retainer cut off her enemy's head and present it respectfully to Lady Ru. Lady Ru's wish to die for the Prince is one she would not refuse; only she has had no way to do it. If the Prince will but open his mouth once and ask Lady Ru, Lady Ru will surely consent; then you will have the tiger tally and can seize Jin Bi's army, go north to relieve Zhao and westward drive back Qin — that is a feat of the Five Hegemons." The Prince followed his plan and asked Lady Ru. Lady Ru did indeed steal Jin Bi's army tally and give it to the Prince. As the Prince set out, Master Hou said: "When a general is in the field, there are commands of his ruler that he does not accept, for the good of the state. If the Prince matches the tallies and Jin Bi does not hand the army over to the Prince but sends to ask the King again, the affair will surely be in danger. My friend the butcher Zhu Hai can go with you; he is a man of strength. If Jin Bi listens, very good; if he does not, you can have him strike him down." At this the Prince wept. Master Hou said: "Is the Prince afraid to die? Why do you weep?" The Prince said: "Jin Bi is a blustering old general; I fear that when I go he will not listen, and then I must kill him. That is why I weep — how could I be afraid to die?" The Prince then asked Zhu Hai. Zhu Hai laughed and said: "I am a butcher who plies the knife in the market-place, yet the Prince has in person called on me several times. The reason I did not return the courtesy was that I thought small civilities of no use. Now the Prince is in urgent need; this is the season for me to give my life." So he went with the Prince. The Prince went by to take leave of Master Hou. Master Hou said: "I ought to follow you, but I am old and cannot. Let me count the days of the Prince's journey, and on the day you reach Jin Bi's army I shall face north and cut my throat, to send the Prince off." The Prince then set out. He reached Ye and, feigning a command of the King of Wei, took over from Jin Bi. Jin Bi matched the tallies but doubted him; raising his hand, he looked at the Prince and said: "I now hold a host of a hundred thousand, camped on the border — a weighty charge of the state. Now you come in a single carriage to replace me; how is this?" He meant not to obey. Zhu Hai, with an iron mace of forty jin in his sleeve, struck Jin Bi dead, and the Prince took command of Jin Bi's army. He drew up the troops and gave orders throughout the army: "Where father and son are both in the army, let the father go home; where elder and younger brother are both in the army, let the elder go home; an only son with no brothers, let him go home and support his parents." He obtained eighty thousand picked men and advanced to attack the Qin army. The Qin army broke off and withdrew, and so he relieved Handan and preserved Zhao. The King of Zhao and Lord Pingyuan came in person to meet the Prince at the border, Lord Pingyuan carrying quiver and arrows on his back to lead the way for the Prince. The King of Zhao bowed twice and said: "Since antiquity no man of worth has come up to the Prince." At this time Lord Pingyuan dared not compare himself with others. When the Prince had parted from Master Hou and reached the army, Master Hou did indeed face north and cut his throat. The King of Wei was angry that the Prince had stolen his army tally and killed Jin Bi under a feigned command, and the Prince knew it himself. Having driven back Qin and preserved Zhao, he had a general lead his army back to Wei, while the Prince alone stayed in Zhao with his retainers. King Xiaocheng of Zhao, grateful to the Prince for seizing Jin Bi's army under a feigned command and preserving Zhao, planned with Lord Pingyuan to enfeoff the Prince with five Fortresses. When the Prince heard of it, his mind grew proud and he wore the look of one who takes credit for his deed. One of his retainers said to the Prince: "There are things that must not be forgotten, and things that must not be remembered. When another has done the Prince a kindness, the Prince must not forget it; when the Prince has done another a kindness, I would have the Prince forget it. Moreover, to feign the King of Wei's command and seize Jin Bi's army to relieve Zhao was a service to Zhao, but towards Wei it was not the act of a loyal subject. For the Prince to grow proud and take credit for it — I privately think the Prince should not." At this the Prince at once reproached himself, as if there were nowhere he could hide. The King of Zhao swept the way and came to meet him in person, performed the rites of a host, and led the Prince towards the western steps. The Prince stepped aside in refusal and went up by the eastern steps. He declared his own fault: he had failed Wei and done no service to Zhao. The King of Zhao kept him at wine until dusk, and could not bring himself to offer the five Fortresses, because of the Prince's self-abasement. In the end the Prince stayed in Zhao. The King of Zhao gave the Prince Hao as his private estate, and Wei too restored Xinling for the Prince's support. The Prince remained in Zhao. The Prince heard that in Zhao there were gentlemen in retirement: Master Mao, hidden among the gamblers, and Master Xue, hidden in the house of a seller of drinks. The Prince wished to see the two men, but the two hid themselves and would not see the Prince. When the Prince learned where they were, he went secretly on foot to keep company with the two, and they were very happy together. When Lord Pingyuan heard of it, he said to his wife: "At first I heard that your brother the Prince had no equal under Heaven; now I hear that he recklessly keeps company with gamblers and sellers of drinks — the Prince is a reckless man, that is all." His wife told the Prince. The Prince then took leave of his sister to go, saying: "At first I heard that Lord Pingyuan was a man of worth, and so I betrayed the King of Wei to relieve Zhao, to answer Lord Pingyuan's expectations. But Lord Pingyuan's company is only a grand display; he does not seek gentlemen. When Wuji was still in Daliang he often heard that these two were worthy men, and on coming to Zhao he feared he would not get to see them. With Wuji keeping their company, I still feared they would not want me; now Lord Pingyuan thinks it a disgrace — he is not worth keeping company with." And he packed to leave. His wife told Lord Pingyuan everything. Lord Pingyuan then took off his cap, apologised, and insisted that the Prince stay. When Lord Pingyuan's household heard of it, half of them left Lord Pingyuan and went over to the Prince, and the gentlemen of all under Heaven went over to the Prince once more; the Prince drew away Lord Pingyuan's retainers. The Prince stayed in Zhao ten years without returning. Qin, hearing that the Prince was in Zhao, sent troops east day and night to attack Wei. The King of Wei was troubled by this and sent envoys to ask the Prince back. The Prince, fearing that the King was angry with him, warned his household: "Whoever dares to carry word for the King of Wei's envoys dies." His guests had all turned their backs on Wei for Zhao, and none dared urge the Prince to return. The two men Master Mao and Master Xue went to see the Prince and said: "The reason the Prince weighs heavily in Zhao and his name is heard among the Lords is solely that there is a Wei. Now Qin attacks Wei; Wei is in extremity and the Prince does not care. Should Qin destroy Daliang and level the ancestral temple of the former kings, with what face could the Prince stand before all under Heaven?" Before they had finished speaking the Prince's colour changed at once; he called for his carriage and hurried home to relieve Wei. The King of Wei saw the Prince, and they wept together; and he gave the seal of Supreme General to the Prince, and the Prince took command. In the thirtieth year of King Anxi of Wei the Prince sent envoys to inform all the Lords. When the Lords heard that the Prince was in command, each sent generals with troops to relieve Wei. The Prince led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai, putting Meng Ao to flight. Then, following up the victory, he pursued the Qin army to Hangu Pass and held the Qin troops in check, so that the Qin troops dared not come out. At this time the Prince's majesty shook all under Heaven, and the retainers of the Lords presented methods of war, to all of which the Prince gave his name; hence the world at large calls them the Prince of Wei's Methods of War. The King of Qin was troubled by this, and sent ten thousand jin of gold into Wei to seek out Jin Bi's former retainers and have them slander the Prince to the King of Wei: "The Prince was ten years in exile abroad; now he is Wei's general, and the generals of the Lords are all under him; the Lords hear only of the Prince of Wei and not of the King of Wei. The Prince also wishes to seize this moment to face south and make himself king; the Lords, in awe of the Prince's majesty, are about to set him up together." Qin several times sent agents of discord, feigning to congratulate the Prince on whether he had yet been set up as King of Wei. The King of Wei heard the slander daily and could not help believing it, and afterwards did indeed send someone to replace the Prince in command. The Prince, knowing that he had a second time been cast aside through slander, pleaded illness and did not attend court; with his guests he drank the night through, drinking strong wine and keeping much company with women. Day and night he made merry with drink for four years, and in the end died of drink. That same year King Anxi of Wei also died. When Qin heard that the Prince was dead, it sent Meng Ao to attack Wei; he took twenty Fortresses, and Dong Commandery was first established. Thereafter Qin ate away at Wei little by little, as a silkworm eats a leaf, and in eighteen years it captured the King of Wei and slaughtered Daliang. When Gaozu was still young and humble, he often heard of the Prince's worth. After he ascended the throne as Son of Heaven, whenever he passed Daliang he always sacrificed to the Prince. In the twelfth year of Gaozu, returning from the attack on Qing Bu, he established five tomb-keeping households for the Prince, to sacrifice to the Prince at the four seasons every year, generation after generation. The Grand Historian says: I passed the ruins of Daliang and sought out what is called the Yi Gate. The Yi Gate was the eastern gate of the Fortress. Among the princes of all under Heaven there have been others who delighted in gentlemen, but that Lord Xinling received recluses of the caves and cliffs, and was not ashamed to associate with those beneath him, had its reason. That his name stood first among the Lords was no empty thing. And Gaozu, whenever he passed, had the people sacrifice to him without cease. Biography of Fan Ju and Cai Ze: Some days later he went in to court and said to King Zhao of Qin: "Among the visitors there is one newly come from east of the mountains called Cai Ze, a man of eloquence, clear on the affairs of the Three Kings, the achievements of the Five Hegemons and the changes of the age — well able to be entrusted with the government of the state of Qin. Your servant has seen a great many men, and none comes up to him; your servant is not his equal. Your servant ventures to report it." King Zhao of Qin summoned him and spoke with him, was greatly pleased, and appointed him Guest Minister. Marquis Ying thereupon pleaded illness and asked to return the seal of Chancellor. King Zhao pressed Marquis Ying to rise, but Marquis Ying then declared himself gravely ill. Fan Ju was dismissed as Chancellor; King Zhao, newly pleased with Cai Ze's plans, then appointed him Chancellor of Qin, and eastward took in the house of Zhou. Cai Ze had been Chancellor of Qin for some months when someone spoke ill of him; fearing execution, he pleaded illness and returned the seal of Chancellor, and was styled Lord Gangcheng. He lived in Qin more than ten years, serving King Zhao, King Xiaowen and King Zhuangxiang. Last he served the First Emperor, and went as Qin's envoy to Yan; after three years Yan sent Heir Apparent Dan as a hostage to Qin. Biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru: The next year the Qin troops went on to besiege Handan, and for more than a year it barely escaped. Thanks to the Lords of Chu and Wei coming to its relief, the siege of Handan was lifted. The King of Zhao, too, because Kuo's mother had spoken beforehand, in the end did not put her to death.
passages.no: 博: the board game liubo. 巿, for 市 "market", so written here and twice below. 257 BC. 247 BC. The chapter is excerpted: the speaker is Fan Ju, and the passage follows his interview with Cai Ze. 应侯: Fan Ju, by his title as Marquis of Ying. The chapter is excerpted: "the next year" counts from the preceding passage of the biography. 公子: the biography calls Wuji "the Prince" throughout. 胜: Lord Pingyuan, Zhao Sheng, naming himself in his message. The Biographies: the biography of the Prince of Wei, Lord Xinling, entire; the passage of the biography of Fan Ju and Cai Ze in which Cai Ze becomes Chancellor and Qin takes in the house of Zhou; and the lines of the biography of Lian Po and Lin Xiangru on the siege of Handan.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传：秦昭王五十年，使王齮围邯郸，急，赵欲杀子楚。子楚与吕不韦谋，行金六百斤予守者吏，得脱，亡赴秦军，遂以得归。赵欲杀子楚妻子，子楚夫人赵豪家女也，得匿，以故母子竟得活。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: In the fiftieth year of King Zhao of Qin, he sent Wang Yi to besiege Handan. As the siege grew pressing, Zhao wished to kill Zichu. Zichu plotted with Lü Buwei, and by giving six hundred jin of gold to the officers who guarded him he got free, fled to the Qin army, and so was able to return. Zhao wished to kill Zichu's wife and child, but Zichu's wife was the daughter of a great house of Zhao and was able to hide, and so mother and child in the end came out alive.
passages.no: 257 BC. 子楚: King Zhuangxiang, under the name the Biography of Lü Buwei gives him at Handan. The Biographies, continued: the passage of the biography of Lü Buwei on Zichu's escape from Handan.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 燕孝王发兵攻打赵国昌城(《赵世家》误作“昌壮”，今据校勘更改），五月拔之。 辨析：《史記》宋刻本仍作昌壯，是否應改？待考。 無骨注:燕国约于此时夺占了赵国河间的一部分，所以后来能献出河间十城(事见《战国纵横家书》) 辨析：原文附：二十五、李园谓辛梧章 秦使辛梧据粱（梁），合秦粱（梁）而攻楚。李园忧之。兵未出，谓辛梧：“以秦之强，有两端之劲，东面而伐楚。于臣也，楚不侍（待）伐割挚马免而西走，秦余（与）楚为上交，秦祸案环（还）中粱（梁）矣。将军必逐于粱（梁），恐诛于秦。将军不见井忌乎？ 为秦据赵而攻燕，拔二城。燕使蔡鸟股符〓去壁，奸（间）赵入秦，以河间十城封秦相文信侯。 文信侯弗敢受，曰：‘我无功。’蔡鸟明日见，带长剑，举其末，视视（示）文信侯曰：‘君曰我无功，君无功，胡不解君之玺，以佩蒙敖（骜）、王〓也？秦王以君为贤，故加君二人之上。今燕献地。此非秦之地也。君弗受，不忠。’文信侯敬若（诺）。言之秦王，秦王令受之。余（与）燕为上交，秦祸案环（还）归于赵矣。秦大举兵东面而赍赵，言毋攻燕。以秦之强，有燕之怒，割勺（赵）必深。赵不能听，逐井忌，诛于秦。今臣窃为将军私计，不如少案（按）之，毋庸出兵，秦未得志于楚，必重粱（梁），粱（梁）未得志于楚，必重秦，是将军两重。天下人无不死者，久者寿。愿将军之察之也。粱（梁）兵未出，楚见粱（梁）之未出兵也，走秦必缓。秦王怒于楚之缓也，怨必深。是将军有（又）重矣。”粱（梁）兵果六月乃出。 卫怀君采取连横之策，背叛魏国。 辨析：此條來源《韓非子·五蠹》：故周去秦为从，期年而举；卫离魏为衡，半岁而亡。是周灭于从，卫亡于衡也。使周、卫缓其从衡之计，而严其境内之治，明其法禁，必其赏罚，尽其地力以多其积，致其民死以坚其城守，天下得其地则其利少，攻其国则其伤大，万乘之国莫敢自顿于坚城之下，而使强敌裁其弊也，此必不亡之术也。舍必不亡之术而道必灭之事，治国者之过也。智困于内而政乱于外，则亡不可振也。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I King Xiao of Yan sent troops to attack Zhao's Changcheng (the Hereditary House of Zhao wrongly has 昌壮; emended here on the basis of collation) and took it in May. Analysis: the Song printed edition of the Shiji still reads 昌壯. Should it be emended? Pending investigation. Ivar's note: Yan at about this time seized part of Zhao's Hejian, which is why it was later able to offer up the ten Fortresses of Hejian (see the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu). Analysis: original text appended: chapter 25, Li Yuan speaks to Xin Wu. Qin sent Xin Wu to hold Liang, to join Qin and Liang in an attack on Chu. Li Yuan was troubled by this. Before the troops had set out he said to Xin Wu: "With Qin's strength and the force of two arms, you face east and attack Chu. As your servant sees it, Chu will not wait to be attacked: it will cede land and bring gifts and hurry west, Qin and Chu will become the closest of allies, and Qin's blow will then fall back upon Liang. The General will surely be driven out of Liang, and I fear put to death by Qin. Has the General not seen the case of Jing Ji? On Qin's behalf he held Zhao and attacked Yan, taking two Fortresses. Yan sent Cai Niao, who with a tally made his way out through the ramparts, passed secretly through Zhao into Qin and offered the ten Fortresses of Hejian as a fief to the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Wenxin. Marquis Wenxin did not dare accept, saying: 'I have no merit.' The next day Cai Niao came to see him wearing a long sword, raised its point and showed it to Marquis Wenxin, saying: 'You say "I have no merit". If you have no merit, why not untie your seal and hang it on Meng Ao or Wang 〓? The King of Qin holds you worthy, and so has set you above those two. Now Yan offers land; this is not Qin's land. If you do not accept it, you are disloyal.' Marquis Wenxin respectfully agreed. He spoke of it to the King of Qin, and the King of Qin ordered him to accept. Qin became Yan's closest ally, and Qin's blow then turned back upon Zhao. Qin raised a great army, faced east and bore down on Zhao, declaring that Yan was not to be attacked. With Qin's strength and Yan's anger, the cutting of Zhao was bound to go deep. Zhao could not bear it; it drove out Jing Ji, and he was put to death by Qin. Now, if your servant may privately plan for the General: better to hold back a little and not send out the troops. So long as Qin has not had its way with Chu, it must value Liang; so long as Liang has not had its way with Chu, it must value Qin — thus the General is valued on both sides. No man under Heaven escapes death; he who lasts long lives long. I wish the General to consider it. While Liang's troops have not set out, Chu, seeing that Liang has not sent out its troops, will be slow to hurry to Qin. The King of Qin, angered at Chu's slowness, will resent it deeply; and so the General is valued still more." Liang's troops did indeed set out only after six months. Lord Huai of Wey adopted the policy of the Horizontal Alliance and turned against Wei. Analysis: this entry derives from Han Feizi, "The Five Vermin": Thus Zhou left Qin for the Vertical Alliance, and within a year was taken; Wey left Wei for the Horizontal, and within half a year perished. So Zhou was destroyed by the Vertical, and Wey perished by the Horizontal. Had Zhou and Wey put off their schemes of Vertical and Horizontal and tightened their governance within their borders, made their laws and prohibitions clear, made their rewards and punishments certain, used the strength of their land to the full to multiply their stores, and brought their people to die for them so as to make their Fortress defences firm, then all under Heaven would have gained little by taking their land and suffered much by attacking their state; no state of ten thousand chariots would have dared wear itself out beneath their firm Fortresses and let a strong enemy cut it down in its weakness. This is the art of certainly not perishing. To abandon the art of certainly not perishing and take the road of certain destruction is the fault of those who govern a state. When wisdom is baffled within and government disordered without, perishing cannot be averted.
passages.no: In the appended chapter the characters in parentheses are the editors' readings of the manuscript graphs before them (粱 read 梁, 侍 read 待, and so on); the translation follows the readings. 割挚马免: no published reading of the phrase was found; 挚 is taken as 贽, "gifts", and the rendering is approximate. 股符〓去壁: 〓 marks a graph illegible in the manuscript. The Wikisource transcription of the text reads 股符胠壁, 胠 "to break open" and 壁 "rampart"; 股 is unexplained, and the rendering is tentative. 王〓: the graph after 王 is illegible in the manuscript. 赍赵 (齎趙 in the transcription): 齎 is probably a loan for 挤, "to press"; the reading is not settled. 文信侯: Lü Buwei, under the title the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu gives him. Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year, with his analyses (辨析) and the texts he adduces: chapter 25 of the Zhanguo Zonghengjia Shu and a passage of the Han Feizi.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）二 韩桓惠王派军收复汝南，夺秦相范雎封地。 辨析：吴良寶：戰國晚期韓國疆域變遷新考 https://history.sohu.com/a/668355186_121124388 《韓非子·定法》云：“應侯攻韓，八年，成其汝南之封”。據《范睢列傳》“秦封范睢以應”，時在秦昭王四十一年（前266年）。《戰國策·秦策三》“應侯失韓之汝南”章“秦昭王謂應侯曰：‘君亡汝南國，其憂乎？’”，諸家多定策文年代在公元前257年信陵君破秦於邯鄲之時。這説明桓惠王十六年時韓國重新奪回了今河南魯山縣東的應地。上引“二十三年襄城令矛”、“六年襄城令戈”等器表明韓國一直佔據今襄城、魯山縣一帶，而《秦始皇本紀》“韓南陽假守騰”的記載，是韓國設置南陽郡（騰暫時代理郡守一職）的最直接證據。 魏安僖王派军进占秦国陶地，又吞并卫国。 《韩非子·五蠹》:“卫离魏为衡，半岁而亡。 《吕氏春秋·审应览》:“当此时也，两周全，其北存，魏举陶削卫，地方六百。 卫怀君入魏觐见，被魏安僖王囚杀。 無骨注:魏国后来又在濮阳扶植卫元君(魏王之婿)与普通封君无异，卫国实已灭亡。 辨析：《史記·衛世家》載懷君三十一年朝魏，又《史記·六國年表（公元對照）》載衛懷君元年為公元前282年，衛懷君三十一年應為公元前252年，同年，魏立衛元君，改元，故衛懷君三十一年為衛元君元年。 赵孝成王大约在这一时期令李牧居代、雁门，防备匈奴。 辨析：時間與本年表觀點不同。 楚国春申君黄歇北伐，灭鲁。 辨析：與《史記·六國年表（公元對照）》不同。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II King Huanhui of Han sent troops to recover Runan, seizing the fief of the Chancellor of Qin, Fan Ju. Analysis: Wu Liangbao, "A new study of the changes in Han's territory in the late Warring States", history.sohu.com/a/668355186_121124388. The Han Feizi, "Fixing the Laws", says: "Marquis Ying attacked Han, and in eight years completed his fief of Runan." According to the Biography of Fan Ju, "Qin enfeoffed Fan Ju with Ying", in the forty-first year of King Zhao of Qin (266 BC). The chapter "Marquis Ying loses Han's Runan" in the Zhanguoce, Strategies of Qin III — "King Zhao of Qin said to Marquis Ying: 'You have lost your state of Runan; does it grieve you?'" — is dated by most scholars to 257 BC, when Lord Xinling defeated Qin at Handan. This shows that in the sixteenth year of Huanhui Han had retaken the territory of Ying, east of modern Lushan County, Henan. The vessels cited above, the "spear of the Sheriff of Xiangcheng, twenty-third year" and the "dagger-axe of the Sheriff of Xiangcheng, sixth year", show that Han held the area of modern Xiangcheng and Lushan Counties throughout, and the record in the Basic Annals of the First Emperor of Qin of "Teng, Acting Magistrate of Han's Nanyang" is the most direct evidence that Han established a Nanyang Commandery (Teng temporarily filling the post of Magistrate of the Commandery). King Anxi of Wei sent troops to occupy Qin's territory of Tao, and annexed Wey. Han Feizi, "The Five Vermin": "Wey left Wei for the Horizontal, and within half a year perished. Lüshi Chunqiu, "Shenying lan": "At this time the two Zhou were intact and its north survived; Wei took Tao and pared Wey, and its land was six hundred li square. Lord Huai of Wey went to Wei for an audience, and was imprisoned and killed by King Anxi of Wei. Ivar's note: Wei later set up Lord Yuan of Wey (the King of Wei's son-in-law) at Puyang, no different from an ordinary enfeoffed lord; Wey had in fact already perished. Analysis: the Hereditary House of Wey in the Shiji records that Lord Huai went to court in Wei in his thirty-first year, and the Shiji Table of the Six States (with Western dates) gives Lord Huai of Wey's first year as 282 BC, so his thirty-first year should be 252 BC; in that year Wei set up Lord Yuan of Wey, who began a new count of years, so that the thirty-first year of Lord Huai of Wey is the first year of Lord Yuan of Wey. King Xiaocheng of Zhao at about this time ordered Li Mu to station himself at Dai and Yanmen as a guard against the Xiongnu. Analysis: the date differs from the view taken in this chronology. Chu's Lord Chunshen, Huang Xie, campaigned north and extinguished Lu. Analysis: differs from the Shiji Table of the Six States (with Western dates).
passages.no: 257 BC. 其北存: rendered literally; the referent of 其 is unclear. Ivar the Boneless' commentary, continued: Han's recovery of Runan, Wei's seizure of Tao and Wey, Li Mu's northern command and Chunshen's conquest of Lu, each with its analysis.

passages.title: Other ancient works (histories)
passages.zh: 其他古籍（史類） 《陕西长安神禾原战国秦陵园大墓发掘简报》：【摘 要】2004～2008年发掘的神禾原战国秦陵大墓,为"亚"字形墓,位于陵园中心位置。大墓虽遭严重的盗扰、焚烧,仍出土精美器物数百件。根据大墓形制、随葬器物及其刻铭,并结合文献资料,推定墓主为战国晚期秦国夏太后。该墓的发掘为战国秦汉时期有关帝王陵墓形制、构筑、制度和文化等诸多方面研究提供了丰富的实物资料。 大墓从葬坑K8出土的马具上刻有纪年文字“五十九年”[4]，该纪年只有东周末代天子周赧王使用过，时为秦昭襄王五十一年（公元前256年）。这意味着神禾原大墓营建时代上限不早于周赧王五十九年，即不早于公元前256年。 战国晚期处于秦都咸阳附近杜县（今长安区沈家桥至杜城村一带）东南的“亚”字形大墓，应是秦国高等级的贵族墓葬。这一时期去世的秦王、后、太子类高等级贵族，葬地多在咸阳或芷阳陵区[6]。而葬地与杜有关的秦的高等级贵族，只有战国晚期的秦始皇的祖母—夏太后[7]。 夏太后是秦孝文王的如夫人，称夏姬，为庄襄王母亲，秦始皇的祖母。庄襄王元年（公元前249年）被尊为夏太后[8]。“始皇七年，庄襄王母夏太后薨。孝文王后曰华阳太后，与孝文王会葬寿陵。夏太后子庄襄王葬芷阳，故夏太后独别葬杜东。”
passages.en: Other ancient works (histories) Preliminary report on the excavation of the great tomb of the Warring States Qin mausoleum precinct at Shenheyuan, Chang'an, Shaanxi: [Abstract] The great tomb of the Warring States Qin mausoleum at Shenheyuan, excavated in 2004–2008, is a tomb of 亚-shaped plan, situated at the centre of the mausoleum precinct. Although the tomb suffered severe looting and burning, several hundred fine objects were still recovered. On the basis of the tomb's form, the grave goods and their inscriptions, together with the written sources, the occupant is inferred to be Queen Dowager Xia of Qin, of the late Warring States period. The excavation of this tomb provides abundant material evidence for the study of many aspects of the form, construction, institutions and culture of royal mausolea in the Warring States, Qin and Han periods. Horse trappings from the tomb's accompanying pit K8 bear the inscribed date "fifty-ninth year" [4]. This year-count was used only by King Nan of Zhou, the last Son of Heaven of Eastern Zhou, and corresponds to the fifty-first year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin (256 BC). This means that the earliest possible date for the construction of the Shenheyuan great tomb is the fifty-ninth year of King Nan of Zhou, that is, no earlier than 256 BC. A 亚-shaped great tomb of the late Warring States south-east of Du County (the area from Shenjiaqiao to Duchengcun in modern Chang'an District), near the Qin capital Xianyang, must be the burial of a high-ranking Qin noble. The kings of Qin, Queens, Heirs Apparent and other high-ranking nobles who died in this period were mostly buried in the Xianyang or Zhiyang mausoleum areas [6]. The only high-ranking Qin noble whose burial place is connected with Du is Queen Dowager Xia of the late Warring States, the grandmother of the First Emperor of Qin [7]. Queen Dowager Xia was a secondary consort of King Xiaowen of Qin, styled Lady Xia 夏姬; she was the mother of King Zhuangxiang and the grandmother of the First Emperor of Qin. In the first year of King Zhuangxiang (249 BC) she was honoured as Queen Dowager Xia [8]. "In the seventh year of the First Emperor, Queen Dowager Xia, the mother of King Zhuangxiang, died. King Xiaowen's Queen, called Queen Dowager Huayang, was buried together with King Xiaowen at Shouling. Queen Dowager Xia's son King Zhuangxiang was buried at Zhiyang, and so Queen Dowager Xia was buried by herself, apart, east of Du."
passages.no: 亚字形: a tomb whose plan, with a ramp on each of the four sides, has the shape of the character 亚. The bracketed numbers are the report's own footnote references. The quotation is from the Basic Annals of the First Emperor of Qin. Other works: the preliminary report on the Shenheyuan tomb at Chang'an, whose dated inscription of the fifty-ninth year ties it to this year.

passages.title: Shiji, supplement: the Eight Treatises
passages.zh: 史記：補：八書 封禅书：其後百二十岁而秦灭周，周之九鼎入于秦。或曰宋太丘社亡，而鼎没于泗水彭城下。
passages.en: Shiji, supplement: the Eight Treatises Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices: One hundred and twenty years after this, Qin extinguished Zhou, and the Nine Tripods of Zhou passed into Qin. Some say that when the altar of the soil at Taiqiu in Song was lost, the tripods sank in Si River below Pengcheng.
passages.no: The chapter is excerpted: "this" is the event of the Treatise's preceding sentence. The Eight Treatises: the sentence of the Treatise on the Feng and Shan Sacrifices on the passing of the Nine Tripods to Qin.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：五十一年，攻陽城。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: In the fifty-first year, attacked Yangcheng.
passages.no: 葉書: the year-by-year record on the bamboo slips of Shuihudi tomb 11, Yunmeng, Hubei, which notes Qin's campaigns beside the events of the tomb occupant's family. It was published in 1978 under the editors' title 编年记; the Collected Qin Slips gives it the title written on the slips themselves, 葉書. The fifty-first year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 256 BC. The subject, Qin, is not expressed; the Basic Annals of Qin record the taking of Yangcheng under the same year. The entry for 256 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips, which counts the year as the fifty-first of King Zhaoxiang of Qin.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：五十二年，周民东亡，其器九鼎入秦。周初亡。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the fifty-second year, the people of Zhou fled east, and their vessels, the Nine Tripods, passed into Qin. Zhou now first perished.
passages.no: The fifty-second year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 255 BC. The Basic Annals of Zhou place the flight of the people of Zhou and the taking of the Nine Tripods under the preceding year, the fifty-ninth of King Nan. 周初亡: the Western Zhou domain was extinguished; the Eastern Zhou domain remained. The Basic Annals for 255 BC: the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the fifty-second year of King Zhaoxiang, which records the end of Zhou a year later than the Basic Annals of Zhou.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 秦：取西周。王稽棄市。 楚：取魯，魯君封於莒。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Qin: Took Western Zhou. Wang Ji was executed in the marketplace. Chu: Took Lu; the Lord of Lu was enfeoffed at Ju.
passages.no: 魯君: Duke Qing of Lu, whom the Table calls the Lord of Lu. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entries for Qin and Chu.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 燕召公世家：三年卒，子今王喜立。 赵世家：十一年，城元氏，县上原。武阳君郑安平死，收其地。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of the Duke of Shao of Yan: In the third year he died, and his son, the present king, Xi, was set up. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the eleventh year, made Yuanshi a Fortress and Shangyuan a County. Lord Wuyang, Zheng Anping, died, and his lands were taken back.
passages.no: The third year of King Xiao of Yan, 255 BC; the king is the unexpressed subject. 今王: so the text, from the standpoint of the record the Shiji draws on. The eleventh year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 255 BC. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the house of Yan, on the death of King Xiao, and the house of Zhao.

passages.title: Shiji IV: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（四：列传） 春申君列传：春申君者，楚人也，名歇，姓黄氏。游学博闻，事楚顷襄王。顷襄王以歇为辩，使於秦。秦昭王使白起攻韩、魏，败之於华阳，禽魏将芒卯，韩、魏服而事秦。秦昭王方令白起与韩、魏共伐楚，未行，而楚使黄歇適至於秦，闻秦之计。当是之时，秦已前使白起攻楚，取巫、黔中之郡，拔鄢郢，东至竟陵，楚顷襄王东徙治於陈县。黄歇见楚怀王之为秦所诱而入朝，遂见欺，留死於秦。顷襄王，其子也，秦轻之，恐壹举兵而灭楚。歇乃上书说秦昭王曰： 天下莫彊於秦、楚。今闻大王欲伐楚，此犹两虎相与斗。两虎相与斗而驽犬受其弊，不如善楚。臣请言其说：臣闻物至则反，冬夏是也；致至则危，累釭是也。今大国之地，遍天下有其二垂，此从生民已来，万乘之地未尝有也。先帝文王、庄王之身，三世不妄接地於齐，以绝从亲之要。今王使盛桥守事於韩，盛桥以其地入秦，是王不用甲，不信威，而得百里之地。王可谓能矣。王又举甲而攻魏，杜大梁之门，举河内，拔燕、酸枣、虚、桃，入邢，魏之兵云翔而不敢捄。王之功亦多矣。王休甲息众，二年而後复之；又并蒲、衍、首、垣，以临仁、平丘，黄、济阳婴城而魏氏服；王又割濮〔磿〕之北，注齐秦之要，绝楚赵之脊，天下五合六聚而不敢救。王之威亦单矣。 王若能持功守威，绌攻取之心而肥仁义之地，使无後患，三王不足四，五伯不足六也。王若负人徒之众，仗兵革之彊，乘毁魏之威，而欲以力臣天下之主，臣恐其有後患也。诗曰“靡不有初，鲜克有终”。易曰“狐涉水，濡其尾”。此言始之易，终之难也。何以知其然也？昔智氏见伐赵之利而不知榆次之祸，吴见伐齐之便而不知干隧之败。此二国者，非无大功也，没利於前而易患於後也。吴之信越也，从而伐齐，既胜齐人於艾陵，还为越王禽三渚之浦。智氏之信韩、魏也，从而伐赵，攻晋阳城，胜有日矣，韩、魏叛之，杀智伯瑶於凿台之下。今王妒楚之不毁也，而忘毁楚之彊韩、魏也，臣为王虑而不取也。 诗曰“大武远宅而不涉”。从此观之，楚国，援也；邻国，敌也。诗云“趯趯〔毚〕免，还犬获之。他人有心，余忖度之”。今王中道而信韩、魏之善王也，此正吴之信越也。臣闻之，敌不可假，时不可失。臣恐韩、魏卑辞除患而实欲欺大国也。何则？王无重世之德於韩、魏，而有累世之怨焉。夫韩、魏父子兄弟接踵而死於秦者将十世矣。本国残，社稷坏，宗庙毁。刳腹绝肠，折颈摺颐，首身分离，暴骸骨於草泽，头颅僵仆，相望於境，父子老弱系脰束手为群虏者相及於路。鬼神孤伤，无所血食。人民不聊生，族类离散，流亡为仆妾者，盈满海内矣。故韩、魏之不亡，秦社稷之忧也，今王资之与攻楚，不亦过乎！ 且王攻楚将恶出兵？王将借路於仇雠之韩、魏乎？兵出之日而王忧其不返也，是王以兵资於仇雠之韩、魏也。王若不借路於仇雠之韩、魏，必攻随水右壤。随水右壤，此皆广川大水，山林谿谷，不食之地也，王虽有之，不为得地。是王有毁楚之名而无得地之实也。 且王攻楚之日，四国必悉起兵以应王。秦、楚之兵构而不离，魏氏将出而攻留、方与、铚、湖陵、砀、萧、相，故宋必尽。齐人南面攻楚，泗上必举。此皆平原四达，膏腴之地，而使独攻。王破楚以肥韩、魏於中国而劲齐。韩、魏之彊，足以校於秦。齐南以泗水为境，东负海，北倚河，而无後患，天下之国莫彊於齐、魏，齐、魏得地葆利而详事下吏，一年之後，为帝未能，其於禁王之为帝有馀矣。 夫以王壤土之博，人徒之众，兵革之彊，壹举事而树怨於楚，迟令韩、魏归帝重於齐，是王失计也。臣为王虑，莫若善楚。秦、楚合而为一以临韩，韩必敛手。王施以东山之险，带以曲河之利，韩必为关内之侯。若是而王以十万戍郑，梁氏寒心，许、鄢陵婴城，而上蔡、召陵不往来也，如此而魏亦关内侯矣。王壹善楚，而关内两万乘之主注地於齐，齐右壤可拱手而取也。王之地一经两海，要约天下，是燕、赵无齐、楚，齐、楚无燕、赵也。然後危动燕、赵，直摇齐、楚，此四国者不待痛而服矣。 昭王曰：“善。”於是乃止白起而谢韩、魏。发使赂楚，约为与国。 黄歇受约归楚，楚使歇与太子完入质於秦，秦留之数年。楚顷襄王病，太子不得归。而楚太子与秦相应侯善，於是黄歇乃说应侯曰：“相国诚善楚太子乎？”应侯曰：“然。”歇曰：“今楚王恐不起疾，秦不如归其太子。太子得立，其事秦必重而德相国无穷，是亲与国而得储万乘也。若不归，则咸阳一布衣耳；楚更立太子，必不事秦。夫失与国而绝万乘之和，非计也。原相国孰虑之。”应侯以闻秦王。秦王曰：“令楚太子之傅先往问楚王之疾，返而後图之。”黄歇为楚太子计曰：“秦之留太子也，欲以求利也。今太子力未能有以利秦也，歇忧之甚。而阳文君子二人在中，王若卒大命，太子不在，阳文君子必立为後，太子不得奉宗庙矣。不如亡秦，与使者俱出；臣请止，以死当之。”楚太子因变衣服为楚使者御以出关，而黄歇守舍，常为谢病。度太子已远，秦不能追，歇乃自言秦昭王曰：“楚太子已归，出远矣。歇当死，原赐死。”昭王大怒，欲听其自杀也。应侯曰：“歇为人臣，出身以徇其主，太子立，必用歇，故不如无罪而归之，以亲楚。”秦因遣黄歇。 歇至楚三月，楚顷襄王卒，太子完立，是为考烈王。考烈王元年，以黄歇为相，封为春申君，赐淮北地十二县。後十五岁，黄歇言之楚王曰：“淮北地边齐，其事急，请以为郡便。”因并献淮北十二县。请封於江东。考烈王许之。春申君因城故吴墟，以自为都邑。 春申君既相楚，是时齐有孟尝君，赵有平原君，魏有信陵君，方争下士，招致宾客，以相倾夺，辅国持权。 春申君为楚相四年，秦破赵之长平军四十馀万。五年，围邯郸。邯郸告急於楚，楚使春申君将兵往救之，秦兵亦去，春申君归。春申君相楚八年，为楚北伐灭鲁，以荀卿为兰陵令。当是时，楚复彊。 赵平原君使人於春申君，春申君舍之於上舍。赵使欲夸楚，为玳瑁簪，刀剑室以珠玉饰之，请命春申君客。春申君客三千馀人，其上客皆蹑珠履以见赵使，赵使大惭。
passages.en: Shiji IV: Biographies Biography of Lord Chunshen: Lord Chunshen was a man of Chu, named Xie, of the clan Huang. He travelled to study and was widely learned, and served King Qingxiang of Chu. King Qingxiang, holding Xie to be eloquent, sent him as envoy to Qin. King Zhao of Qin had sent Bai Qi to attack Han and Wei; he defeated them at Huayang and captured the Wei general Mang Mao, and Han and Wei submitted and served Qin. King Zhao of Qin was just then ordering Bai Qi to join Han and Wei in an attack on Chu, and before he had set out the Chu envoy Huang Xie happened to arrive in Qin and learned of Qin's plan. At that time Qin had already, earlier, sent Bai Qi to attack Chu; he had taken the Commanderies of Wu and Qianzhong, taken Yan and Ying, and reached Jingling in the east, and King Qingxiang of Chu had moved his seat east to Chen County. Huang Xie had seen how King Huai of Chu, lured by Qin into coming to court, had been deceived and kept in Qin until he died. King Qingxiang was his son; Qin thought little of him, and Xie feared that it would raise its troops in a single stroke and extinguish Chu. Xie therefore sent up a letter to persuade King Zhao of Qin: "Under Heaven none is stronger than Qin and Chu. Now I hear that the great King wishes to attack Chu. This is like two tigers fighting each other: when two tigers fight, the worthless dog profits from their exhaustion. Better to be on good terms with Chu. Let your servant set out his argument. Your servant has heard that when a thing reaches its limit it turns back, as winter and summer do; and that what is heaped to the limit is in danger, as stacked pieces are. Now the great state's territory reaches both ends of all under Heaven; since there have been people, no land of ten thousand chariots has ever been so. In the persons of the former kings, King Wen and King Zhuang, for three generations you never rashly extended your lands to touch Qi, so as to cut the waist of the Vertical league. Now the King has Sheng Qiao hold office in Han, and Sheng Qiao brings its land into Qin: thus without using armour or displaying might the King has gained a hundred li of land. The King may be called able. The King also raised armour and attacked Wei, shut the gates of Daliang, took Henei, took Yan, Suanzao, Xu and Tao, and entered Xing, and Wei's troops hovered like clouds and dared not come to the rescue. The King's achievements are many indeed. The King rested his armour and gave his people respite, and after two years took it up again; he also annexed Pu, Yan, Shou and Yuan, and bore down on Ren and Pingqiu; Huang and Jiyang shut their Fortresses, and the house of Wei submitted. The King also cut off the land north of Puli, pinned the waist between Qi and Qin, and severed the spine between Chu and Zhao; all under Heaven joined five times and gathered six, and dared not come to the rescue. The King's might has been exerted to the full. "If the King can hold on to his achievements and keep his majesty, curb the urge to attack and seize and fatten the ground of humanity and right, so that there is no trouble to come, then the Three Kings will no longer lack a fourth, nor the Five Hegemons a sixth. If instead the King relies on the multitude of his people and the strength of his arms, and rides the prestige of having broken Wei, to subject the rulers of all under Heaven by force, your servant fears there will be trouble to come. The Odes say: 'None but has a beginning; few can have an end.' The Changes say: 'The fox crosses the water and wets its tail.' This says that beginnings are easy and endings hard. How do we know it is so? Of old the Zhi saw the profit of attacking Zhao and did not foresee the calamity of Yuci; Wu saw the convenience of attacking Qi and did not foresee the defeat at Gansui. These two states did not lack great achievements; they sank into the profit before them and made light of the trouble behind. Wu, trusting Yue, went on to attack Qi, and having beaten the men of Qi at Ailing, on its return was captured by the King of Yue at the shore of Sanzhu. The Zhi, trusting Han and Wei, went on to attack Zhao and assaulted the Fortress of Jinyang; victory was only days away when Han and Wei turned on them and killed Zhi Bo Yao beneath the Zao Terrace. Now the King begrudges that Chu is not destroyed, and forgets that destroying Chu would strengthen Han and Wei. Your servant, planning for the King, would not have it. "The Odes say: 'Great arms do not go far afield to trespass.' Seen in this light, the state of Chu is a support, and the neighbouring states are enemies. The Odes say: 'Hopping, hopping the wily hare; it meets a dog and is caught. What is in another's mind, I can fathom.' Now the King midway trusts that Han and Wei mean him well; this is exactly Wu's trusting of Yue. Your servant has heard that an enemy must not be indulged, and a moment must not be lost. Your servant fears that Han and Wei speak humbly to be rid of their peril but in truth mean to deceive the great state. Why? The King has no kindness of generations' standing toward Han and Wei, but a grudge heaped up over generations. Fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers of Han and Wei have died at Qin's hands heel upon heel for nearly ten generations. Their homelands are ravaged, their altars of soil and grain overthrown, their ancestral temples destroyed. Bellies ripped open and bowels cut out, necks broken and jaws wrenched, heads parted from bodies, bones exposed in the marshes, skulls lying stiff within sight of one another across the borders; fathers and sons, old and young, roped by the neck and bound at the hands, driven in herds of captives, follow one another along the roads. Their ghosts and spirits are forlorn and wounded, with none to offer them blood sacrifice. The people cannot live, clans are scattered, and those who have fled to become servants and concubines fill all within the seas. So that Han and Wei have not perished is the worry of Qin's altars of soil and grain; and now the King would furnish them with means and attack Chu with them — is that not a mistake! "Moreover, when the King attacks Chu, by what road will he send out his troops? Will the King borrow a road through Han and Wei, his sworn enemies? From the day the troops set out the King will worry that they will not return; that is the King lending his troops to his enemies Han and Wei. If the King does not borrow a road through his enemies Han and Wei, he must attack the lands on the right bank of Sui River. The right bank of Sui River is all broad rivers and great waters, mountain forests and ravines, land that yields no food; though the King should hold it, it would not count as gaining land. Thus the King would have the name of destroying Chu without the substance of gaining land. "Moreover, on the day the King attacks Chu, the four states will surely raise all their troops to answer the King. While the troops of Qin and Chu are locked together and cannot disengage, the house of Wei will march out and attack Liu, Fangyu, Zhi, Huling, Dang, Xiao and Xiang, and the old land of Song will be theirs entirely. The men of Qi, facing south, will attack Chu, and the Si country will surely be taken. These are all open plains with roads on four sides, rich and fertile land, and they would be left to attack it unopposed. The King would break Chu only to fatten Han and Wei in the central states and to strengthen Qi. The strength of Han and Wei would then suffice to contend with Qin. Qi, with Si River for its border on the south, the sea at its back on the east and the River to lean on in the north, would have nothing to fear behind it; of the states under Heaven none would be stronger than Qi and Wei. Qi and Wei, having gained land and secured its profit, and attending carefully to their lesser officers, in a year's time might not yet be able to become Emperor, but would be more than able to prevent the King from becoming Emperor. "With the breadth of the King's territory, the multitude of his people and the strength of his arms, to raise one campaign and plant a grudge in Chu, and so drive Han and Wei to carry the weight of the imperial title over to Qi — that is the King miscalculating. If your servant plans for the King, nothing is better than to be on good terms with Chu. If Qin and Chu unite as one and bear down on Han, Han must fold its hands. If the King spreads out the defences of the eastern mountains and girds himself with the advantage of the bend of the River, Han must become a Marquis within the Passes. If then the King garrisons Zheng with a hundred thousand, the house of Liang will turn cold at heart; Xu and Yanling will shut their Fortresses, and Shangcai and Shaoling will no longer come and go; and so Wei too will be a Marquis within the Passes. Once the King is on good terms with Chu, two lords of ten thousand chariots within the Passes will turn their arms upon Qi, and Qi's western lands may be taken with folded hands. The King's land would run in one stretch from sea to sea, binding all under Heaven: then Yan and Zhao would be without Qi and Chu, and Qi and Chu without Yan and Zhao. After that, threaten and shake Yan and Zhao, and rock Qi and Chu outright, and these four states will submit without waiting to be hurt." King Zhao said: "Good." Thereupon he halted Bai Qi and sent his excuses to Han and Wei. He sent envoys with gifts to Chu and bound it as an allied state. Huang Xie received the covenant and returned to Chu, and Chu sent Xie with the Heir Apparent, Wan, as hostages to Qin; Qin kept them for several years. King Qingxiang of Chu fell ill, and the Heir Apparent could not return. Now the Heir Apparent of Chu was on good terms with the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Ying, and so Huang Xie spoke to Marquis Ying: "Is the Chancellor of State truly a friend to the Heir Apparent of Chu?" Marquis Ying said: "I am." Xie said: "Now the King of Chu is unlikely to rise from his sickness, and Qin would do best to send his Heir Apparent home. If the Heir Apparent is set on the throne, his service to Qin will surely be weighty and his gratitude to the Chancellor of State without end; that is to befriend an allied state and lay up a ruler of ten thousand chariots. If he is not sent home, he is merely a commoner of Xianyang; Chu will set up another Heir Apparent, who will surely not serve Qin. To lose an allied state and break off the friendship of a ruler of ten thousand chariots is no plan. I wish the Chancellor of State to consider it carefully." Marquis Ying reported it to the King of Qin. The King of Qin said: "Let the Heir Apparent of Chu's Tutor go first to inquire after the King of Chu's illness; when he returns we shall plan it." Huang Xie planned for the Heir Apparent of Chu: "Qin keeps the Heir Apparent because it wants to gain some advantage by it. Now the Heir Apparent has no means yet to benefit Qin, and Xie is deeply anxious about it. And Lord Yangwen's two sons are at court; if the King should die and the Heir Apparent is not there, Lord Yangwen's son will surely be set up as successor, and the Heir Apparent will never serve the ancestral temple. Better to flee Qin and go out with the envoy; your servant begs to stay behind and answer for it with his life." The Heir Apparent of Chu accordingly changed his clothes and, as the Chu envoy's driver, went out through the Pass, while Huang Xie kept the lodging and constantly made excuses of illness. Judging that the Heir Apparent was already far away and Qin could not overtake him, Xie then spoke for himself to King Zhao of Qin: "The Heir Apparent of Chu has gone home; he is already far away. Xie deserves death; I beg to be granted death." King Zhao was greatly angered and was ready to let him kill himself. Marquis Ying said: "Xie, as a subject, gave his own life for his master's sake; when the Heir Apparent is set up he will surely employ Xie. So it is better to send him home without blame, to befriend Chu." Qin accordingly sent Huang Xie back. Xie had been in Chu three months when King Qingxiang of Chu died and the Heir Apparent, Wan, was set up: this was King Kaolie. In the first year of King Kaolie he made Huang Xie Chancellor, enfeoffed him as Lord Chunshen, and granted him twelve Counties of the land north of the Huai. Fifteen years later Huang Xie said to the King of Chu: "The land north of the Huai borders Qi, and its affairs are pressing; it would be better made a Commandery." And he gave back the twelve Counties north of the Huai, asking to be enfeoffed in Jiangdong. King Kaolie consented. Lord Chunshen accordingly fortified the old ruins of Wu and made them his seat. When Lord Chunshen had become Chancellor of Chu, at that time Qi had Lord Mengchang, Zhao had Lord Pingyuan and Wei had Lord Xinling, all vying to humble themselves before gentlemen and to attract retainers, so as to outdo one another, support their states and hold power. In the fourth year of Lord Chunshen's chancellorship of Chu, Qin destroyed Zhao's army of more than four hundred thousand at Changping. In the fifth year it besieged Handan. Handan sent word of its peril to Chu; Chu sent Lord Chunshen with troops to relieve it, the Qin troops also withdrew, and Lord Chunshen returned. In the eighth year of his chancellorship Lord Chunshen campaigned north for Chu and extinguished Lu, and made Xun Qing Sheriff of Lanling. At this time Chu was strong again. Lord Pingyuan of Zhao sent a man to Lord Chunshen, and Lord Chunshen lodged him in the best quarters. The Zhao envoy wished to show off before Chu: he had tortoiseshell hairpins made and sword scabbards adorned with pearls and jade, and asked to meet Lord Chunshen's retainers. Lord Chunshen's retainers numbered more than three thousand, and his chief guests all came to see the Zhao envoy shod in pearl-studded slippers; the Zhao envoy was greatly ashamed.
passages.no: 累釭: so the text; the three-commentary edition reads 累棊, "stacked gaming-pieces", which is translated. 濮磿: 磿 is supplied from the three-commentary edition. Xu Guang: the Pu flows north into the Ji at Juye; the Suoyin: a place-name, near the Pu. 单: read 殚 (Xu Guang); the Suoyin: "exhausted — the King's might has been fully exerted." 大武远宅而不涉: rendered with the Zhengyi, "a great army does not go far afield on campaign." 趯趯毚兔，还犬获之: 毚 is supplied from the three-commentary edition, which also reads 还; 免 is for 兔. 注地於齐: the Suoyin, "注 means to cut at it with troops." 右壤: the Zhengyi, "the lands north and south of Jizhou", that is, Qi's western border on the Ji. 262 BC. The eighth year of King Kaolie, 255 BC. The Suoyin: the Table has the taking of Lu and the enfeoffment of its lord at Ju in this year, and Lu's extinction in the fourteenth. 关: the Hangu Pass, Qin's eastern gate. The Biographies: the biography of Lord Chunshen of Chu, from his origins and his letter to King Zhao of Qin to his eighth year as Chancellor, the year of the conquest of Lu, and the visit of the Zhao envoy.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 秦相蔡泽受诽谤，遂称病免相，秦昭襄王任命杜仓为相。 辨析： 《史記》范雎蔡泽列传：後数日，入朝，言於秦昭王曰：“客新有从山东来者曰蔡泽，其人辩士，明於三王之事，五伯之业，世俗之变，足以寄秦国之政。臣之见人甚众，莫及，臣不如也。臣敢以闻。”秦昭王召见，与语，大说之，拜为客卿。应侯因谢病请归相印。昭王彊起应侯，应侯遂称病笃。范雎免相，昭王新说蔡泽计画，遂拜为秦相，东收周室。 蔡泽相秦数月，人或恶之，惧诛，乃谢病归相印，号为纲成君。居秦十馀年，事昭王、孝文王、庄襄王。卒事始皇帝，为秦使於燕，三年而燕使太子丹入质於秦。 觀點不同在於從“東收周室”之前到“數月”“歸相印”之後的時間點，有沒有到秦昭王五十二年？
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I The Chancellor of Qin, Cai Ze, was slandered, and so pleaded illness and was relieved of the chancellorship; King Zhaoxiang of Qin appointed Du Cang Chancellor. Analysis: Shiji, Biography of Fan Ju and Cai Ze: Some days later he went in to court and said to King Zhao of Qin: "Among the visitors there is one newly come from east of the mountains called Cai Ze, a man of eloquence, clear on the affairs of the Three Kings, the achievements of the Five Hegemons and the changes of the age — well able to be entrusted with the government of the state of Qin. Your servant has seen a great many men, and none comes up to him; your servant is not his equal. Your servant ventures to report it." King Zhao of Qin summoned him and spoke with him, was greatly pleased, and appointed him Guest Minister. Marquis Ying thereupon pleaded illness and asked to return the seal of Chancellor. King Zhao pressed Marquis Ying to rise, but Marquis Ying then declared himself gravely ill. Fan Ju was dismissed as Chancellor; King Zhao, newly pleased with Cai Ze's plans, then appointed him Chancellor of Qin, and eastward took in the house of Zhou. Cai Ze had been Chancellor of Qin for some months when someone spoke ill of him; fearing execution, he pleaded illness and returned the seal of Chancellor, and was styled Lord Gangcheng. He lived in Qin more than ten years, serving King Zhao, King Xiaowen and King Zhuangxiang. Last he served the First Emperor, and went as Qin's envoy to Yan; after three years Yan sent Heir Apparent Dan as a hostage to Qin. The difference of view lies in the point in time, from before "eastward took in the house of Zhou" to after the "some months" and the returning of the seal of Chancellor: does it reach the fifty-second year of King Zhao of Qin?
passages.no: Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: Cai Ze's fall and Du Cang's appointment as Chancellor of Qin, with the passage of the Shiji on which the dating turns.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）二 秦相杜仓攻楚，楚国令尹春申君策动“天下共割韩上地十城以谢秦”，秦国于是罢兵。 辨析：詳情見左側春申君列傳。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II The Chancellor of Qin, Du Cang, attacked Chu; the Chief Minister of Chu, Lord Chunshen, contrived that "all under Heaven together cede ten Fortresses of Han's upper lands to make amends to Qin", and Qin thereupon called off its troops. Analysis: for the details see the Biography of Lord Chunshen to the left.
passages.no: That is, §4 of this year, the preceding column of the chronology. Ivar the Boneless' commentary, continued: Du Cang's attack on Chu and the cession of ten Fortresses of Han's upper lands that ended it.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：[五十二]年，王稽、張禄死。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: In the [fifty-second] year, Wang Ji and Zhang Lu died.
passages.no: The fifty-second year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 255 BC. The square brackets are the editors': the graphs are damaged on the slip and restored. 张禄: the name Fan Ju went by in Qin. The Chronicle gives his death in the same year as Wang Ji's execution, which the Table records. The entry for 255 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the deaths of Wang Ji and Zhang Lu, that is, Fan Ju.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：五十三年，天下来宾。魏后，秦使摎伐魏，取吴城。韩王入朝，魏委国听令。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the fifty-third year, all under Heaven came to pay homage. Wei was late; Qin sent Jiu to attack Wei and took Wucheng. The King of Han came to court, and Wei entrusted its state to Qin and took its orders.
passages.no: The fifty-third year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 254 BC. 来宾: came as guests, that is, in submission. The Basic Annals for 254 BC: the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the fifty-third year of King Zhaoxiang.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 鲁周公世家：十九年，楚伐我，取徐州。 赵世家：十二年，邯郸〔廥〕烧。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of the Duke of Zhou of Lu: In the nineteenth year, Chu attacked us and took Shuzhou. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the twelfth year, the fodder-store at Handan burned.
passages.no: The nineteenth year of Duke Qing of Lu, 254 BC. 徐州: the Suoyin, citing the Shuowen's 䣄, "a lower town of Zhu, east of Lu", gives the pronunciation of the character as that of 舒, shu; hence Shuzhou. The twelfth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 254 BC. 廥 is supplied from the three-commentary edition, which reads 邯郸廥烧; Xu Guang: a stable; the Suoyin: a store of hay and straw, destroyed by fire. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the house of Lu, on the loss of Shuzhou to Chu, and the house of Zhao.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：[五十]三年，吏誰從軍。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: In the [fifty-]third year, the officer Shui went with the army.
passages.no: The fifty-third year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 254 BC; the bracketed graphs are the editors' restoration of damage on the slip. The entry for 254 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the first of its entries on the tomb occupant's own family.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：五十四年，王郊见上帝于雍。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the fifty-fourth year, the King performed the suburban sacrifice to the High God at Yong.
passages.no: The fifty-fourth year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 253 BC; the King is King Zhaoxiang. The Basic Annals for 253 BC: the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the fifty-fourth year of King Zhaoxiang.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 楚：徙於鉅陽。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Chu: Moved to Juyang.
passages.no: 徙: the removal of the court; Xu Guang on the Hereditary House of Chu cites the Table's entry as "in the tenth year moved to Juyang", the tenth year of King Kaolie being this year. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entry for Chu alone.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：五十四年。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: Fifty-fourth year.
passages.no: The fifty-fourth year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 253 BC; the Chronicle gives the year with no entry under it. The entry for 253 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the year alone, with nothing recorded under it.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 卫康叔世家：怀君三十一年，朝魏，魏囚杀怀君。魏更立嗣君弟，是为元君。元君为魏婿，故魏立之。 赵世家：十四年，平原君赵胜死。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Kang Shu of Wey: In the thirty-first year of Lord Huai, he went to court in Wei, and Wei imprisoned and killed Lord Huai. Wei instead set up the younger brother of Lord Si: this was Lord Yuan. Lord Yuan was a son-in-law of Wei, and so Wei set him up. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the fourteenth year, Lord Pingyuan, Zhao Sheng, died.
passages.no: 252 BC, by the Table's count from Lord Huai's first year, 282 BC. The fourteenth year of King Xiaocheng of Zhao, 252 BC. The Suoyin notes that the Table places the death in the fifteenth year. The entries of the Hereditary Houses for this year: the house of Wey, on the killing of Lord Huai and the setting up of Lord Yuan, and the house of Zhao, on the death of Lord Pingyuan.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：五十五年。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: Fifty-fifth year.
passages.no: The fifty-fifth year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 252 BC; the Chronicle gives the year with no entry under it. The entry for 252 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the year alone, with nothing recorded under it.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦本纪：五十六年秋，昭襄王卒，子孝文王立。尊唐八子为唐太后，而合其葬于先王。韩王衰绖入吊祠，诸侯皆使其将相来吊祠，视丧事。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of Qin: In the autumn of the fifty-sixth year, King Zhaoxiang died, and his son King Xiaowen was set up. He honoured the Bazi consort Tang as Queen Dowager Tang and buried her together with the late king. The King of Han, in hempen mourning dress, came in to condole and sacrifice, and the Lords all sent their generals and ministers to come and condole and sacrifice, and to attend to the funeral.
passages.no: The fifty-sixth and last year of King Zhaoxiang of Qin, 251 BC. The Basic Annals for 251 BC: the entry of the Basic Annals of Qin under the fifty-sixth year of King Zhaoxiang, the year of his death.

passages.title: Shiji II: Tables
passages.zh: 史记（二：表） 趙：平原君卒。 楚：柱國景伯死。 燕：伐趙，趙破我軍，殺栗腹。
passages.en: Shiji II: Tables Zhao: Lord Pingyuan died. Chu: The Pillar of the State Jing Bo died. Yan: Attacked Zhao; Zhao defeated our army and killed Li Fu.
passages.no: 我: the Table speaks from the standpoint of the state whose column it is, so "our army" is Yan's; the subject of 伐趙, "attacked Zhao", is likewise Yan. The row of the Table of the Six States for this year: the entries for Zhao, Chu and Yan.

passages.title: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses
passages.zh: 史记（三：世家） 燕召公世家：今王喜四年，秦昭王卒。燕王命相栗腹约欢赵，以五百金为赵王酒。还报燕王曰：“赵王壮者皆死长平，其孤未壮，可伐也。”王召昌国君乐闲问之。对曰：“赵四战之国，其民习兵，不可伐。”王曰：“吾以五而伐一。”对曰：“不可。”燕王怒，群臣皆以为可。卒起二军，车二千乘，栗腹将而攻鄗，卿秦攻代。唯独大夫将渠谓燕王曰：“与人通关约交，以五百金饮人之王，使者报而反攻之，不祥，兵无成功。”燕王不听，自将偏军随之。将渠引燕王绶止之曰：“王必无自往，往无成功。”王蹴之以足。将渠泣曰：“臣非以自为，为王也！”燕军至宋子，赵使廉颇将，击破栗腹于鄗。乐乘破卿秦于代。乐闲奔赵。廉颇逐之五百余里，围其国。燕人请和，赵人不许，必令将渠处和。燕相将渠以处和。赵听将渠，解燕围。 楚世家：十二年，秦昭王卒，楚王使春申君吊祠于秦。 赵世家：十五年，以尉文封相国廉颇为信平君。燕王令丞相栗腹约驩，以五百金为赵王酒，还归，报燕王曰：“赵氏壮者皆死长平，其孤未壮，可伐也。”王召昌国君乐闲而问之。对曰：“赵，四战之国也，其民习兵，伐之不可。”王曰：“吾以众伐寡，二而伐一，可乎？”对曰：“不可。”王曰：“吾即以五而伐一，可乎？”对曰：“不可。”燕王大怒。群臣皆以为可。燕卒起二军，车二千乘，栗腹将而攻鄗，卿秦将而攻代。廉颇为赵将，破杀栗腹，虏卿秦、乐闲。 魏世家：二十六年，秦昭王卒。 韩世家：二十二年，秦昭王卒。
passages.en: Shiji III: Hereditary Houses Hereditary House of Duke Shao of Yan: In the fourth year of the present king, Xi, King Zhao of Qin died. The King of Yan ordered the Chancellor Li Fu to conclude friendly relations with Zhao, and with five hundred jin of gold he feasted the King of Zhao. He returned and reported to the King of Yan: "Of the King of Zhao's men, those in their prime all died at Changping, and their orphans are not yet grown; he can be attacked." The king summoned Lord Changguo, Yue Jian, and asked him. He replied: "Zhao is a state at war on four sides; its people are practised in arms. It cannot be attacked." The king said: "I shall attack with five against one." He replied: "It cannot be done." The King of Yan was angry, and the assembled ministers all held that it could be done. In the end he raised two armies, two thousand chariots: Li Fu led one and attacked Hao, and Qing Qin attacked Dai. Alone the Grand Master Jiang Qu said to the King of Yan: "To open the Passes to another and bind oneself to him in friendship, to feast another's king with five hundred jin of gold, and then, when the envoy has reported back, to turn and attack him — that is ill-omened, and the troops will have no success." The King of Yan did not listen, and himself led a detached army behind them. Jiang Qu took hold of the King of Yan's seal-ribbon to stop him, saying: "Your Majesty must on no account go yourself; if you go there will be no success." The king kicked him away with his foot. Jiang Qu wept and said: "Your servant does this not for himself but for Your Majesty!" The Yan army reached Songzi. Zhao sent Lian Po in command; he struck and defeated Li Fu at Hao. Yue Cheng defeated Qing Qin at Dai. Yue Jian fled to Zhao. Lian Po pursued them more than five hundred li and besieged their capital. The men of Yan sued for peace; the men of Zhao would not allow it, and insisted that Jiang Qu be made to handle the peace. Yan made Jiang Qu Chancellor to handle the peace. Zhao heeded Jiang Qu and raised the siege of Yan. Hereditary House of Chu: In the twelfth year, King Zhao of Qin died, and the King of Chu sent Lord Chunshen to condole and sacrifice in Qin. Hereditary House of Zhao: In the fifteenth year, the Chancellor of State Lian Po was enfeoffed with Weiwen as Lord Xinping. The King of Yan ordered the Chancellor Li Fu to conclude friendly relations, and with five hundred jin of gold he feasted the King of Zhao; he went back and reported to the King of Yan: "Of the men of Zhao, those in their prime all died at Changping, and their orphans are not yet grown; Zhao can be attacked." The king summoned Lord Changguo, Yue Jian, and asked him. He replied: "Zhao is a state at war on four sides; its people are practised in arms. To attack it cannot be done." The king said: "If I attack the few with the many, two against one, will it do?" He replied: "It will not." The king said: "Then if I attack with five against one, will it do?" He replied: "It will not." The King of Yan was greatly angered. The assembled ministers all held that it could be done. Yan in the end raised two armies, two thousand chariots: Li Fu led one and attacked Hao, and Qing Qin led one and attacked Dai. Lian Po was Zhao's general; he defeated and killed Li Fu and captured Qing Qin and Yue Jian. Hereditary House of Wei: In the twenty-sixth year, King Zhao of Qin died. Hereditary House of Han: In the twenty-second year, King Zhao of Qin died.
