The Prince heard that in Zhao there were gentlemen in retirement: Master Mao, hidden among the gamblers, and Master Xue, hidden in the house of a seller of drinks. The Prince wished to see the two men, but the two hid themselves and would not see the Prince. When the Prince learned where they were, he went secretly on foot to keep company with the two, and they were very happy together. When Lord Pingyuan heard of it, he said to his wife: "At first I heard that your brother the Prince had no equal under Heaven; now I hear that he recklessly keeps company with gamblers and sellers of drinks — the Prince is a reckless man, that is all." His wife told the Prince. The Prince then took leave of his sister to go, saying: "At first I heard that Lord Pingyuan was a man of worth, and so I betrayed the King of Wei to relieve Zhao, to answer Lord Pingyuan's expectations. But Lord Pingyuan's company is only a grand display; he does not seek gentlemen. When Wuji was still in Daliang he often heard that these two were worthy men, and on coming to Zhao he feared he would not get to see them. With Wuji keeping their company, I still feared they would not want me; now Lord Pingyuan thinks it a disgrace — he is not worth keeping company with." And he packed to leave. His wife told Lord Pingyuan everything. Lord Pingyuan then took off his cap, apologised, and insisted that the Prince stay. When Lord Pingyuan's household heard of it, half of them left Lord Pingyuan and went over to the Prince, and the gentlemen of all under Heaven went over to the Prince once more; the Prince drew away Lord Pingyuan's retainers. The Prince stayed in Zhao ten years without returning. Qin, hearing that the Prince was in Zhao, sent troops east day and night to attack Wei. The King of Wei was troubled by this and sent envoys to ask the Prince back. The Prince, fearing that the King was angry with him, warned his household: "Whoever dares to carry word for the King of Wei's envoys dies." His guests had all turned their backs on Wei for Zhao, and none dared urge the Prince to return. The two men Master Mao and Master Xue went to see the Prince and said: "The reason the Prince weighs heavily in Zhao and his name is heard among the Lords is solely that there is a Wei. Now Qin attacks Wei; Wei is in extremity and the Prince does not care. Should Qin destroy Daliang and level the ancestral temple of the former kings, with what face could the Prince stand before all under Heaven?" Before they had finished speaking the Prince's colour changed at once; he called for his carriage and hurried home to relieve Wei. The King of Wei saw the Prince, and they wept together; and he gave the seal of Supreme General to the Prince, and the Prince took command. In the thirtieth year of King Anxi of Wei the Prince sent envoys to inform all the Lords. When the Lords heard that the Prince was in command, each sent generals with troops to relieve Wei. The Prince led the troops of five states and defeated the Qin army at Hewai, putting Meng Ao to flight. Then, following up the victory, he pursued the Qin army to Hangu Pass and held the Qin troops in check, so that the Qin troops dared not come out. At this time the Prince's majesty shook all under Heaven, and the retainers of the Lords presented methods of war, to all of which the Prince gave his name; hence the world at large calls them the Prince of Wei's Methods of War. The King of Qin was troubled by this, and sent ten thousand jin of gold into Wei to seek out Jin Bi's former retainers and have them slander the Prince to the King of Wei: "The Prince was ten years in exile abroad; now he is Wei's general, and the generals of the Lords are all under him; the Lords hear only of the Prince of Wei and not of the King of Wei. The Prince also wishes to seize this moment to face south and make himself king; the Lords, in awe of the Prince's majesty, are about to set him up together." Qin several times sent agents of discord, feigning to congratulate the Prince on whether he had yet been set up as King of Wei. The King of Wei heard the slander daily and could not help believing it, and afterwards did indeed send someone to replace the Prince in command. The Prince, knowing that he had a second time been cast aside through slander, pleaded illness and did not attend court; with his guests he drank the night through, drinking strong wine and keeping much company with women. Day and night he made merry with drink for four years, and in the end died of drink. That same year King Anxi of Wei also died. When Qin heard that the Prince was dead, it sent Meng Ao to attack Wei; he took twenty Fortresses, and Dong Commandery was first established. Thereafter Qin ate away at Wei little by little, as a silkworm eats a leaf, and in eighteen years it captured the King of Wei and slaughtered Daliang. When Gaozu was still young and humble, he often heard of the Prince's worth. After he ascended the throne as Son of Heaven, whenever he passed Daliang he always sacrificed to the Prince. In the twelfth year of Gaozu, returning from the attack on Qing Bu, he established five tomb-keeping households for the Prince, to sacrifice to the Prince at the four seasons every year, generation after generation. The Grand Historian says: I passed the ruins of Daliang and sought out what is called the Yi Gate. The Yi Gate was the eastern gate of the Fortress. Among the princes of all under Heaven there have been others who delighted in gentlemen, but that Lord Xinling received recluses of the caves and cliffs, and was not ashamed to associate with those beneath him, had its reason. That his name stood first among the Lords was no empty thing. And Gaozu, whenever he passed, had the people sacrifice to him without cease.
passages.no: 公子: the Biography calls Wuji "the Prince" throughout. The passage, from his stay in Zhao to the historian's judgement, is the one already given under 256 BC (§4), repeated here for the year it dates: the thirtieth year of King Anxi, 247 BC, of his return and the victory at Hewai. 247 BC. The King of Qin of the slander is King Zhuangxiang, in whose last year the Prince took command; the four years of drinking and the Prince's death fall under King Zheng. The second half of the Biography of the Prince of Wei, Lord Xinling: his ten years in Zhao, his return to command the five states against Qin in the thirtieth year of King Anxi, the slander that undid him, and his death; told in full under 256 BC and repeated here for the year of the victory at Hewai.

passages.title: Shiji V: Biographies
passages.zh: 史记（五：列传） 吕不韦列传：庄襄王即位三年，薨，太子政立为王，尊吕不韦为相国，号称“仲父”。秦王年少，太后时时窃私通吕不韦。不韦家僮万人。 当是时，魏有信陵君，楚有春申君，赵有平原君，齐有孟尝君，皆下士喜宾客以相倾。吕不韦以秦之彊，羞不如，亦招致士，厚遇之，至食客三千人。是时诸侯多辩士，如荀卿之徒，著书布天下。吕不韦乃使其客人人著所闻，集论以为八览、六论、十二纪，二十馀万言。以为备天地万物古今之事，号曰吕氏春秋。布咸阳市门，悬千金其上，延诸侯游士宾客有能增损一字者予千金。 始皇帝益壮，太后淫不止。吕不韦恐觉祸及己，乃私求大阴人嫪毐以为舍人，时纵倡乐，使毐以其阴关桐轮而行，令太后闻之，以啗太后。太后闻，果欲私得之。吕不韦乃进嫪毐，诈令人以腐罪告之。不韦又阴谓太后曰：“可事诈腐，则得给事中。”太后乃阴厚赐主腐者吏，诈论之，拔其须眉为宦者，遂得侍太后。太后私与通，绝爱之。有身，太后恐人知之，诈卜当避时，徙宫居雍。嫪毐常从，赏赐甚厚，事皆决於嫪毐。嫪毐家僮数千人，诸客求宦为嫪毐舍人千馀人。 李斯列传：李斯者，楚上蔡人也。年少时，为郡小吏，见吏舍厕中鼠食不絜，近人犬，数惊恐之。斯入仓，观仓中鼠，食积粟，居大庑之下，不见人犬之忧。於是李斯乃叹曰：“人之贤不肖譬如鼠矣，在所自处耳！” 乃从荀卿学帝王之术。学已成，度楚王不足事，而六国皆弱，无可为建功者，欲西入秦。辞於荀卿曰：“斯闻得时无怠，今万乘方争时，游者主事。今秦王欲吞天下，称帝而治，此布衣驰骛之时而游说者之秋也。处卑贱之位而计不为者，此禽鹿视肉，人面而能强行者耳。故诟莫大於卑贱，而悲莫甚於穷困。久处卑贱之位，困苦之地，非世而恶利，自讬於无为，此非士之情也。故斯将西说秦王矣。” 至秦，会庄襄王卒，李斯乃求为秦相文信侯吕不韦舍人；不韦贤之，任以为郎。李斯因以得说，说秦王曰：“胥人者，去其几也。成大功者，在因瑕衅而遂忍之。昔者秦穆公之霸，终不东并六国者，何也？诸侯尚众，周德未衰，故五伯迭兴，更尊周室。自秦孝公以来，周室卑微，诸侯相兼，关东为六国，秦之乘胜役诸侯，盖六世矣。今诸侯服秦，譬若郡县。夫以秦之彊，大王之贤，由灶上骚除，足以灭诸侯，成帝业，为天下一统，此万世之一时也。今怠而不急就，诸侯复彊，相聚约从，虽有黄帝之贤，不能并也。”秦王乃拜斯为长史，听其计，阴遣谋士赍持金玉以游说诸侯。诸侯名士可下以财者，厚遗结之；不肯者，利剑刺之。离其君臣之计，秦王乃使其良将随其後。秦王拜斯为客卿。 会韩人郑国来间秦，以作注溉渠，已而觉。秦宗室大臣皆言秦王曰：“诸侯人来事秦者，大抵为其主游间於秦耳，请一切逐客。”李斯议亦在逐中。斯乃上书曰： 臣闻吏议逐客，窃以为过矣。昔缪公求士，西取由余於戎，东得百里奚於宛，迎蹇叔於宋，来丕豹、公孙支於晋。此五子者，不产於秦，而缪公用之，并国二十，遂霸西戎。孝公用商鞅之法，移风易俗，民以殷盛，国以富彊，百姓乐用，诸侯亲服，获楚、魏之师，举地千里，至今治彊。惠王用张仪之计，拔三川之地，西并巴、蜀，北收上郡，南取汉中，包九夷，制鄢、郢，东据成皋之险，割膏腴之壤，遂散六国之从，使之西面事秦，功施到今。昭王得范睢，废穰侯，逐华阳，彊公室，杜私门，蚕食诸侯，使秦成帝业。此四君者，皆以客之功。由此观之，客何负於秦哉！向使四君卻客而不内，疏士而不用，是使国无富利之实而秦无彊大之名也。 今陛下致昆山之玉，有随、和之宝，垂明月之珠，服太阿之剑，乘纤离之马，建翠凤之旗，树灵鼍之鼓。此数宝者，秦不生一焉，而陛下说之，何也？必秦国之所生然後可，则是夜光之璧不饰朝廷，犀象之器不为玩好，郑、卫之女不充後宫，而骏良駃騠不实外厩，江南金锡不为用，西蜀丹青不为采。所以饰後宫充下陈娱心意说耳目者，必出於秦然後可，则是宛珠之簪，傅玑之珥，阿缟之衣，锦绣之饰不进於前，而随俗雅化佳冶窈窕赵女不立於侧也。夫击甕叩缶弹筝搏髀，而歌呼呜呜快耳者，真秦之声也；郑、卫、桑间、昭、虞、武、象者，异国之乐也。今弃击甕叩缶而就郑卫，退弹筝而取昭虞，若是者何也？快意当前，適观而已矣。今取人则不然。不问可否，不论曲直，非秦者去，为客者逐。然则是所重者在乎色乐珠玉，而所轻者在乎人民也。此非所以跨海内制诸侯之术也。 臣闻地广者粟多，国大者人众，兵彊则士勇。是以太山不让土壤，故能成其大；河海不择细流，故能就其深；王者不卻众庶，故能明其德。是以地无四方，民无异国，四时充美，鬼神降福，此五帝、三王之所以无敌也。今乃弃黔首以资敌国，卻宾客以业诸侯，使天下之士退而不敢西向，裹足不入秦，此所谓“藉寇兵而赍盗粮”者也。 夫物不产於秦，可宝者多；士不产於秦，而原忠者众。今逐客以资敌国，损民以益雠，内自虚而外树怨於诸侯，求国无危，不可得也。 秦王乃除逐客之令，复李斯官，卒用其计谋。官至廷尉。二十馀年，竟并天下，尊主为皇帝，以斯为丞相。夷郡县城，销其兵刃，示不复用。使秦无尺土之封，不立子弟为王，功臣为诸侯者，使後无战攻之患。
passages.en: Shiji V: Biographies Biography of Lü Buwei: King Zhuangxiang died in the third year after his accession; the Heir Apparent, Zheng, was set up as king, and he honoured Lü Buwei as Chancellor of State, styling him "Second Father". The King of Qin was young, and the Queen Dowager from time to time had secret relations with Lü Buwei. Buwei's household slaves numbered ten thousand. At this time Wei had Lord Xinling, Chu had Lord Chunshen, Zhao had Lord Pingyuan and Qi had Lord Mengchang, all of whom humbled themselves before gentlemen and delighted in retainers, each striving to outdo the others. Lü Buwei, for all Qin's strength, was ashamed to fall short of them, and he too drew gentlemen to him and treated them generously, until his retainers reached three thousand. At that time there were many disputants among the Lords, such as Xun Qing and his kind, who wrote books and spread them over all under Heaven. Lü Buwei therefore had each of his guests write down what he had heard, and gathered their discourses into the Eight Surveys, Six Discourses and Twelve Records, more than two hundred thousand words. Holding that it comprised the affairs of heaven and earth, of the myriad things and of ancient and modern times, he called it Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals. He displayed it at the market gate of Xianyang, hung a thousand jin of gold above it, and invited the travelling gentlemen and retainers of the Lords: whoever could add or take away a single character would be given the thousand jin. As the First Emperor grew to manhood, the Queen Dowager's licence did not cease. Lü Buwei, fearing that it would be found out and disaster fall on himself, privately sought out a man of great member, Lao Ai, and made him a household retainer; at times, letting the players and musicians loose, he had Ai walk with a wheel of tong wood hung on his member, and let the Queen Dowager hear of it, so as to bait her. The Queen Dowager heard, and as expected wished to have him in secret. Lü Buwei then presented Lao Ai, and had someone falsely accuse him of an offence meriting castration. Buwei also said to the Queen Dowager in private: "If the castration can be feigned, he can be had as a palace attendant." The Queen Dowager then secretly made rich gifts to the officer in charge of castrations, who passed false sentence on him, plucked out his beard and eyebrows and made him a eunuch; and so he came to attend the Queen Dowager. She had secret relations with him and loved him beyond measure. She became pregnant and, fearing that it would be known, feigned a divination that she should avoid the season, and moved her palace to Yong. Lao Ai was always in attendance, the rewards given him were very rich, and all matters were decided by Lao Ai. Lao Ai's household slaves numbered several thousand, and the guests who sought office by becoming Lao Ai's household retainers more than a thousand. Biography of Li Si: Li Si was a man of Shangcai in Chu. In his youth he was a petty officer of the Commandery. He saw that the rats in the privy of the officers' quarters ate filth and, being near men and dogs, were constantly startled and frightened by them. Then Si went into the granary and watched the rats there: they ate the stored grain, lived under the great eaves, and had no fear of men or dogs. At this Li Si sighed: "Whether a man is worthy or worthless is like the case of the rats: it lies in where he places himself!" He then studied the arts of emperors and kings under Xun Qing. When his studies were complete, he judged that the King of Chu was not worth serving and that the Six States were all weak, with no chance of achievement among them, and wished to go west into Qin. Taking leave of Xun Qing he said: "Si has heard that when one meets one's hour one must not be idle. Now the lords of ten thousand chariots are contending for their hour, and it is the travellers who have the management of affairs. Now the King of Qin wishes to swallow all under Heaven and rule under the title of Emperor; this is the hour for commoners to gallop, and the harvest-time of the travelling persuaders. One who sits in a humble and lowly station and makes no plan for himself is a beast staring at meat, with a man's face and able only to walk upright. So there is no greater disgrace than lowliness, no greater sorrow than want. To stay long in a humble station and in straitened circumstances, carping at the age and hating gain, entrusting oneself to inaction: that is not the true feeling of a gentleman. Therefore Si will go west and persuade the King of Qin." He arrived in Qin just as King Zhuangxiang died. Li Si then sought to become a household retainer of the Chancellor of Qin, Marquis Wenxin Lü Buwei; Buwei thought him able and appointed him a Court Gentleman. Li Si thereby got his chance to speak, and said to the King of Qin: "The petty man is one who lets slip his moment. Those who achieve great deeds do so by seizing on a flaw and being ruthless in following it through. In former days, when Duke Mu of Qin was hegemon, why did he never in the end annex the Six States to the east? Because the Lords were still many and the virtue of Zhou had not yet declined, so the Five Hegemons rose in turn and each in turn honoured the house of Zhou. Since Duke Xiao of Qin, the house of Zhou has sunk low, the Lords have swallowed one another, east of the Pass there are six states, and Qin has ridden its victories and made the Lords its servants for six reigns now. Today the Lords submit to Qin as if they were its Commanderies and Counties. With Qin's strength and the Great King's worth, it would be like sweeping the dust off a stove: enough to wipe out the Lords, complete the imperial task and bring all under Heaven under one rule. This is the one chance in ten thousand generations. If now you are idle and do not hasten to finish it, the Lords will grow strong again and gather to swear the Vertical Alliance, and though you had the worth of the Yellow Emperor you could not annex them." The King of Qin then appointed Si Senior Clerk, followed his plan, and secretly sent out schemers bearing gold and jade to work on the Lords. Those famous men of the Lords who could be brought down with wealth he bound to himself with rich gifts; those who would not, he stabbed with a sharp sword. Having laid his plans to divide rulers from ministers, the King of Qin then sent his good generals in their wake. The King of Qin appointed Si Guest Minister. It happened that Zheng Guo, a man of Han, came to spy on Qin by building an irrigation canal, and after a time this was discovered. The royal clan and great ministers of Qin all said to the King of Qin: "The men of the Lords who come to serve Qin for the most part only travel here to spy on Qin for their masters; we ask that all guests be expelled without exception." Li Si was counted among those to be expelled. Si then submitted a memorial, saying: "Your servant has heard that the officers are deliberating the expulsion of the guests; in my humble view this is a mistake. In former days Duke Mu sought gentlemen: in the west he took You Yu from the Rong, in the east he got Baili Xi from Wan, he welcomed Jian Shu from Song, and he brought Pi Bao and Gongsun Zhi from Jin. These five were not born in Qin, yet Duke Mu used them, annexed twenty states and became hegemon over the Western Rong. Duke Xiao used the laws of Shang Yang, changed the ways and altered the customs; the people prospered and multiplied, the state grew rich and strong, the hundred clans were glad to be employed and the Lords submitted in friendship; he captured the armies of Chu and Wei and took a thousand li of land, and to this day the state is well governed and strong. King Hui used the plans of Zhang Yi: he took the lands of Sanchuan, in the west annexed Ba and Shu, in the north gathered in Shang Commandery, in the south took Hanzhong, encompassed the Nine Yi and brought Yan and Ying under control; in the east he seized the fastness of Chenggao and cut off the fat and fertile soil; and so he scattered the Vertical Alliance of the Six States and made them face west and serve Qin, and the benefit of his deeds reaches to this day. King Zhao got Fan Ju, deposed Marquis Rang and expelled Huayang, strengthened the ducal house and barred the private gates, nibbled away at the Lords like a silkworm, and brought Qin to the imperial task. These four lords all owed their success to guests. Seen in this light, how have the guests failed Qin? Had the four lords rejected the guests and not admitted them, kept gentlemen at a distance and not used them, the state would have had none of the substance of wealth and profit, and Qin none of its name for strength and greatness. "Now Your Majesty obtains the jade of Kunshan, possesses the treasures of Sui and He, hangs up the bright-moon pearl, wears the sword Tai'e, rides the horses of Xianli, raises banners of kingfisher-phoenix plumes and sets up drums of magic alligator hide. Of these several treasures Qin produces not one, yet Your Majesty delights in them: why? If only what the state of Qin produces will do, then the jade disc that shines by night would not adorn the court, vessels of rhinoceros horn and ivory would not be toys and pleasures, the women of Zheng and Wey would not fill the harem, and fine steeds and jueti would not stock the outer stables; the gold and tin of Jiangnan would not be used, nor the cinnabar and azurite of Western Shu for colouring. If what adorns the harem and fills the lower ranks, delighting the heart and pleasing the eye and ear, must come from Qin before it will do, then hairpins of Wan pearls, ear-pendants set with seed-pearls, robes of E gauze and ornaments of brocade and embroidery would not be brought before you, and the lovely, bewitching, graceful women of Zhao, elegant and refined after the fashion, would not stand at your side. Striking pots and beating jars, plucking the zither and slapping the thigh, and howling "wu, wu" to delight the ear: that is the true music of Qin; the music of Zheng, Wey and Sangjian, the Zhao, Yu, Wu and Xiang, are the music of other countries. Now you cast aside the striking of pots and the beating of jars and take up Zheng and Wey, put away the plucking of the zither and take the Zhao and Yu: why so? Because they please you here and now and suit the eye, that is all. But in taking men you do not do so. You ask not whether they will do or not, you weigh not the crooked and the straight; whoever is not of Qin must go, whoever is a guest is expelled. So then what is prized is women, music, pearls and jade, and what is held light is the people. This is not the way to bestride all within the seas and control the Lords. "Your servant has heard that where the land is broad the grain is plentiful, where the state is great the people are many, and where the arms are strong the soldiers are brave. Thus Taishan does not refuse the clods of earth, and so can achieve its greatness; the rivers and seas do not pick and choose among the little streams, and so can achieve their depth; a true king does not reject the common multitude, and so can make his virtue shine. Thus the land has no four quarters and the people no foreign country; the four seasons are full and fair and the gods and spirits send down blessing: this is why the Five Emperors and the Three Kings had no rival. Now instead you cast off the black-headed people to supply the enemy states, and turn away retainers to build up the Lords, making the gentlemen of all under Heaven draw back and not dare to face west, binding their feet so that they do not enter Qin: this is what is called "lending arms to the bandit and carrying provisions to the thief". "Things not produced in Qin that may be treasured are many; gentlemen not born in Qin who wish to be loyal are numerous. Now to expel the guests to supply the enemy states, to lose your people to strengthen your foes, emptying yourself within and planting resentment among the Lords without, and then to seek a state free of danger: it cannot be done." The King of Qin then rescinded the order expelling the guests and restored Li Si to his office, and in the end used his plans. He rose in office to Commandant of Justice. In twenty-odd years Qin at last annexed all under Heaven, honoured its ruler as Emperor, and made Si Chancellor. The Fortresses of the Commanderies and Counties were levelled and their weapons melted down, to show that they would not be used again. Qin was made to have not a foot of land in fief; no sons or brothers were set up as kings, no meritorious ministers as Lords, so that afterwards there should be no trouble of wars and attacks.
passages.no: 247 BC, this year; the Basic Annals (§1) give the day, Bingwu of the fifth month. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: Zheng was then thirteen. The two Biographies run on from this point far past the year: the matter of Lao Ai falls in the king's early years and ends with Ai's revolt and death in 238 BC and Buwei's fall in 237 BC; Li Si's memorial is dated by the Zhengyi to the king's tenth year, 237 BC, and his Biography closes with the unification of 221 BC. The passages are given whole here, where the chronology meets them. 仲父: the Zhengyi: 仲 is 中, the middle; a second father; on the model of Duke Huan of Qi, who made Guan Zhong his 仲父. The Zhengyi, from the Table: Lord Pingyuan died in King Zhaoxiang's fifty-sixth year (251 BC), Lord Xinling in the First Emperor's fourth (243 BC), and Li Yuan killed Lord Chunshen in his ninth (238 BC); Lord Mengchang died after King Zhaoxiang's twenty-fourth year (283 BC), the earliest of the four. The Suoyin cites Wang Shao, "Mengchang and Chunshen had long been dead", and answers that by the Table and the Biographies Mengchang and Pingyuan died somewhat earlier, but Xinling's command of the five states against Qin at Hewai falls in King Zhuangxiang's reign, when Buwei was already Chancellor, and Chunshen and Buwei were contemporaries, each Chancellor for over ten years, so that he cannot be said to have been long dead. 八览、六论、十二纪: the Suoyin names the eight Surveys (有始, 孝行, 慎大, 先识, 审分, 审应, 离俗, 时君), the six Discourses (开春, 慎行, 贵直, 不苟, 以顺, 士容) and the twelve Records, one for each month, beginning with 孟春; the two hundred thousand-odd words make twenty-six juan. 吕氏春秋: Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals, the compilation of Lü Buwei's retainers in twenty-six juan; quoted under 256 BC (§7). The Suoyin: the Dilizhi's Weicheng County in Youfufeng is the old Xianyang, renamed Xincheng by Emperor Gao and Weicheng by Emperor Jing; 咸 means "all", the place lying north of the Wei and south of the northern slope, on the 阳 side of both water and hill. 始皇帝: the Biography names the young king by his later title. 桐轮: the Zhengyi: a small cart wheel made of tong wood. 腐罪: the Zhengyi: 腐 is read fu; the palace punishment, 宫刑, of the convict. The Zhengyi: the old city of Yong lies seven li south of Yong County in Qizhou, with the Da Zheng Palace of the Qin capital. The Suoyin: the Dilizhi's Shangcai County in Runan, "the old state of Cai, fief of Shu Du, King Wu of Zhou's brother; at the eighteenth generation Marquis Ping moved to Xincai", both in Runan; two generations later Marquis Zhao moved to Xiacai, in Pei; in the time of the Six States it was Chu land, hence "Shangcai of Chu". 郡小吏: the Suoyin: a petty clerk of a district 乡小史; Liu: in charge of the district's documents. 游者主事: the Suoyin: in an age when the lords of ten thousand chariots contend for mastery, the travelling persuaders can win merit and fame and are given charge of affairs; Liu's reading, "travel among the Lords and seek a strong master to serve", twists the text and is wrong. 秋: the Zhengyi: in autumn all things ripen; in a time of contention the persuaders too are ripe. 禽鹿视肉: the Suoyin: 禽鹿 means birds and beasts, which know only to stare at meat and eat it; the Zhuangzi and Master Su say "a man who does not learn is like one who stares at meat and eats", and Yang Xiong's Fayan "a man who does not learn, how does he differ from a beast?"; one who cannot persuade and win honour is as the beasts, having a man's face and able only to walk upright. 诟: the Zhengyi: read hou; shame. 非世: the Suoyin: 非 is to censure, the "unbridled discourse of men out of office". The Zhengyi: to censure the age's wealth and rank, to hate its honours and gains and entrust oneself to inaction is not the gentleman's true feeling; it is that his strength cannot attain them. 247 BC: the point at which Li Si's story meets this year. What follows, his rise under King Zheng and the memorial of 237 BC, belongs to the following years. 胥人者，去其几也: the Suoyin: 胥人 is like 胥吏, petty men; 去 is to lose; 几 is the first stirring of movement; the gentleman sees the stirring and acts without waiting out the day, while the petty man does not know the moment of stirring and so always loses his time; Liu's gloss of 几 as "strong" is wrong. The Zhengyi reads 胥 as 相, "mutually", and 几 as 察, "to examine": the Six States east of the Pass stand against Qin as rivals, and the secret affairs of their rulers and ministers all have flaws by which great deeds may be achieved if one bears with them ruthlessly. 因瑕衅而遂忍之: the Suoyin: where the Lords have flaws, steel the heart and cut them away; "so I shall urge Qin to annex the world". 六世: the Zhengyi: Duke Xiao, Duke Huiwen, King Wu, King Zhao, King Xiaowen and King Zhuangxiang. 灶上骚除: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 骚 read as 埽; the Suoyin: Qin's annexing of the world would be like the cook sweeping the dirt from the stove top, no difficulty at all. 注溉渠: the Zhengyi: the Zheng Guo canal rose twenty-five li south-west of Yunyang County in Yongzhou, drawn from Zhongshan westward at Hukou, and ran along the northern hills east into the Luo, three hundred-odd li, to water the fields; Han, hard pressed by Qin's arms, sent the water engineer Zheng Guo to spy on Qin by building the canal, to waste its labour and keep it from attacking eastward. 一切逐客: the Suoyin: 一切 is "as one rule", to expel them all; 切 is as a sharp knife cutting, one stroke of the axe severing everything; those who gloss 一切 in the Hanshu as "for the time being" have not got it. The Zhengyi: in the First Emperor's tenth year (237 BC). The memorial is the 谏逐客书, the remonstrance against the expulsion of the guests. 缪公: Duke Mu 穆公 as the memorial writes him. The Suoyin: the Basic Annals of Qin say Duke Xian of Jin sent Baili Xi to Qin as a bride-servant with Duke Mu's wife; Xi fled to Wan, and rustics of Chu seized him. The Zhengyi cites the Xinxu: Baili Xi, a man of Wan in Chu, served in Yu; when Yu fell he entered Qin, and was called the Grand Master of the Five Rams' Skins. The Suoyin: the Basic Annals also have Baili Xi tell Duke Mu, "I am not the equal of my friend Jian Shu, who is worthy but unknown to the age", whereupon the duke welcomed him with rich gifts and made him Senior Grand Master; "from Song" has no known source. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Jian Shu was a man of Qizhou, then travelling in Song, hence welcomed from Song. The Suoyin: Pi Bao's flight from Jin to Qin is plain in the Zuo Tradition; Gongsun Zhi is Zi Sang, a Grand Master of Qin, and his coming from Jin has no known source. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Gongsun Zhi was a man of Qizhou who travelled in Jin and later returned to Qin. 并国二十: the Suoyin: the Basic Annals say Duke Mu, on You Yu's counsel, attacked the king of the Rong, added twelve states and opened a thousand li of land, becoming hegemon over the Western Rong; here the merits of all five are summed, hence "twenty"; texts that alter it to "twelve" are wrong. The Suoyin: in King Hui's time Zhang Yi, as Chancellor, asked to attack Han and send troops down to Sanchuan to menace the two Zhou; Sima Cuo asked to attack Shu, the king agreed, and Shu was destroyed; after Yi's death King Wu wished to open the road to Sanchuan and had Gan Mao take Yiyang. All is credited to Zhang Yi here because he was Chancellor of Qin, and because he first asked to attack Sanchuan. The Zhengyi: in King Hui's tenth year (328 BC) Wei ceded the fifteen Counties of Shang Commandery. The Zhengyi: in King Hui's thirteenth year (of his second reckoning, 312 BC) Qin attacked Chu's Hanzhong and took six hundred li of land. 九夷: the Suoyin: the Yi belonging to Chu; the Dilizhi's Jiangling County in Nan Commandery is "the old Ying, capital of Chu", and its Yicheng County "the old Yan". The Zhengyi: the Yi are the annexing of Ba and Shu, the gathering in of Shang Commandery, the taking of Hanzhong and the attacks on Yiqu and Danli; the Nine Yi are properly the nine kinds of Eastern Yi, and the phrase is a figure of style. The Zhengyi: Sishui County 氾水县 of Henan 河南府, in the names of the Tang. 华阳: Lord Huayang 华阳君, Mi Rong. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: 华 in one text 叶. 蚕食: the Suoyin cites Gao You on the Huainanzi: to eat up, leaving nothing. The Zhengyi: Kungang lies four hundred li north-east of the state of Khotan (于阗), and the ridge yields jade. 随、和之宝: the pearl of the Marquis of Sui and the jade disc of Bian He. The Zhengyi cites the Kuodizhi: Mount Fen, also called Kunshan and Duanshe Hill, "the hill of the severed snake", lies twenty-five li north of Sui County in Suizhou; the Shuoyuan: the Marquis of Sui on a journey met a great snake cut in two and, suspecting it was uncanny, had it dressed with medicine; the snake was able to go, and the place was named for it; after a year the snake brought him a bright pearl an inch across, pure white and shining, called the pearl of Sui. The disc of Bian He the First Emperor made the seal of state handed down. 太阿: the Jijie: see the Biography of Su Qin. The Suoyin cites the Yuejueshu: the King of Chu summoned Ou Yezi and Gan Jiang to make three iron swords, Ganjiang, Moye and Tai'e. 纤离: the Jijie cites Xu Guang: Xianli and Pushao are both names of fine horses; the Suoyin: both horse names, Xu following the Sunqingzi. 灵鼍之鼓: the Jijie cites Zheng Xuan on the Yueling: alligator hide can be stretched over drums. 駃騠: the Suoyin gives the reading jue-ti; the Zhoushu, "the true north offers jueti"; the Guangya, "a kind of horse"; Guo Pu on the Shanglin fu, "born three days and it outruns its mother". 西蜀: Shu, the Chengdu plain. 下陈: the Suoyin: the rear ranks; Master Yan, "I have two daughters and wish to have them enter among the lower ranks". 宛珠之簪，傅玑之珥: the Suoyin: 宛 read yuan, to wind pearls round the hairpin; 傅 read fu; 傅玑 is to set seed-pearls on the ear-pendant, 珥 being the ear-plug and 玑 a pearl that is not round; or 宛珠 is the pearl of Sui, Sui lying south of the Han and Wan near it; women's ornaments, none of them things Qin possesses. 阿缟: the Jijie cites Xu Guang: Dong'e County of Qi, whence silks come. 随俗雅化: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 随俗 in one text 修使; the Suoyin: refined and adaptable, able to suit the common taste. 击甕叩缶: the Suoyin cites the Shuowen: 甕 a water jar; 缶 an earthen vessel, which the men of Qin beat to keep time to music. 昭、虞、武、象: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, 昭 in one text 韶; the dances of Shun, of King Wu and the Xiang. 太山: Mount Tai. The Suoyin cites the Guanzi, "the sea does not refuse water and so achieves its greatness; the mountain does not refuse earth and stones and so achieves its height", and the Wenzi, "the sage does not refuse the words of the firewood-carrier, and so widens his name". 资: the Suoyin: 给, to supply. 藉寇兵而赍盗粮: the Suoyin gives the readings and cites the Shuowen, 赍 is to carry and present; 赍 or 资, the sense the same. The Jijie cites the Xinxu: Si, among those expelled, submitted his memorial of remonstrance on the road; it reached the First Emperor, who sent men after him as far as Liyi and brought him back. The unification of 221 BC and the imperial title; the Biography's summary runs to the end of the First Emperor's reign. The Biography of Lü Buwei from King Zhuangxiang's death: Buwei as Chancellor of State and Second Father to the young king, his three thousand retainers and Master Lü's Spring and Autumn Annals, and the matter of Lao Ai and the Queen Dowager; and the Biography of Li Si from his birth at Shangcai to his arrival in Qin in this year, his counsel to King Zheng, the memorial against the expulsion of the guests, and his rise to Chancellor.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）一 魏、楚、燕攻齐;魏取平陆，楚取齐南阳，燕取聊城。 辨析：此條出處或是《史記·鲁仲连邹阳列传》。然而原文時間只有信陵君竊符救趙的“其後二十馀年”，具體時間點不詳。 齐安平君田单率军围攻聊城。 辨析：此條出處或是《史記·鲁仲连邹阳列传》。然而原文時間只有信陵君竊符救趙的“其後二十馀年”，具體時間點不詳。 楚、魏两国放弃攻齐，谋划合纵攻秦。 辨析：此條出處或是《史記·鲁仲连邹阳列传》。然而原文時間只有信陵君竊符救趙的“其後二十馀年”，具體時間點不詳。 《史記·鲁仲连邹阳列传》：適会魏公子无忌夺晋鄙军以救赵，击秦军，秦军遂引而去。 於是平原君欲封鲁连，鲁连辞让者三，终不肯受。平原君乃置酒，酒酣起前，以千金为鲁连寿。鲁连笑曰：“所贵於天下之士者，为人排患释难解纷乱而无取也。即有取者，是商贾之事也，而连不忍为也。”遂辞平原君而去，终身不复见。 其後二十馀年，燕将攻下聊城，聊城人或谗之燕，燕将惧诛，因保守聊城，不敢归。齐田单攻聊城岁馀，士卒多死而聊城不下。鲁连乃为书，约之矢以射城中，遗燕将。书曰： 吾闻之，智者不倍时而弃利，勇士不却死而灭名，忠臣不先身而後君。今公行一朝之忿，不顾燕王之无臣，非忠也；杀身亡聊城，而威不信於齐，非勇也；功败名灭，後世无称焉，非智也。三者世主不臣，说士不载，故智者不再计，勇士不怯死。今死生荣辱，贵贱尊卑，此时不再至，原公详计而无与俗同。 且楚攻齐之南阳，魏攻平陆，而齐无南面之心，以为亡南阳之害小，不如得济北之利大，故定计审处之。今秦人下兵，魏不敢东面；衡秦之势成，楚国之形危；齐弃南阳，断右壤，定济北，计犹且为之也。且夫齐之必决於聊城，公勿再计。今楚魏交退於齐，而燕救不至。以全齐之兵，无天下之规，与聊城共据期年之敝，则臣见公之不能得也。且燕国大乱，君臣失计，上下迷惑，栗腹以十万之众五折於外，以万乘之国被围於赵，壤削主困，为天下僇笑。国敝而祸多，民无所归心。今公又以敝聊之民距全齐之兵，是墨翟之守也。食人炊骨，士无反外之心，是孙膑之兵也。能见於天下。虽然，为公计者，不如全车甲以报於燕。车甲全而归燕，燕王必喜；身全而归於国，士民如见父母，交游攘臂而议於世，功业可明。上辅孤主以制群臣，下养百姓以资说士，矫国更俗，功名可立也。亡意亦捐燕弃世，东游於齐乎？裂地定封，富比乎陶、卫，世世称孤，与齐久存，又一计也。此两计者，显名厚实也，原公详计而审处一焉。 且吾闻之，规小节者不能成荣名，恶小耻者不能立大功。昔者管夷吾射桓公中其钩，篡也；遗公子纠不能死，怯也；束缚桎梏，辱也。若此三行者，世主不臣而乡里不通。乡使管子幽囚而不出，身死而不反於齐，则亦名不免为辱人贱行矣。臧获且羞与之同名矣，况世俗乎！故管子不耻身在縲绁之中而耻天下之不治，不耻不死公子纠而耻威之不信於诸侯，故兼三行之过而为五霸首，名高天下而光烛邻国。曹子为鲁将，三战三北，而亡地五百里。乡使曹子计不反顾，议不还踵，刎颈而死，则亦名不免为败军禽将矣。曹子弃三北之耻，而退与鲁君计。桓公朝天下，会诸侯，曹子以一剑之任，枝桓公之心於坛坫之上，颜色不变，辞气不悖，三战之所亡一朝而复之，天下震动，诸侯惊骇，威加吴、越。若此二士者，非不能成小廉而行小节也，以为杀身亡躯，绝世灭後，功名不立，非智也。故去感忿之怨，立终身之名；弃忿悁之节，定累世之功。是以业与三王争流，而名与天壤相弊也。原公择一而行之。 燕将见鲁连书，泣三日，犹豫不能自决。欲归燕，已有隙，恐诛；欲降齐，所杀虏於齐甚众，恐已降而後见辱。喟然叹曰：“与人刃我，宁自刃。”乃自杀。聊城乱，田单遂屠聊城。归而言鲁连，欲爵之。鲁连逃隐於海上，曰：“吾与富贵而诎於人，宁贫贱而轻世肆志焉。”
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I Wei, Chu and Yan attacked Qi: Wei took Pinglu, Chu took Qi's Nanyang, and Yan took Liaocheng. Analysis: the source of this item is perhaps the Shiji, Biographies of Lu Zhonglian and Zou Yang. But the only date in the text is "twenty-odd years after" Lord Xinling's theft of the tally to save Zhao, and the exact point in time is not known. Tian Dan, Lord Anping of Qi, led an army to besiege Liaocheng. Analysis: the source of this item is perhaps the Shiji, Biographies of Lu Zhonglian and Zou Yang. But the only date in the text is "twenty-odd years after" Lord Xinling's theft of the tally to save Zhao, and the exact point in time is not known. Chu and Wei gave up attacking Qi and planned a Vertical Alliance to attack Qin. Analysis: the source of this item is perhaps the Shiji, Biographies of Lu Zhonglian and Zou Yang. But the only date in the text is "twenty-odd years after" Lord Xinling's theft of the tally to save Zhao, and the exact point in time is not known. Shiji, Biographies of Lu Zhonglian and Zou Yang: It happened just then that the Prince of Wei, Wuji, seized Jin Bi's army to relieve Zhao and attacked the Qin army, and the Qin army withdrew. Thereupon Lord Pingyuan wished to enfeoff Lu Lian; Lu Lian declined three times and in the end would not accept. Lord Pingyuan then gave a banquet, and when the wine was flowing he rose, came forward and offered Lu Lian a thousand jin of gold for his long life. Lu Lian laughed and said: "What is prized in a gentleman of all under Heaven is that he removes troubles, resolves difficulties and settles disorders for others, and takes nothing for it. If he takes something, that is the business of merchants, and Lian cannot bring himself to do it." So he took leave of Lord Pingyuan and departed, and never saw him again as long as he lived. Twenty-odd years later, a general of Yan attacked and took Liaocheng. Someone of Liaocheng slandered him to Yan, and the general of Yan, fearing execution, held Liaocheng and did not dare return. Tian Dan of Qi attacked Liaocheng for more than a year; many of his soldiers died, yet Liaocheng did not fall. Lu Lian then wrote a letter, tied it to an arrow and shot it into the Fortress, to be delivered to the general of Yan. The letter said: "I have heard that the wise man does not turn his back on the hour and throw away advantage, the brave man does not shun death and destroy his name, and the loyal minister does not put himself first and his lord after. Now you are acting on a single morning's anger, with no thought for the King of Yan's being left without his minister: that is not loyalty. To be killed and lose Liaocheng, your might unproven against Qi: that is not courage. With your deeds undone and your name wiped out, and nothing for later ages to tell of: that is not wisdom. Men of these three kinds the rulers of the age do not take as ministers, and the persuaders do not record; therefore the wise man does not deliberate twice, and the brave man does not flinch from death. Now life and death, glory and disgrace, high and low, honour and baseness: this hour will not come again. I wish you to consider it carefully and not go along with the common run. "Moreover, Chu attacked Qi's Nanyang and Wei attacked Pinglu, yet Qi has no mind to turn south: it holds the harm of losing Nanyang to be small, not to compare with the great gain of winning Jibei, and so it has fixed its plan and deals with the matter accordingly. Now the men of Qin have sent down their troops and Wei dares not face east; the Horizontal Alliance with Qin is formed and the position of the state of Chu is in danger; Qi gives up Nanyang, cuts off its right-hand lands and settles Jibei: its plan is still to go through with it. And since Qi is set on deciding the matter at Liaocheng, do not deliberate again. Now Chu and Wei have both withdrawn from Qi, and the relief from Yan does not come. Against the whole strength of Qi, with no design from all under Heaven, holding out with Liaocheng in its exhaustion of a full year: your servant sees that you cannot succeed. Moreover, the state of Yan is in great disorder, ruler and ministers have lost their counsel, high and low are bewildered; Li Fu with a host of a hundred thousand was broken five times abroad, a state of ten thousand chariots was besieged by Zhao, its land pared away and its ruler in straits, the laughing-stock of all under Heaven. The state is exhausted and its troubles many, and the people have no one to turn to. Now you, with the people of worn-out Liao, hold off the whole strength of Qi: that is the defence of Mo Di. Eating men and cooking bones, and the soldiers have no thought of turning against you: those are the troops of Sun Bin. Your ability is seen by all under Heaven. Even so, if I were to plan for you, it would be better to bring your chariots and armour back whole and report to Yan. If the chariots and armour return whole to Yan, the King of Yan will surely rejoice; if you return in person whole to your state, the soldiers and people will greet you as a father and mother, your friends will bare their arms and speak of you to the age, and your deeds will be made plain. Above you will support an orphaned ruler in controlling the body of ministers; below you will nourish the hundred clans and furnish the persuaders; you will set the state right and change its customs, and your name and deeds can be established. Or if you have no mind for that, will you not abandon Yan, cast off the age and go east to Qi? Land would be carved out and a fief fixed for you, with wealth to match Tao and Wey; generation after generation you would call yourselves lords, enduring as long as Qi: that is another plan. These two plans bring an illustrious name and solid substance. I wish you to consider them carefully and to settle on one. "Moreover, I have heard that he who is scrupulous over small points cannot achieve a glorious name, and he who shrinks from small shames cannot establish great deeds. In former days Guan Yiwu shot at Duke Huan and hit the hook of his belt: that was usurpation; he abandoned Prince Jiu and could not die for him: that was cowardice; he was bound in fetters and shackles: that was disgrace. A man of these three conducts the rulers of the age do not take as minister, and his own village does not receive. Had Master Guan stayed shut in prison and never come out, died and never returned to Qi, his name too could not have escaped being that of a disgraced man of base conduct. Slaves and bondwomen would have been ashamed to share a name with him, how much more the common run of the age! But Master Guan was not ashamed to be in bonds, he was ashamed that all under Heaven was not in order; he was not ashamed not to have died for Prince Jiu, he was ashamed that his might was unproven among the Lords; and so, carrying the faults of three conducts, he became the first of the Five Hegemons, his name high in all under Heaven and his light shining on the neighbouring states. Master Cao, as general of Lu, fought three battles and was three times routed, and lost five hundred li of land. Had Master Cao not looked back in his counsels nor turned on his heel in his deliberations, but cut his throat and died, his name too could not have escaped being that of a defeated general, a captured commander. Master Cao put aside the shame of his three routs and withdrew to take counsel with the lord of Lu. When Duke Huan was receiving the homage of all under Heaven and assembling the Lords, Master Cao, trusting to a single sword, held it to Duke Huan's breast upon the altar mound; his colour did not change, his speech did not falter, and what three battles had lost he recovered in a single morning; all under Heaven was shaken, the Lords were struck with fear, and his might reached to Wu and Yue. These two gentlemen were not unable to achieve small scruples and carry out small points; they held that to be killed and lose one's body, to cut off one's line and destroy one's posterity, with no name or deed established, is not wisdom. Therefore they set aside the resentments of sudden anger and established a lifelong name; they cast off the points of indignant honour and fixed deeds for generations to come. Thus their achievements vie in the current with the Three Kings', and their names will wear out only with heaven and earth. I wish you to choose one of these and act on it." When the general of Yan saw Lu Lian's letter he wept for three days, wavering and unable to decide. He wished to return to Yan, but there was already a breach and he feared execution; he wished to surrender to Qi, but he had killed and captured very many of Qi's men and feared that after surrendering he would be humiliated. With a deep sigh he said: "Rather than let another put the blade to me, I will put it to myself." And he killed himself. Liaocheng fell into disorder, and Tian Dan then put Liaocheng to the sword. On his return he spoke of Lu Lian and wished to ennoble him. Lu Lian fled and hid himself by the sea, saying: "Rather than be rich and honoured and bend to others, I would be poor and lowly, make light of the age and follow my own will."
passages.no: The rescue of Zhao was in 257 BC (told under 256 BC, §4), so "twenty-odd years after" would fall in the 230s; but the Jijie on the passage cites Xu Guang, by the Table, placing Tian Dan's attack on Liaocheng ten-odd years after Changping (260 BC), that is in the 240s, and the Suoyin notes that the "thirty-odd years" of some texts is an error. The compiler enters the three items here with their date left open. The passage follows Lu Zhonglian's refusal to let Zhao honour Qin as Emperor during the siege of Handan; the relief of Zhao is told under 256 BC (§4). The Jijie cites Xu Guang: by the Table, Tian Dan's attack on Liaocheng is ten-odd years after Changping. The Suoyin: Xu Guang, following the Table, puts it ten-odd years after Changping; the reading "thirty-odd years" is wrong. The Zhengyi on Liaocheng: now a County of Bozhou, in the names of the Tang. 却死: the Suoyin: to avoid death. The Suoyin on Qi's Nanyang: Qi's lands north of the Huai and on the Si; on Pinglu: a town on the western border, and the Zhengyi: a County of Yanzhou in the names of the Tang; on Jibei: the land of Liaocheng. The Zhengyi: Qi has no mind to attack Chu and Wei to the south, holding the harm at Nanyang and Pinglu small beside the gain of Liaocheng, which it will surely attack. 衡秦之势成: the Suoyin: Qin and Qi were at peace at this time, hence the phrase. The Suoyin: Qi gives up the lands on the Si that Chu attacked, cuts off the right-hand land that Wei attacked, Pinglu, leaving it unrelieved, and bends its purpose to attacking Liaocheng and settling Jibei. 交退: the Suoyin: 交 is "both"; earlier Chu attacked Nanyang and Wei Pinglu; now both armies have withdrawn and Yan's relief does not come, so the position is perilous. The Jijie cites Xu Guang: this event is ten years from Changping. Li Fu's defeat by Zhao and the siege of Yan are told under 251 BC. The Zhengyi: as Mo Di defended Song and repulsed the Chu army. The Zhengyi: Sun Bin could so comfort his soldiers that they had no second thoughts. 资说士: the Suoyin: having nourished the people, he also furnishes the persuaders, aiming in the end at a strong state; Liu reads 说士 as 锐士, "crack troops", which is plausible but it is better to keep the character. 矫国更俗: the Suoyin: he wishes the general of Yan to return to Yan, set the state's affairs right and reform its corrupt customs. 亡意: the Suoyin: 亡 is read wu, "none": if you have no mind at all to return to Yan, then abandon Yan and go east to Qi. 陶、卫: the Suoyin: Yan Du's note on the Zhanguoce takes Tao as Tao Zhu Gong and Wey as Prince Jing of Wey, wrongly; Wang Shao: Wei Ran was enfeoffed at Tao and Lord Shang was surnamed Wey, and the comparison is with these. Neither is tagged, the names standing for the men. 称孤: 孤, "the orphan", is the self-designation of the ruler of a state; to call oneself so is to rule. 遗公子纠: the Suoyin: 遗 is to abandon, abandoning Prince Jiu to serve Xiaobai. The Zhengyi: Guan Zhong was Tutor to Prince Jiu, whom Lu killed; not following him in death was cowardice. 臧获: the Jijie cites the Fangyan: between Jing and the Huai, the sea and Mount Dai, Yan and Qi, a male slave is abused as 臧 and a female as 获. The Zhengyi: Duke Huan of Qi was the first to receive from King Xiang of Zhou the sacrificial meat of Kings Wen and Wu, the red bow and arrows and the great carriage, hence first of the Five Hegemons. 曹子: the Suoyin: the Lu general Cao Mei 曹昧, that is Cao Mo 曹沫. His three defeats and the covenant of Ke fall under Duke Zhuang of Lu, 681 BC. 枝桓公之心: the Suoyin: 枝 is 拟, to point at. Ivar the Boneless' commentary on the year: the attacks of Wei, Chu and Yan on Qi, Tian Dan's siege of Liaocheng, and Chu and Wei's turn from Qi to an alliance against Qin, each with the Biographies of Lu Zhonglian and Zou Yang adduced as the probable source, their date left open; and the passage itself, Lu Zhonglian's refusal of reward and his letter to the general of Yan in Liaocheng.

passages.title: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II
passages.zh: 无骨论点补充（以及辨析）二 晋阳叛秦，复归赵。 辨析：《史記》與漢簡皆作秦王政元年。 魏军夺取韩国管地。 辨析：此條出處不詳。
passages.en: Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis II Jinyang revolted against Qin and returned to Zhao. Analysis: the Shiji and the Han slips both place this in the first year of King Zheng of Qin. The Wei army seized Han's land of Guan. Analysis: the source of this item is not known.
passages.no: 漢簡: the compiler does not say which slips. 246 BC. The Basic Annals of the First Emperor: "In the first year Jinyang revolted; the general Meng Ao attacked and settled it." The item will be met under that year. Ivar the Boneless' second column: the revolt of Jinyang, which the sources put in the following year, and Wei's seizure of Han's Guan, of unknown source.

passages.title: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips
passages.zh: 《秦简牍合集》（一）睡虎地竹简 葉書：莊王三年，莊王死。
passages.en: Collected Qin Slips I: the Shuihudi bamboo slips Chronicle: Third year of King Zhuang. King Zhuang died.
passages.no: The third year of King Zhuangxiang of Qin, 247 BC, whom the Chronicle calls King Zhuang. The Basic Annals (§1) give the day: Bingwu of the fifth month. The entry for 247 BC in the Chronicle of the Shuihudi slips: the death of King Zhuang.

passages.title: Hujiacaochang Western Han slips: the Suiji (Annual Record)
passages.zh: 胡家草场西汉简牍《岁纪》 三年，泰上皇死。王齮將軍歸。
passages.en: Hujiacaochang Western Han slips: the Suiji (Annual Record) Third year. The Grand Supreme Emperor died. General Wang Yi returned.
passages.no: The third year of King Zhuangxiang, 247 BC. 泰上皇: King Zhuangxiang, under the title given him after his death, which the Suiji uses throughout (see 249 BC, excavated texts §3). 王齮將軍歸: Wang Yi, written 王龁 in the Basic Annals, which have him attacking Shangdang this year (§1, §2); his return from the campaign is recorded only here. The entry for 247 BC in the Suiji (Annual Record) of the Hujiacaochang slips: the death of the Grand Supreme Emperor, as it calls King Zhuangxiang, and the return of General Wang Yi.

passages.title: Shiji I: Basic Annals
passages.zh: 史记（一：本纪） 秦始皇本纪：年十三岁，庄襄王死，政代立为秦王。当是之时，秦地已并巴、蜀、汉中，越宛有郢，置南郡矣；北收上郡以东，有河东、太原、上党郡；东至荥阳，灭二周，置三川郡。吕不韦为相，封十万户，号曰文信侯。招致宾客游士，欲以并天下。李斯为舍人。蒙骜、王齮、麃公等为将军。王年少，初即位，委国事大臣。 晋阳反，元年，将军蒙骜击定之。
passages.en: Shiji I: Basic Annals Basic Annals of the First Emperor of Qin: When he was thirteen, King Zhuangxiang died, and Zheng took his place as King of Qin. At this time Qin's territory had already annexed Ba, Shu and Hanzhong, and, passing beyond Wan, held Ying, where Nan Commandery had been set up; in the north it had taken in Shang Commandery and the lands east of it, and held the Commanderies of Hedong, Taiyuan and Shangdang; in the east it reached Xingyang, having wiped out the two Zhou and set up Sanchuan Commandery. Lü Buwei was Chancellor, enfeoffed with a hundred thousand households and styled Marquis Wenxin. He drew retainers and travelling gentlemen to him, meaning by them to annex all under Heaven. Li Si was a household retainer. Meng Ao, Wang Yi, Lord Biao and others were Generals. The king was young and newly on the throne, and left the affairs of state to the great ministers. Jinyang revolted; in the first year the General Meng Ao attacked and settled it.
passages.no: 年十三岁: King Zhuangxiang died in 247 BC; Zheng's first year as king is this year, 246 BC. 二周: the Western and Eastern Zhou domains, extinguished in 256 and 249 BC (see those years). 舍人: the Jijie cites Wen Ying: the title of a petty officer in charge of the stables; or, retainers in attendance are called sheren. 王齮: the Jijie cites Xu Guang, one text 齕. The Suoyin: Meng Ao was a man of Qi, father of Meng Wu and grandfather of Meng Tian; Wang Yi is Wang He 王齕, who in King Zhao's forty-ninth year replaced the Grand Master Ling in attacking Zhao. The Zhengyi gives the reading of 齮 as yi (魚綺反); Liu Bozhuang reads it qi. 麃公: the Jijie cites Ying Shao, Biao is a Qin town; the Suoyin: probably the lord of the town of Biao, his surname and name lost to history; the Zhengyi: 麃 read biao (彼苗反), probably a County town of Qin, and a Grand Master is called 公 as in the Chu system. 246 BC. The Table (§2) and the Hereditary House of Zhao (§3) record the taking of Jinyang. The Basic Annals of the First Emperor at his accession: the extent of Qin at the start of the reign, Lü Buwei as Chancellor and Marquis Wenxin with Li Si in his household, the generals Meng Ao, Wang Yi and Lord Biao, and in the first year the revolt of Jinyang and Meng Ao's settling of it.

passages.title: c. 1260 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1260年 盘庚去世后，其弟小辛、小乙先后即位；到了小乙之子武丁即位时，中商文化正式过渡为殷墟一期。 朱开沟族群的主体离开了鄂尔多斯地区，南迁陕北并对关中地区的商文化产生了一定影响；朱开沟的典型器物——蛇纹鬲，在耀县北村、扶风壹家堡等商文化遗址中均有出土。部分学者视其为方方。 武丁在位时期，也对渭水流域的方国、部族进行了一系列征伐；自中商以来，关中地区的商文化越来越具有地方特色，武丁派遣军队征伐犬方，或是商王朝尝试重新加强对西土控制力的一个缩影。 甲骨卜辞中的“周方”，常被认为是后来建立周朝的周人；商王武丁在位前期，相当于考古意义上的殷墟一期，漆水河流域出现了郑家坡文化，其遗址与周原地区的京当型商文化交错分布。与此同时，孙家类型出现在彬州、旬邑一带，其文化面貌近似郑家坡文化，两者均有被学者视为先周文化的说法。
passages.en: c. 1260 BC After Pan Geng's death his younger brothers Xiao Xin and Xiao Yi succeeded in turn; by the accession of Xiao Yi's son Wu Ding, the Middle Shang culture had formally passed into Yinxu Phase I. The main body of the Zhukaigou people left the Ordos region and moved south into northern Shaanxi, exerting a certain influence on the Shang culture of the Guanzhong region; the characteristic Zhukaigou vessel, the snake-pattern li, has been unearthed at Shang-culture sites such as Beicun in Yao County and Yijiabu in Fufeng. Some scholars take them to be the Fang. During Wu Ding's reign a series of campaigns was also made against the fang states and tribes of the Wei River valley; since the Middle Shang the Shang culture of Guanzhong had taken on an ever more local character, and Wu Ding's dispatch of armies against the Quanfang may be an epitome of the Shang court's attempt to tighten its hold on the western lands once more. The "Zhoufang" of the oracle-bone inscriptions is generally taken to be the Zhou people who later founded the Zhou dynasty. In the earlier part of King Wu Ding's reign, corresponding in archaeological terms to Yinxu Phase I, the Zhengjiapo culture appeared in the valley of the Qishui River, its sites interspersed with those of the Jingdang-type Shang culture of the Zhouyuan region. At the same time the Sunjia type appeared around Binzhou and Xunyi, close in its cultural character to the Zhengjiapo culture; both have been regarded by scholars as Proto-Zhou culture.
passages.no: The Shang in the time of Wu Ding, about 1260 BC: the passage from the Middle Shang to Yinxu Phase I, the Zhukaigou people's move from the Ordos into Shaanxi, Wu Ding's campaigns in the Wei valley, and the first appearance of the cultures taken to be the Zhou.

passages.title: c. 1260–1235 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1260年—公元前1235年 甲骨卜辞显示，商王武丁在统治的早期，逐一征服亘方、缶、基方、湔方等国，实现了对晋南地区的控制。 考古表明，进入晚商殷墟一期后，桓台史家遗址的土著文化因素被商文化所取代；殷墟甲骨卜辞中有一位叫做子画的王族成员，于武丁初年被封在东方，其封地也被称为画。部分学者认为子画受封是为了镇守商王朝新征服的土地。 武丁在征讨晋南地区的方国后，继而与雀征讨沚方与辔方；按卜辞的方位描述，这两者皆与𢀛方相邻。戉在武丁统治的早期发动过叛乱，同样为雀所征讨。沚方在被商王朝征服后，其首领沚馘成为了武丁的臣属，替武丁守卫西疆，又出兵协助武丁讨伐巴方，并镇压东部的谭国叛乱。 在此之后，武丁又发动大军击败了𢀛方的盟友土方。武丁的配偶妇好是征伐土方的统帅之一，甲骨卜辞有“呼妇好伐土方”的记录；妇好也在武丁统治的早期有过征伐夷方、巴方等国的记载。武丁的另外一位配偶妇耕也曾出征龙方。 在入侵商朝的方国中，大多数的方国侵扰地点分布虽广，但每次入侵的规模都比较小；然𢀛方则不然，不仅入侵频率高，造成的破坏也非常大，时常联合东面的土方一同进攻商王朝。部分学者认为𢀛方与考古意义上的石楼类型遗存有关，与其在中商时期便不断向晋中地区扩展势力或有一定联系。 武丁在击败土方之后，开始对𢀛方展开攻势，然而在征伐的卜辞记载中，妇好并未见载；部分学者据此判断妇好去世于征土方之后，征𢀛方之前。 在考古层面上，殷墟一期时汉江地区的商文化趋于消失，但产自南方的青铜资源仍然大量涌现于殷商统治中心，这说明商王朝仍然致力于维持对南方的部族进行间接控制；为了确保“铜路”的安全通畅，武丁在位时发起了南征行动，对虎方、方进行了讨伐。殷墟一期卜辞中有武丁和望乘征方的内容，此后其在卜辞记录中未再见载，推测已被消灭。
passages.en: c. 1260–1235 BC The oracle-bone inscriptions show that King Wu Ding of Shang, in the early part of his reign, conquered one after another the Gengfang, Fou, the Jifang, the Jianfang and other states, and gained control of the southern Shanxi region. Archaeology shows that with the Late Shang Yinxu Phase I the indigenous cultural elements at the Shijia site in Huantai were replaced by Shang culture; the Yinxu oracle-bone inscriptions have a member of the royal clan called Zi Hua, enfeoffed in the east in Wu Ding's first years, whose fief was likewise called Hua. Some scholars hold that Zi Hua was enfeoffed to guard the land the Shang court had newly conquered. After his campaigns against the fang states of southern Shanxi, Wu Ding went on, with Que, to campaign against the Zhifang and the Peifang; by the inscriptions' description of their position, both bordered the Qiongfang. Yue rose in revolt early in Wu Ding's reign and was likewise put down by Que. After the Zhifang was conquered by the Shang court, its chief Zhi Guo became Wu Ding's vassal, guarding the western frontier for him, sending troops to help him attack the Bafang, and putting down the revolt of the state of Tan in the east. After this Wu Ding raised a great army and defeated the Qiongfang's ally, the Tufang. Wu Ding's consort Fu Zi was one of the commanders of the campaign against the Tufang; the oracle-bone inscriptions record "calling on Fu Zi to attack the Tufang". Fu Zi is also recorded, in the early part of Wu Ding's reign, as campaigning against the Yifang, the Bafang and other states. Another consort of Wu Ding, Fu Geng, also went out against the Longfang. Of the fang states that raided the Shang, most raided at widely scattered points but on a small scale each time; not so the Qiongfang, whose raids were frequent and highly destructive, and which often joined with the Tufang to its east in attacking the Shang court. Some scholars connect the Qiongfang with the remains of the Shilou type in archaeological terms, which may have some bearing on its steady extension of its power into the central Shanxi region from the Middle Shang period onward. After defeating the Tufang, Wu Ding opened his offensive against the Qiongfang; but Fu Zi does not appear in the inscriptions recording that campaign, and some scholars conclude from this that she died after the campaign against the Tufang and before that against the Qiongfang. On the archaeological level, in Yinxu Phase I the Shang culture of the Hanjiang region was fading away, yet bronze metals from the south still flowed in quantity into the centre of Yin Shang rule, which shows that the Shang court was still at pains to keep indirect control over the peoples of the south; to secure the "copper road", Wu Ding in his reign launched a southern expedition and attacked the Hufang and the Moufang. The Yinxu Phase I inscriptions record Wu Ding and Wang Cheng campaigning against the Moufang, which thereafter appears no more in the inscriptions and is presumed to have been destroyed.
passages.no: 𢀛方: the graph is 工 over 口 (𢀛), which the site's font lacks, so it is drawn. The state is read Qiongfang; some transcribe it 工方. 呼妇好伐土方: an oracle-bone formula, 呼 "call on" being the verb by which the king commands a subordinate to act; the inscription is the divination charge, not a narrative. 方: the graph, 中 with a doubled vertical stroke, has no Unicode code point and is drawn; read mou. Wu Ding's wars as the oracle-bone inscriptions and archaeology show them, from about 1260 to 1235 BC: the conquest of southern Shanxi, Zi Hua's fief in the east, the campaigns of Que, Zhi Guo, Fu Zi and Fu Geng in the west, the defeat of the Tufang and the offensive against the Qiongfang, and the southern expedition that secured the copper road against the Hufang and the Moufang.

passages.title: c. 1260–1235 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前1260年—公元前1235年 约公元前1260年： 魏营子文化承接夏家店下层文化发展。 围坊三期文化发展形成围坊类型。 约公元前1250年： 庙台子类型兴起，与大城墩类型、吴城文化等文化被不同学者认做为虎方；路家河文化、石地坝文化与周梁玉桥文化兴起。
passages.en: c. 1260–1235 BC: archaeological appearances c. 1260 BC: The Weiyingzi culture developed in succession to the Lower Xiajiadian culture. The Weifang Phase III culture developed into the Weifang type. c. 1250 BC: The Miaotaizi type arose; it, the Dachengdun type, the Wucheng culture and other cultures have each been taken by different scholars to be the Hufang. The Lujiahe culture, the Shidiba culture and the Zhouliangyuqiao culture arose.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, under their own dates: in the north-east, about 1260 BC, the Weiyingzi culture succeeding the Lower Xiajiadian, and the Weifang type formed within the Weifang Phase III culture; on the middle Yangtze, about 1250 BC, the Miaotaizi type, one of the cultures identified with the Hufang, and the Lujiahe, Shidiba and Zhouliangyuqiao cultures.

passages.title: c. 1235 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1235年 晚商文化进入殷墟二期，其早段大致与武丁执政的中晚期相当。 从殷墟二期开始，被众多学者视为“羌方文化”的刘家文化开始强势崛起；其族群向东进入周原地区，加速了京当型商文化的衰退。 李家崖文化与西岔文化兴起；部分学者据《周易》中的记载与清涧李家崖遗址内出土的陶文推断鬼方或是李家崖文化。 晚商文化大城墩类型在盘庚迁殷后逐渐走向衰亡；大城墩四期文化兴起。 魏营子文化发展形成小白阳类型。 吴城文化承接石灰山文化发展。
passages.en: c. 1235 BC Late Shang culture entered Yinxu Phase II, whose early stage corresponds roughly to the middle and later part of Wu Ding's reign. From Yinxu Phase II the Liujia culture, regarded by many scholars as the "Qiangfang culture", began a strong rise; its people moved east into the Zhouyuan region, hastening the decline of the Jingdang-type Shang culture. The Lijiaya culture and the Xicha culture arose; some scholars, from the record in the Zhouyi and the pottery inscriptions unearthed at the Lijiaya site in Qingjian, infer that the Guifang may be the Lijiaya culture. The Dachengdun type of Late Shang culture gradually went into decline and died out after Pan Geng's move to Yin; the Dachengdun Phase IV culture arose. As the Weiyingzi culture developed, the Xiaobaiyang type took shape within it. The Wucheng culture took over from the Shihuishan culture and carried its development forward.
passages.no: 《周易》: the lines on Gaozong's campaign against the Guifang, in the hexagrams Jiji 既济 (third line) and Weiji 未济 (fourth line); Gaozong is Wu Ding. The Late Shang about 1235 BC, at the opening of Yinxu Phase II: the rise of the Liujia culture and its people's move into the Zhouyuan, the Lijiaya and Xicha cultures and the question of the Guifang, the decline of the Dachengdun type, the Xiaobaiyang type, and the Wucheng culture.

passages.title: c. 1230–1150 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1230年—公元前1150年 商王朝征伐𢀛方的战争时断时续，旷日持久，直到武丁在位的末期，仍有卜问“擒𢀛方”一类的卜辞，此后不再见于卜辞记录；在考古方面，石楼类型的物质遗存在殷墟二期遭受重创，柳林高红遗址内的大型夯土建筑废弃，呈现出萎靡不振的状态，这些现象似乎可以和武丁征𢀛方联系起来。 殷墟二期以后，晋中地区出现了一些规格较高的商文化贵族墓葬，其中灵石旌介与浮山桥北的商墓中出土的青铜器铭文经辨析应为属于商王辖下的丙国和先国；部分学者认为商王分封丙、先二国是为了巩固征伐𢀛方的胜利果实，以求西北稳定。 太子孝己先于武丁去世。在战国时期的文献中，他被描述成孝子的典范，汉代以后的文献进一步丰富了孝己的故事；在考古方面，孝己在武丁前中期的卜辞被称为“小王”，到了武丁统治的晚期，孝己去世，其称呼添加了日名，祭祀时称“小王己”。 根据传世文献记载，武丁在位长达五十九年；武丁晚年准备立小儿子祖甲为继承人，然而祖甲却认为兄长祖庚理当继位，所以违背父命，逃匿民间。 武丁驾崩后，祖庚顺利继承王位，在位七年，死后传位于祖甲；近代以来，学者们通过对殷墟中甲骨卜辞的整理与分析，发现祖甲在位时进行了一系列的改革，如建立周祭制度、简化祀典、裁减贞人等，强化了王权，确保了商王朝的政治稳定。 在殷墟二期晚段，商文化基本退出了关中西部。
passages.en: c. 1230–1150 BC The Shang court's war against the Qiongfang went on by fits and starts and dragged out over many years; down to the last years of Wu Ding's reign there are still inscriptions divining about "capturing the Qiongfang" and the like, after which it is no longer seen in the inscriptional record. On the archaeological side, the material remains of the Shilou type suffered heavy damage in Yinxu Phase II: the large rammed-earth buildings at the Gaohong site in Liulin were abandoned, and the type shows a state of decline. These phenomena, it seems, can be connected with Wu Ding's campaigns against the Qiongfang. After Yinxu Phase II a number of aristocratic tombs of Shang culture, of fairly high rank, appeared in the central Shanxi region; among them, the inscriptions on the bronzes from the Shang tombs at Jingjie in Lingshi and Qiaobei in Fushan have been shown on analysis to belong to the states of Bing and Xian, under the Shang king. Some scholars hold that the Shang king enfeoffed the two states of Bing and Xian to secure the fruits of the victory over the Qiongfang and so keep the north-west stable. The Heir Apparent Xiao Ji died before Wu Ding. In the texts of the Warring States period he is described as the model of a filial son, and texts from the Han onward enriched the story of Xiao Ji further. On the archaeological side, Xiao Ji is called the "Junior King" in the inscriptions of the early and middle part of Wu Ding's reign; in the late part of Wu Ding's reign Xiao Ji died, a day name was added to his style, and in sacrifice he is called "Junior King Ji". According to the transmitted texts, Wu Ding was on the throne for as long as fifty-nine years. In his last years Wu Ding prepared to make his youngest son Zu Jia his successor; but Zu Jia held that his elder brother Zu Geng ought by right to succeed, and so, going against his father's command, he fled and hid among the people. After Wu Ding's death Zu Geng succeeded to the throne without difficulty; he reigned seven years and at his death passed the throne to Zu Jia. In modern times scholars, by ordering and analysing the oracle-bone inscriptions from Yinxu, have found that Zu Jia carried out a series of reforms in his reign, such as establishing the cyclical sacrifice system, simplifying the sacrificial canon and reducing the number of diviners, which strengthened the royal power and secured the political stability of the Shang court. In the late stage of Yinxu Phase II, Shang culture for the most part withdrew from the western Guanzhong.
passages.no: 传世文献: the Documents, "Wuyi" 无逸, gives Gaozong fifty-nine years on the throne; Zu Jia's flight among the people is Ma Rong's reading of the same chapter. From Wu Ding's last wars to the reforms of Zu Jia, about 1230 to 1150 BC: the end of the war with the Qiongfang and the decline of the Shilou type, the states of Bing and Xian in central Shanxi, the Heir Apparent Xiao Ji, the succession of Zu Geng and Zu Jia, and the withdrawal of Shang culture from the western Guanzhong.

passages.title: c. 1230–1150 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前1230年—公元前1150年 约公元前1200年： 美沙里类型下限；韩国中西部进入可乐洞、欣岩里、驿三洞阶段。同时，虎谷洞二期文化兴起。 寺洼文化徐家碾遗址出现。
passages.en: c. 1230–1150 BC: archaeological appearances c. 1200 BC: The Misa-ri type reached its lower limit; central-western South Korea entered the stage of Garak-dong, Heunam-ri and Yeoksam-dong. At the same time the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture arose. The Xujianian site of the Siwa culture appeared.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, about 1200 BC: in Korea, the end of the Misa-ri type, the stage of Garak-dong, Heunam-ri and Yeoksam-dong and the rise of the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture; and the Xujianian site of the Siwa culture.

passages.title: c. 1150 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1150年 祖甲去世后，其子廪辛、康丁先后继位。而与相对和平的祖甲时期不同，涉及战争的卜辞内容在廪辛、康丁时期重新变得频繁起来。到祖甲之子廪辛即位时，日益壮大的羌方已开始对商王朝的西土造成了严重的威胁；随着刘家文化的强势东进，不仅是商文化退出了关中西部，刚有发展势头的郑家坡文化也受到了冲击。 考古表明，殷墟二、三期之交，晚期朱开沟文化与李家崖文化因素向南传播，与关中文化交融形成了淳化地区的枣树沟脑类型和黑豆嘴类型遗存。部分学者认为这或许与廪辛、康丁卜辞中再度壮大的方有所关联；在祖甲时期的卜辞中，涉及战争的内容虽然很少，但几乎都和方的侵扰相关。到了廪辛、康丁在位时期，其侵扰亦频次加剧。也有学者主张将其与传世文献中逼迫周太王从豳地南迁至岐周的“薰鬻戎狄”对应起来。 青海青铜文化进入中期晚段；张家园上层文化兴起。
passages.en: c. 1150 BC After Zu Jia's death his sons Lin Xin and Kang Ding succeeded in turn. Unlike the relatively peaceful time of Zu Jia, inscriptions concerned with war became frequent again under Lin Xin and Kang Ding. By the accession of Zu Jia's son Lin Xin, the ever-growing Qiangfang had begun to pose a serious threat to the western lands of the Shang court; with the strong eastward advance of the Liujia culture, not only did Shang culture withdraw from the western Guanzhong, but the Zhengjiapo culture, which had only just begun to gather momentum, was hit as well. Archaeology shows that at the turn from Yinxu Phase II to Phase III, elements of the late Zhukaigou culture and the Lijiaya culture spread south and, blending with the cultures of Guanzhong, formed the remains of the Zaoshugounao type and the Heidouzui type in the Chunhua region. Some scholars think this may be connected with the Fang, grown strong once more in the inscriptions of Lin Xin and Kang Ding; in the inscriptions of Zu Jia's time what concerns war is very little, yet nearly all of it has to do with the raids of the Fang. By the reigns of Lin Xin and Kang Ding its raids, too, had grown more frequent. Other scholars propose to identify it with the "Xunyu Rong and Di" of the transmitted texts, who forced King Tai of Zhou to move south from Bin to Qi Zhou. The Bronze Age cultures of Qinghai entered the late stage of their middle period; the Upper Zhangjiayuan culture arose.
passages.no: 薰鬻戎狄: the Basic Annals of Zhou have the 薰育戎狄 attack Gugong Danfu, who is King Tai; the Mencius writes 獯鬻. The reigns of Lin Xin and Kang Ding, about 1150 BC: the Qiangfang's threat to the western lands and the eastward advance of the Liujia culture, the Zaoshugounao and Heidouzui types of the Chunhua region and the question of the Fang and the Xunyu, and the Bronze Age cultures of Qinghai and the Upper Zhangjiayuan culture.

passages.title: c. 1150–1088 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1150年—公元前1088年 三期卜辞大部分与羌方交战的内容都属于廪辛之弟康丁统治时期；与武丁时期不同，康丁时期的卜辞少见甚至不见选将和登人聚众，反而多见“戍”与“行”投入战斗，这反映此时的军队已有较为固定的编制。除此之外，卜辞中还有康丁发动附属部族以及方国军队征伐羌方的记录。 从康丁对羌方作战之前的卜问内容来看，不乏其对作战方略的详细考虑；另一方面，这些卜辞也反映了羌方侵袭的严重性，以至于康丁要谨慎行事，并多次征调戍军、臣属部族和方国增援西土。除羌方以外，康丁还要应对来自方方的侵扰，但面对方的侵扰，商王朝的手段以防御为主，这可能与当时的首要打击目标并非方而是羌方有关。 除了应对羌方和方，康丁在位时还征讨过东南部的危方；这一时期，西部的虘方、辔方、絴方、兹方也改变了自武丁征伐后的友好态度，转而与商朝为敌，康丁未能将他们重新征服。 康丁去世后，其子武乙即位；在康丁时入寇的西部方国中，辔方放弃敌对，转而臣服商王朝，虘方和兹方不见于武乙时期的卜辞，具体情况不明，羌方和絴方在武乙卜辞中各有一条被商军征讨的记录，其后絴方表示臣服。 武乙在位时期另一个比较重要的事件，是姬周族群的迁徙；根据传世文献记载，周人的先公——古公亶父与武乙所处年代大致相当，受“薰鬻戎狄”所迫，率领部众从豳地南迁至岐山脚下的周原，并在抵达后迎娶姜姓之女。亶父带领民众革除戎俗，并开垦荒地、建造城郭，又设置五官有司，完善政治制度，使周人日渐强大。后世亦追尊亶父为太王。 考古表明，殷墟二、三期之交，分布于泾河中上游的碾子坡类型和孙家类型遗存向南传播，与漆水河流域的郑家坡文化融合。郑家坡文化于是得以迅速扩张，并与刘家文化因素趋同发展。至于豳地原有的孙家类型则为断泾二期所取代。 《史记·周本纪》称周太王有三个儿子，长子太伯、次子仲雍、少子季历，其中季历是太王的正妃太姜所生；《列女传》则认为太伯、仲雍、季历三兄弟的生母都是太姜。季历娶太任为妻，生子昌，即是后来的周文王。 按《史记》的记载，太王欲立季历为储君，以传位于昌，于是太伯和仲雍主动出奔至南方的蛮夷之地，并以“句吴”为号，建立吴国；部分学者认为太伯和仲雍并没有逃到南方的蛮夷之地，而是统帅部分的周族，在山西的平陆建立了虞国，以筹划翦灭殷商。另一批学者则不认同这种观点，并主张太伯、仲雍最初立国的地点在江西赣江流域，在西周初改封到江苏宁镇地区，其分支则被迁回中原，另封虞国。 部分学者指出，虽然卜辞中并没有商周的直接冲突的记录，但仍然能找到一些“间接证据”，如武乙曾征伐过西部的召方，或在西周初年召公奭的采邑召城，或在更北部的絴方、方方附近。 除了应对西部敌对方国的侵扰外，本阶段的商王朝还征伐过徐、淮地区的夷方；这些军事行动在规模上虽不如帝辛时的征战，但也可被视作商王朝重新将战略重心转向东方的前兆。 除此之外，鲁北地区也是此时商王朝在东部用兵的重点区域；考古表明，殷墟三期晚段，鲁北地区的珍珠门文化分布范围有所退缩，商文化则向东扩展到了弥河的流域，以青州苏埠屯墓葬群为典型代表。部分学者推测，该地便是传世文献所载的蒲姑国。 在包含鲁北和沧州东部地区的渤海沿岸，横跨二百五十公里的范围内发现了十多个盐业聚落群，每个聚落群由十几处至几十处制盐作坊组成，规模宏大；部分学者认为该阶段的商王朝经略东部地区、开辟水陆通道，很可能是为了控制鲁北海盐和保障长江下游的铜、锡原料顺利北运。可见，晚商三期的商王朝经略重点转向东方，应该亦有出于对经济效益的考量。 武乙在西狩时“雷暴震死”；部分学者认为这可能与其西征召方失利有关。此后，其子文丁继位。 尽管卜辞显示康丁、武乙这两代商王在抗击西部的敌对方国的战争中取得了一定成果，但在考古层面上，却并未发现有商文化据点随着这些军事胜利而重新出现在西安以西；晋中地区遗址的商文化因素亦在殷墟三期以后逐渐消退，石楼类型的影响力则重新加强，正是在此时期，周人开始扩展势力范围。 考古表明，先周文化因素在殷墟三期后出现于晋陕高原的众多遗址中，甚至传播到了晋中盆地。部分学者认为此种现象可能与季历征伐戎狄相关；季历在渭河沿线用兵，传世文献中只有攻灭毕程氏一则记录。季历其他见载的征伐行动，基本上都是针对晋陕高原的戎狄部族。 文丁在位的第二年，季历继续征伐狄戎，以鬼戎为踏板讨伐燕京戎，但以失败告终。隔年，季历又伐余无之戎，获得胜利，被文丁命为牧师；接下来的数年内，季历称王，反复在山西地区讨伐戎狄，终让商王朝感到了威胁，被文丁囚禁而死。
passages.en: c. 1150–1088 BC Most of what the Yinxu Phase III inscriptions have on fighting with the Qiangfang belongs to the reign of Kang Ding, younger brother of Lin Xin; unlike those of Wu Ding's time, the inscriptions of Kang Ding's time seldom or never show the choosing of commanders and the levying and mustering of men, and show instead, again and again, the "garrisons" and the "columns" being sent into battle, which reflects an army that by now had a fairly fixed organisation. Besides this, the inscriptions also record Kang Ding calling out dependent tribes and the armies of fang states to attack the Qiangfang. To judge from what Kang Ding divined about before fighting the Qiangfang, there was no lack of detailed thought on his part about the plan of campaign; on the other hand, these inscriptions also reflect how serious the Qiangfang's raids were, so much so that Kang Ding had to act with caution, and many times called up garrison troops, subject tribes and fang states to reinforce the western lands. Besides the Qiangfang, Kang Ding also had to deal with the raids of the Fang; but in the face of the Fang's raids the measures of the Shang court were mainly defensive, which may be because the chief target at the time was not the Fang but the Qiangfang. Besides dealing with the Qiangfang and the Fang, Kang Ding in his reign also campaigned against the Weifang in the south-east; in this period the Cuofang, the Peifang, the Xiangfang and the Zifang in the west also gave up the friendly attitude they had kept since Wu Ding's campaigns and turned against the Shang, and Kang Ding was unable to conquer them again. After Kang Ding's death his son Wu Yi came to the throne; of the western fang states that had raided in Kang Ding's time, the Peifang gave up its hostility and submitted to the Shang court; the Cuofang and the Zifang are not seen in the inscriptions of Wu Yi's time, and what became of them is not known; the Qiangfang and the Xiangfang each have one record in Wu Yi's inscriptions of being attacked by the Shang army, after which the Xiangfang declared its submission. Another event of some importance in Wu Yi's reign was the migration of the Ji Zhou people; according to the transmitted texts, the Zhou people's former lord Gugong Danfu, who lived at roughly the same time as Wu Yi, was pressed by the "Xunyu Rong and Di" and led his people south from Bin to the Zhouyuan at the foot of Qishan, and after arriving took to wife a woman of the Jiang surname. Danfu led the people in doing away with Rong customs, opened up waste land and built Fortresses and outer walls, and set up the five offices with their officers, bringing the system of government to completion, so that the Zhou people grew stronger day by day. Later ages also honoured Danfu posthumously as King Tai. Archaeology shows that at the turn from Yinxu Phase II to Phase III the remains of the Nianzipo type and the Sunjia type, distributed on the middle and upper reaches of Jing River, spread south and merged with the Zhengjiapo culture of the Qishui River valley. The Zhengjiapo culture was thereby able to expand rapidly, and developed in convergence with elements of the Liujia culture. As for the Sunjia type that had been in Bin, it was replaced by Duanjing Phase II. The Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says that King Tai of Zhou had three sons, the eldest Taibo, the second Zhongyong and the youngest Jili, of whom Jili was born of King Tai's principal consort Tai Jiang; the Lienüzhuan, however, holds that Tai Jiang was the mother of all three brothers, Taibo, Zhongyong and Jili. Jili took Tai Ren to wife, and she bore him a son, Chang, who was the later King Wen of Zhou. By the account of the Shiji, King Tai wished to make Jili his heir so that the throne might pass to Chang, and so Taibo and Zhongyong of their own accord fled to the lands of the barbarians in the south, took "Gouwu" as their style, and founded the state of Wu; some scholars hold that Taibo and Zhongyong did not flee to the lands of the barbarians in the south at all, but led a part of the Zhou people and founded the state of Yu at Pinglu in Shanxi, in order to plan the destruction of Yin Shang. Another group of scholars does not accept this view, and maintains that the place where Taibo and Zhongyong first founded their state was in the Ganjiang valley in Jiangxi, that at the beginning of the Western Zhou they were re-enfeoffed in the Ning–Zhen region of Jiangsu, and that a branch of them was moved back to the Central Plains and separately enfeoffed as the state of Yu. Some scholars point out that although the inscriptions have no record of direct conflict between Shang and Zhou, some "indirect evidence" can still be found: Wu Yi, for instance, campaigned against the Shaofang of the west, which lay either at Shao Fortress, the fief of Shi, Duke of Shao, in the first years of the Western Zhou, or further north, near the Xiangfang and the Fang. Besides dealing with the raids of the hostile fang states of the west, the Shang court in this stage also campaigned against the Yifang of the Xu and Huai region; these operations did not match in scale the campaigns of Di Xin's time, but they can still be seen as a foreshadowing of the Shang court's turning the weight of its strategy to the east once more. Besides this, the northern Shandong region too was a chief area of the Shang court's use of arms in the east at this time; archaeology shows that in the late stage of Yinxu Phase III the range of the Zhenzhumen culture in northern Shandong shrank somewhat, while Shang culture extended east as far as the Mi River valley, of which the Subutun cemetery at Qingzhou is the typical example. Some scholars conjecture that this place is the state of Pugu recorded in the transmitted texts. Along the Bohai coast, taking in northern Shandong and the eastern part of the Cangzhou region, more than ten clusters of salt-making settlements have been found over a stretch of two hundred and fifty kilometres, each cluster made up of from a dozen or so to several dozen salt workshops, on a grand scale; some scholars hold that the Shang court's management of the east in this stage, and its opening of routes by water and land, were very probably meant to control the sea salt of northern Shandong and to keep the copper and tin of the lower Yangtze moving north without hindrance. It can be seen that when the Shang court of Late Shang Phase III turned the weight of its effort to the east, considerations of economic gain must also have played a part. Wu Yi, on a hunt in the west, was "struck dead in a thunderstorm"; some scholars think this may be connected with the failure of his western campaign against the Shaofang. After this his son Wen Ding succeeded to the throne. Although the inscriptions show that Kang Ding and Wu Yi, two generations of Shang kings, had some success in their wars against the hostile fang states of the west, on the archaeological level no strongholds of Shang culture are found reappearing west of Xi'an in the wake of these victories; the Shang cultural elements at the sites of the central Shanxi region likewise faded away by degrees after Yinxu Phase III, while the influence of the Shilou type grew strong again; and it was in just this period that the Zhou people began to extend their sphere of power. Archaeology shows that after Yinxu Phase III elements of Proto-Zhou culture appear at many sites on the Shanxi–Shaanxi plateau, and spread even as far as the central Shanxi basin. Some scholars think this may be connected with Jili's campaigns against the Rong and Di; of Jili's use of arms along Wei River the transmitted texts have only one record, the destruction of the Bicheng clan. Jili's other recorded campaigns were nearly all directed against the Rong and Di tribes of the Shanxi–Shaanxi plateau. In the second year of Wen Ding's reign Jili went on with his campaigns against the Di and Rong; using the Gui Rong as a stepping-stone he attacked the Yanjing Rong, but this ended in defeat. Two years later Jili attacked the Rong of Yuwu as well and was victorious, and was appointed mushi by Wen Ding; in the years that followed Jili took the title of King and campaigned again and again against the Rong and Di in the Shanxi region, until at last the Shang court felt threatened, and he was imprisoned by Wen Ding and died.
passages.no: 列女传: the Biographies of Exemplary Women, compiled by Liu Xiang of the Western Han. 帝辛: the last king of Shang, the Zhou 纣 of the later texts. 雷暴震死: the Basic Annals of Yin have 武乙猎于河渭之间，暴雷，武乙震死. 牧师: the Bamboo Annals, where Wen Ding is Tai Ding, have under his second year 周人伐燕京之戎，周师大败 and under his fourth 周人伐余无之戎，克之。周王季命为殷牧师. The reigns of Kang Ding, Wu Yi and Wen Ding, about 1150 to 1088 BC: the wars with the Qiangfang and the other fang states of the west; the move of the Zhou under Gugong Danfu from Bin to the Zhouyuan, and the accounts of Taibo and Zhongyong; the Shang court's turn to the east and the salt-making settlements of the Bohai coast; and Jili's campaigns against the Rong and Di, down to his imprisonment and death under Wen Ding.

passages.title: c. 1150–1088 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前1150年—公元前1088年 约公元前1100年： 寺洼文化进入中期一段，发展形成九站类型；寺洼山类型下限。 双房文化、新城子文化承接于家上层文化与马城子文化发展。 新岩里二期文化与金滩里青铜时代一期文化兴起。 虎谷洞三期文化承接虎谷洞二期文化发展。 三星堆四期文化承接三星堆文化发展。 辛店文化进入晚期。
