passages.en: c. 1150–1088 BC: archaeological appearances c. 1100 BC: The Siwa culture entered the first stage of its middle period, and as it developed the Jiuzhan type took shape within it; the Siwashan type reached its lower limit. The Shuangfang culture and the Xinchengzi culture took over from the Upper Yujia culture and the Machengzi culture and carried their development forward. The Sinam-ri Phase II culture and the Geumtan-ri Bronze Age Phase I culture arose. The Beomui-guseok Phase III culture took over from the Beomui-guseok Phase II culture and carried its development forward. The Sanxingdui Phase IV culture took over from the Sanxingdui culture and carried its development forward. The Xindian culture entered its late period.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, about 1100 BC: the Jiuzhan type of the Siwa culture; the Shuangfang and Xinchengzi cultures; in Korea, the Sinam-ri Phase II, Geumtan-ri Bronze Age Phase I and Beomui-guseok Phase III cultures; the Sanxingdui Phase IV culture; and the late period of the Xindian culture.

passages.title: c. 1088–1046 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1088年—公元前1046年 周王季历遇害后，其子昌继任周国君主，即周文王。商王文丁也在不久后去世，其子帝乙即位，而晚商亦进入了最后一期：殷墟四期。 古本《竹书纪年》记载：“帝乙处殷，二年，周人伐商。”部分学者认为，这是季历被杀后商周矛盾激化的表现；至于周人此次伐商的结果，则因周人力量不足而不可能取得成功。于是受挫后的周文王重新检讨了内外政策，转而与殷商和好，并致力于扭转力量对比。 就考古层面而言，进入殷墟四期后，商文化一方面在东部地区繁荣发展，另一方面则在西部地区日渐式微；在郑家坡文化与刘家文化融合形成了岐、丰地区的晚期先周文化后，原本与商文化联系紧密的晋中地区考古亦呈现出空白状。这一阶段，帝乙曾征伐过盂方。 淮夷文化承接大城墩四期文化发展。 帝乙去世后，其子帝辛继位；在考古层面上，出土的宰椃角铭文示帝辛在位至少二十有五年，但目前尚未发现帝辛的统治末年大肆征伐东夷的考古证据。不过，在帝辛在位的前中期，确实有征夷方的卜辞以及相关金文记录。 帝辛征伐夷方的军事行动，已经一年多的筹划准备后进行的“十祀征夷方”最为著名；帝辛十祀九月甲午的卜辞显示帝辛准备与靠近夷方的攸国的侯喜一同征伐夷方，并在出征前于王畿“大邑商”举行了告祭仪式。 十祀十一月，帝辛抵达危地。十二月初，与攸侯喜会师，并从癸酉日开始和夷方交战。根据卜辞记载，十日后，夷方似乎一时退却。之后帝辛率军抵达了淮河沿岸并征服林方；到了正月的丙午日，商军再与夷方交战。胜利后，帝辛率军在十一祀的二月由攸国踏上归途回师。 注：进军路线的“淮”亦可释为“潍”，故有两说。 除了“十祀征夷方”以外，帝辛还发动了“十五祀征夷方”，佐证来自商末小臣艅犀尊的铭文：“王赐小臣艅夔贝，隹王来征夷方，隹王十祀又五，彡日。”另有几则年月不明的商末卜辞及金文材料亦与征夷方相关。 在对外用兵的同时，帝辛也对内加强王权，严格地奉行祭祀先王、先妣的“周祭制度”；与其他奉行周祭制度的先王相比，帝辛为了集中王权，将打压旁系宗亲从祭祀层面延伸到了政治层面，加大重用小臣的力度并疏远旧贵，黄组卜辞中小臣任事内容多于旧贵职官，可为佐证。如此一来，商朝政坛上长期以来的平衡被打破，导致了商王朝固有的制度运转不畅，破坏了政治体系的稳定性。 另外，帝辛亦多接纳四方逃亡人口，加剧了与各族、各方国的矛盾，周文王则反其道而行之，明确提出了“有亡荒阅”政策，即搜捕逃亡人口，送还原主，借此笼络了殷商国内各族与附属方国。 据传世文献记载，在周国发展蒸蒸日上时，周王昌被帝辛诱捕囚禁于羑里。后来，经周国大臣七年间的收买与进献，文王才得以被释放回国，并被帝辛命为“西伯”。 据《史记·周本纪》记载，虞、芮两国发生了争端，相持不下，于是找周文王裁决。两国之君抵达周国后，见民风崇尚礼让，便惭愧而归，不再相争。此事很快传播开来，诸侯皆曰：“西伯盖受命之君！”部分学者认为文王决断“虞芮争讼”，是一种发动宗亲与国，宣扬“受命”舆论的手段。 据《逸周书·程寤篇》记载，文王因夫人太姒奇异的梦境而举行禳灾的仪式，与太子发“拜受吉梦”，以表示从“皇上帝”接收了殷商天命；周人因而视此年为“受命之年”。史载文王在“受命之年”决断“虞芮争讼”，第二年讨伐犬戎，第三年伐密须，并在灭密须的次年讨伐了耆国。文王在伐耆之后又伐邘，阻断了殷商王畿西部的天然屏障。 殷商旧贵和帝辛之间的矛盾日趋激化，而忙于压服国内贵族的帝辛，或许一时无法对周人的行动做出反应；山西地区的众多殷商属国，如吕国等，大致也在这一时期倒向了周人。 周文王的下一个目标，则是打通前往东方的主通道，扫除崇国；西安市灞桥区的老牛坡遗址被部分学者认为属于崇国，而根据碳十四测年结果，该遗址约在商末遭到废弃，遗址内的中型木椁墓被严重破坏，无一幸免，墓主遗骸遭到扬弃，随葬品十有八九皆无存。这或许是周人对崇侯虎及其宗族的一种报复行为。 根据上博楚简《容成氏》记载，文王降伏的邦国还有丰、镐、郍、鹿等；伊、洛以及豫西地区，大致在这一时期被周文王纳入了势力范围。一系列征伐行动结束后，周文王迁都丰邑，并于第二年去世。周文王去世后，太子发继位，是为周武王。 据传世文献记载，武王即王位数年后大举起兵攻商，带着文王的神位声言奉父命出征，又派人联络各地氏族部落在盟津观兵；部分学者认为文王受命七年而崩，又认为武王沿用受命纪年，未曾改元。按此推算，则《史记》中观兵盟津的“九年”，实际是武王在位的第二年。另一批学者持反对意见，指出先秦文献中记载武王实有“元祀”等独立纪年。 按“武王改元说”的观点，从武王即位到观兵盟津足有九年之久，在此期间，周人放缓了文王后期的持续扩张的势头，转而经营丰邑、建造镐京；至于商朝方面，在周人势力已逼近王畿的情况下，即使帝辛需要解决国内宗亲旧族离心的问题，也不得不腾出手来对周人采取反制措施了。 在《左传》中提及的“黎之蒐”，或许就是帝辛为应对周邦攻势而采取的军事部署；帝辛将军队开到耆（黎）国，举行阅兵、组织演习，借此彰显武力，使耆国重新倒向殷商。 若采信《左传》的“黎之蒐”，那么后续的“东夷叛之”则亦应该发生在帝辛统治的后期；考古证据表明，几则无纪年的“征夷方”金文材料不排除可将商夷战争持续至帝辛二十一祀乃至更晚的可能性。如果以上推论成立，那么发生在“黎之蒐”后不久的东夷反叛，很可能扰乱了帝辛的计划，导致无法进一步化解周人势力对王畿的威胁。 另一方面，周人也不甘于失去对黎国的控制，所以在完成内部整合、准备充分后，周人再度征伐黎国，将其一举讨平；清华简《耆夜》有载：“武王八年，征伐耆，大戡之。” 据《史记·周本纪》记载：武王观兵盟津，“不期而会盟津者八百诸侯”，参加会盟的诸侯纷纷要求立刻伐纣灭商，武王对他们说：“女未知天命，未可也。”于是便率军返回；部分学者认为，武王这次“观兵盟津”有演习性质，以便熟悉路程和地形，将来能以洛师作为前进基地，顺利渡河北上。 据传世文献记载，武王“观兵盟津”后不久，殷商统治集团内部出现了严重的撕裂。帝辛为压制反对自己的贵族，采取了非常极端的手段；最终的结果是：王子比干被杀，箕子被囚，太师疵、少师彊等人直接投奔周国。武王认为时机已经成熟，便通告同盟诸侯：“殷有重罪，不可以不毕伐！” 武王十一年一月癸巳日，周军率领戎车三百、虎贲三千、甲士四万五千人正式出发；同盟方国的军队前来与周军会合，武王作《太誓》以告诸侯、众士。周军在戊午日渡过黄河后，于二月癸亥日夜间抵达殷商别都朝歌郊外的牧野；据《国语·周语》记载：癸亥日的夜里下了一场雨，周军冒雨列阵，第二天甲子日的拂晓，武王在阵前作《牧誓》，宣告帝辛罪状。 按照《逸周书·克殷》所载，在牧野之战中，帝辛的军队被周军精锐冲垮而败北，帝辛于甲子日当晚于鹿台自焚；亦有说法认为帝辛被生擒后斩杀。
passages.en: c. 1088–1046 BC After Jili, King of Zhou, was killed, his son Chang succeeded him as ruler of the state of Zhou; he is King Wen of Zhou. Wen Ding, King of Shang, also died not long after, and his son Di Yi came to the throne; and the Late Shang entered its last phase, Yinxu Phase IV. The old-text Bamboo Annals records: "Di Yi resided at Yin. In his second year the men of Zhou attacked Shang." Some scholars hold that this shows the conflict between Shang and Zhou sharpening after Jili was killed; as for the outcome of this attack on Shang, the Zhou people's strength was not enough and it cannot have succeeded. And so King Wen of Zhou, after this setback, reviewed his policies at home and abroad afresh, turned to making peace with Yin Shang, and set himself to reversing the balance of strength. On the archaeological level, after the opening of Yinxu Phase IV Shang culture on the one hand flourished in the east, and on the other dwindled day by day in the west; after the Zhengjiapo culture and the Liujia culture had merged to form the late Proto-Zhou culture of the Qi (岐) and Feng region, the archaeology of the central Shanxi region, once closely tied to Shang culture, likewise shows a blank. In this stage Di Yi campaigned against the Yufang. The Huaiyi culture took over from the Dachengdun Phase IV culture and carried its development forward. After Di Yi's death his son Di Xin succeeded to the throne; on the archaeological level, the inscription of the unearthed Zai Hao jiao shows that Di Xin was on the throne for at least twenty-five years, but so far no archaeological evidence has been found of great campaigns against the Dongyi in the last years of Di Xin's rule. In the early and middle part of Di Xin's reign, however, there are indeed oracle-bone inscriptions on campaigning against the Yifang, and records in bronze inscriptions that bear on it. Of Di Xin's military operations against the Yifang, the best known is the "campaign against the Yifang in the tenth si", carried out after more than a year of planning and preparation; the inscription of Jiawu of September in Di Xin's tenth si shows Di Xin preparing to campaign against the Yifang together with Xi, Marquis of the state of You, which lay close to the Yifang, and holding, before setting out, a rite of announcement sacrifice in the royal domain, at the "Great Settlement Shang". In November of the tenth si Di Xin reached Wei (危). At the beginning of December he joined forces with Xi, Marquis of You, and from the day Guiyou began fighting the Yifang. By the record of the inscriptions, ten days later the Yifang seems for a time to have fallen back. After that Di Xin led his army to the banks of Huai River and conquered the Linfang; on Bingwu of January the Shang army fought the Yifang again. After the victory Di Xin, in February of the eleventh si, set out from You homebound with his army. Note: the "Huai" (淮) of the line of march can also be read as "Wei" (潍), so that there are two accounts. Besides the "campaign against the Yifang in the tenth si", Di Xin also launched a "campaign against the Yifang in the fifteenth si"; the evidence comes from the inscription of the rhinoceros zun of the Lesser Minister Yu, of the end of Shang: "The King bestowed on the Lesser Minister Yu cowries of Kui. It was when the King came to campaign against the Yifang; it was the King's fifteenth si, the day of the rong sacrifice." Several further oracle-bone and bronze inscriptions of the end of Shang, their year and month unknown, also bear on the campaigns against the Yifang. While using arms abroad, Di Xin also strengthened the royal power at home, strictly keeping up the "cyclical sacrifice system" of sacrifices to the former kings and their consorts; compared with the other former kings who kept the cyclical sacrifice system, Di Xin, in order to concentrate the royal power, carried the suppression of the collateral branches of the royal clan from the level of sacrifice over to the level of politics, made ever greater use of Lesser Ministers and kept the old nobility at a distance, as is borne out by the Huang-group inscriptions, in which the employment of Lesser Ministers on affairs outweighs the offices of the old nobility. In this way the balance long kept in the politics of the Shang was broken, the established institutions of the Shang court ceased to run smoothly, and the stability of the political system was undermined. In addition, Di Xin took in many fugitives from every quarter, which sharpened his conflicts with the clans and the fang states; King Wen of Zhou did the opposite, and expressly put forward the policy "Make great inquisition for fugitives", that is, to hunt down fugitives and send them back to their masters, by which he won over the clans within Yin Shang and its dependent fang states. According to the transmitted texts, while the state of Zhou was thriving, Chang, King of Zhou, was lured, seized and imprisoned at Youli by Di Xin. Later, after seven years of bribes and gifts from the ministers of Zhou, King Wen was at last released to return to his state, and was appointed "Chief of the West" by Di Xin. According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou, a dispute arose between the two states of Yu (虞) and Rui, neither of which would give way, and so they went to King Wen of Zhou for a ruling. When the rulers of the two states arrived in Zhou and saw that the ways of the people prized courtesy and yielding, they went home ashamed and contended no more. The matter soon spread abroad, and the Lords all said: "The Chief of the West must be the ruler who has received the Mandate!" Some scholars hold that King Wen's settling of the "suit of Yu and Rui" was a means of rousing his kinsmen and allied states and of spreading abroad the talk of his "receiving the Mandate". According to the Yi Zhou Shu, Awakening at Cheng, King Wen, because of a strange dream of his consort Tai Si, held a rite to avert calamity and, with the Heir Apparent Fa, "bowed and received the auspicious dream", to show that he had received from the "August High God" the Mandate of Heaven that had been Yin Shang's; the Zhou people therefore regarded this year as the "year of receiving the Mandate". History records that in the "year of receiving the Mandate" King Wen settled the "suit of Yu and Rui", in the second year attacked the Quan Rong, in the third year attacked Mixu, and in the year after destroying Mixu attacked the state of Qi (耆). After attacking Qi, King Wen went on to attack Yu (邘), cutting off the natural barrier west of Shang. The conflict between the old nobility of Yin Shang and Di Xin grew sharper by the day, and Di Xin, busy forcing the nobles at home into submission, was perhaps for the time unable to respond to what the Zhou people were doing; the many dependent states of Yin Shang in the Shanxi region, the state of Lü and others, also went over to the Zhou people at about this time. King Wen of Zhou's next aim was to open the main road to the east and sweep away the state of Chong; the Laoniupo site in Baqiao District, Xi'an, is held by some scholars to belong to the state of Chong, and by the results of radiocarbon dating the site was abandoned about the end of Shang; the medium-sized tombs with wooden chambers within the site were badly wrecked, not one being spared, the remains of the tomb occupants were thrown out, and of the grave goods eight or nine parts in ten are gone. This was perhaps an act of revenge by the Zhou people on Hu, Marquis of Chong, and his clan. According to the Rongchengshi of the Shanghai Museum Chu slips, the states subdued by King Wen also included Feng, Hao, Nuo, Lu and others; Yi River, Luo River and the western Henan region were brought into King Wen of Zhou's sphere of power at about this time. When this series of campaigns was over King Wen of Zhou moved his capital to the settlement of Feng, and died the year after. After King Wen of Zhou's death the Heir Apparent Fa succeeded to the throne; he is King Wu of Zhou. According to the transmitted texts, some years after coming to the throne King Wu raised a great army to attack Shang, carrying King Wen's spirit tablet and declaring that he marched at his father's command, and sent men to bring the clans and tribes of every region together for a review of arms at Meng Ford; some scholars hold that King Wen died seven years after receiving the Mandate, and that King Wu went on with the count of years from the Mandate and never began a count of his own. Reckoned in this way, the "ninth year" of the review of arms at Meng Ford in the Shiji is in fact the second year of King Wu's reign. Another group of scholars takes the opposite view, pointing out that the pre-Qin texts record King Wu as having a count of years of his own, such as a "first si". On the view that "King Wu began a count of his own", fully nine years passed from King Wu's accession to the review of arms at Meng Ford, and in this time the Zhou people slackened the continuous expansion of King Wen's later years and turned to the ordering of the settlement of Feng and the building of Haojing; as for the Shang, with the power of the Zhou people already pressing on the royal domain, Di Xin, even though he had the disaffection of his kinsmen and the old clans at home to deal with, had no choice but to free his hands and take countermeasures against the Zhou people. The "review of Li" mentioned in the Zuozhuan was perhaps the military disposition Di Xin made in answer to the Zhou state's offensive; Di Xin moved his army up to the state of Qi (Li), held a review of troops and organised manoeuvres, and by this show of force brought the state of Qi back over to Yin Shang. If the "review of Li" of the Zuozhuan is accepted, then "the Dongyi revolted from him" that follows it should likewise have happened in the later part of Di Xin's rule; the archaeological evidence shows that several undated bronze inscriptions on "campaigning against the Yifang" do not rule out the possibility that the war between Shang and the Yifang went on to Di Xin's twenty-first si or even later. If the above inference holds, then the revolt of the Dongyi, coming not long after the "review of Li", very probably upset Di Xin's plans, so that he could do nothing further to remove the threat of the Zhou people's power to the royal domain. On the other side, the Zhou people for their part were not willing to lose control of the state of Li, and so, once their internal consolidation was complete and their preparations fully made, the Zhou people campaigned against the state of Li a second time and put it down at one stroke; the Qiye of the Tsinghua slips records: "In King Wu's eighth year he campaigned against Qi and greatly conquered it." According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou: when King Wu reviewed his arms at Meng Ford, "the Lords who met at Meng Ford without appointment were eight hundred"; the Lords who took part in the meeting one after another demanded that Zhou (纣) be attacked and Shang destroyed at once, and King Wu said to them: "You do not yet know the Mandate of Heaven; it cannot be done yet." And with that he led his army back; some scholars hold that this "review of arms at Meng Ford" of King Wu's was in the nature of a manoeuvre, to learn the road and the ground, so that in future he could use Luoshi as a forward base and cross the river northwards without difficulty. According to the transmitted texts, not long after King Wu's "review of arms at Meng Ford" a grave split appeared within the ruling group of Yin Shang. To hold down the nobles who opposed him, Di Xin took very extreme measures; the final outcome was that Prince Bigan was killed, Jizi was imprisoned, and the Grand Preceptor Ci, the Junior Preceptor Qiang and others went straight over to the state of Zhou. King Wu judged that the time was ripe, and proclaimed to the allied Lords: "Yin has committed grave crimes; it cannot but be attacked to the end!" On Guisi of January in King Wu's eleventh year the Zhou army formally set out, with three hundred war chariots, three thousand Tiger Braves and forty-five thousand armoured men; the armies of the allied fang states came to join the Zhou army, and King Wu made the Great Declaration to address the Lords and all the gentlemen. After crossing the Yellow River on the day Wuwu, the Zhou army reached Muye, outside Zhaoge, the secondary capital of Yin Shang, in the night of Guihai of February; according to the Guoyu, Discourses of Zhou, rain fell in the night of Guihai and the Zhou army drew up its lines in the rain, and at daybreak the next day, Jiazi, King Wu made the Speech at Mu before the lines, proclaiming Di Xin's crimes. By the account of the Yi Zhou Shu, Conquest of Yin, in the battle of Muye Di Xin's army was broken by the charge of the picked troops of Zhou and was defeated, and Di Xin burned himself to death on Lu Terrace on the evening of that same day, Jiazi; there is also an account that Di Xin was taken alive and then beheaded.
passages.no: 帝乙处殷，二年，周人伐商: a fragment of the old-text Bamboo Annals preserved in the Taiping Yulan, juan 83. 帝辛: the last king of Shang, the Zhou 纣 of the later texts; the name 纣 is used once below. 小臣艅犀尊: the vessel is in the Asian Art Museum, San Francisco, whose translation is followed for the first clause; the Museum reads 夷方 as Renfang, takes 来征 as the King's return from the campaign, and takes 隹王十祀又五，彡日 as the King's fifteenth sacrificial day in the rong-ritual cycle. 有亡荒阅: Legge's translation; the law of King Wen as the Zuozhuan gives it under Duke Zhao's seventh year, 周文王之法曰：有亡荒阅，所以得天下也. Du Yu reads 荒 as great and 阅 as to search. 西伯: after Legge's title for the chapter 西伯戡黎 of the Documents, "The Chief of the West's Conquest of Li". 黎之蒐: after Legge. The Zuozhuan, Duke Zhao, fourth year, has 商纣为黎之蒐，东夷叛之, in Legge "Chow of the Shang dynasty held the review of Le, and the E of the east revolted from him". 太誓, 牧誓: chapters of the Documents, where 太誓 is written 泰誓; the English titles are Legge's. From the death of Jili to the fall of Shang, about 1088 to 1046 BC: Di Yi and the opening of Yinxu Phase IV; Di Xin's campaigns against the Yifang and his strengthening of the royal power; King Wen's imprisonment at Youli, the receiving of the Mandate and his campaigns down to the move to Feng; and King Wu's review of arms at Meng Ford, the split within Yin Shang and the battle of Muye.

passages.title: c. 1046–1036 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1046年—公元前1036年 帝辛死后，武王的下一步行动是实现对殷商王畿的彻底控制；据《逸周书》记载，武王在甲子日傍晚进入朝歌后，就派遣太公率军抵御帝辛的臣子方来。三天后的丁卯日，太公得胜归来，基本扑灭了殷商王畿的残余抵抗势力。 在殷墟王畿，除方来等残存抵抗势力，殷商的宗亲旧族，多无心与周军对抗；据《左传》记载，帝辛的庶兄微子启主动向武王请降，武王亲自替微子启松绑，收下他含着的玉璧，随后命他返回封邑微地。 据《逸周书·克殷》所载，武王在殷商王畿举行了社祭，把帝辛子武庚封在殷邑，命三弟管叔鲜辅佐；武王安排召公去释放被囚禁的箕子，又安排毕叔与康叔去释放了被帝辛囚禁的宗族族人，并命闳夭封比干之墓。武王征召殷商王畿的大小贵族，在殷邑郊外会面，武王对他们发表训诫，即《商誓》。 陕西临潼出土的西周青铜器利簋铭文表明，武王在辛未日，也就是克商的七天后已经离开了殷商王畿，抵达阑师；据《逸周书·世俘》记载，武王令吕他征伐越戏方、侯来伐陈地的靡集、百弇伐韦、陈本伐磿、百韦伐宣方，新荒伐蜀，六路皆捷。在取得胜利后，武王率军返回镐京，于四月庚戌日举行了献俘仪式。辛亥日，祭祀上天，伐纣战争至此完成。 武王克商后的统治较为短暂，至多三年。在此期间，武王对“先代之后”以及宗亲功臣进行了分封。 在“先代之后”中，夏、殷两代王族后裔，共三国受封，合称为“三恪”；此“三恪”的“舜后”是陈国，“夏后”是杞国，至于“殷后”，初为受封于邶的帝辛子武庚。后武庚作乱被讨平，周公又命帝辛庶兄微子启“代殷后”，宋国便成为了“三恪”之一。除此之外，亦有如炎黄之后、尧后等受封。 除管叔鲜在克商之初被派辅佐武庚之外，武王亦增派了另外两位胞弟，蔡叔度和霍叔处，设置“三监”以对殷民进行监督，并拆分了殷商王畿；周武王还把几位胞弟分封在曹、郜、郕等地，又封太公吕尚于营丘，讨平莱夷并建立齐国，在东土立足。 至周初，姜姓人群成规模地进入泾河中、上游，与来自西周王畿腹地的周人在泾河干流与支流马莲河的甘肃灵台、崇信与宁县、合水、环县地区共存。 武王去世后，其子成王即位，周公姬旦承武王遗命而“代行天子事”，发布命令皆称“王命”；正在东方监管殷民的管叔、蔡叔极其不满，随即展开了对抗。 至于霍叔，部分学者认为可能只是被两位兄长裹挟，并非动乱的主要发起者，所以早期的文献大多加以忽略；随着管蔡二人公然对抗周公，帝辛之子武庚也在殷邑起兵。 传统说法大多认为管蔡与武庚联合作乱，但部分的学者根据清华简《系年》的记载推断管蔡起初或只单纯反对周公，并未勾结武庚，原殷商王畿地区的贵族、遗民看到周国宗室内讧，便杀死了留在殷邑的周人属吏、军士，拥戴武庚叛乱。 据《尚书大传》记载，奄国和蒲姑的君主亦有派人通告武庚举事。 管、蔡宣称“公将不利于孺子”，让周朝其他重臣乃至成王本人，对周公摄政心生怀疑；周公一方面极力陈述自己的用心良苦，另一方面表示绝不姑息作乱之人。 周公东征的第一年，主要是在遏制管、蔡以及殷商旧族的攻势；周公坐镇洛地，其子伯禽则率军插入管叔封国的后方，而其他邦君诸侯也配合了周公的行动：温、檀两国扼控着从殷商王畿南下伊洛地区的交通要道，原、雍两国扼控着太行山南麓的隘口，姬姓黎国则镇守着太行山西侧的上党台地，在它们的封锁之下，殷商王畿的叛军也是一筹莫展。 在济水沿线，先前周军东拓的产物——齐、郕、曹、郜等国更是牵制了以奄国、蒲姑为代表的亲商方国，使它们无法有效支援殷商王畿。 在东征的第二年，周公彻底击败管、蔡，管叔或被处死、或自杀，蔡叔或被囚，或与霍叔同遭流放。 在管、蔡败亡后，周公继而挥师攻克了殷邑，武庚向北逃窜；根据安阳小屯发掘所见的柱烬以及基址的红烧土，可以得知殷都在最终废弃时经历了火灾。殷墟王陵以及王陵区以外的绝大多数贵族墓葬也在周公东征的期间集体遭到了破坏性盗掘，晚商殷墟四期彻底结束。 成王对周公的误会消除后，到东征的第三年便亲自参与了“践奄”的重大战役。另一方面，成王派遣太保召公奭率军讨伐北逃的武庚；尽管武庚被追上杀死，但仍然有一部分残党继续北逃，召公率军队追击，直抵燕地，经营据点。后来召公班师，成王就封召公之子克为匽侯。 先前北京地区已有箕子宗族北迁建立的㠱国，根据考古铭文中匽侯赏赐㠱侯族人的内容来看，这一支殷商遗民与匽国的关系较为融洽；至于武庚之乱的残党，或许逃到了更靠北一点的地方，例如孤竹国，而西周初辽西遗存中的殷商式器物可能与其有关。 奄国被攻破后，原本避难于此的帝辛之臣飞廉继续向东逃窜，周军追击到海边，将他杀死；成王又把包括飞廉族人在内的奄国遗民西迁到朱圉山，命令他们抵御“奴虘之戎”。 消灭奄国以后，周公又率军征伐了东夷丰伯之国与蒲姑国；这两国应是在太公的配合下消灭的，所以后来都被成王增封给齐国。此后，周公广伐南国。 几个主要的亲商方国覆亡后，东部地区的纪、薛等国也倒向了周人；据《逸周书》记载，周公还征服了东夷的“熊盈族十有七国”，不过，东夷的大国徐国似乎并未受到重创，后来周公之子伯禽迁封于东方，依然要和徐国斗争。 东征胜利后，周公把一批拥戴武庚叛乱的殷商旧贵迁往九毕，即有重兵屯驻的洛地附近，以便在新都洛邑建成后可以就近管控；因为他们先前反抗周人的统治，也被称为“顽民”。 周公于摄政的第五年营建成周洛邑，其后有更多的殷商旧族被迁到附近安置。周公还重申了安抚政策，使有德之人会被选入王廷供职，而其他迁居洛邑的殷民，也能分到田地。 除了成周洛邑以外，还有部分殷商旧族被迁往周原、丰镐安置；与洛邑的“顽民”不同，这些旧族大多是愿意与周人合作的一派，早在武王克商之初，他们就被陆续迁往西土。 至于殷商王畿，仍有众多未被迁徙的遗民。周公让胞弟康叔封去管辖居留原地的殷商遗民，成王亲政后，嘉奖康叔的功劳，召他回朝担任司寇。 与殷商王畿情况有些类似，商奄的故地后来迁走了一批“顽民”后，还是有众多遗民居留原地，于是令伯禽迁居东方以巩固周公东征的胜利结果。但在许国都城附近，仍然留有一块鲁国的“飞地”许田，作为鲁国君主至洛朝觐时的临时驻地。
passages.en: c. 1046–1036 BC After Di Xin's death, King Wu's next step was to bring the royal domain of Yin Shang wholly under his control; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, King Wu, after entering Zhaoge on the evening of the day Jiazi, at once sent Taigong with an army to hold off Fang Lai, a minister of Di Xin. Three days later, on the day Dingmao, Taigong came back victorious, having for the most part put out what resistance remained in the royal domain of Yin Shang. In the royal domain of Yinxu, apart from Fang Lai and the other remnants of resistance, the kinsmen and old clans of Yin Shang for the most part had no heart to stand against the Zhou army; according to the Zuozhuan, Weizi Qi, Di Xin's elder brother by a secondary consort, came of his own accord to offer his surrender to King Wu, and King Wu with his own hands loosed Weizi Qi's bonds, accepted the jade disc he held in his mouth, and then ordered him back to his fief, the land of Wei (微). By the account of the Yi Zhou Shu, Conquest of Yin, King Wu held a sacrifice at the altar of the soil in the royal domain of Yin Shang, enfeoffed Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, at the settlement of Yin, and ordered his third brother Guanshu Xian to assist him; King Wu sent the Duke of Shao to release the imprisoned Jizi, sent Bishu and Kangshu to release the kinsmen whom Di Xin had imprisoned, and ordered Hong Yao to raise a mound over the tomb of Bigan. King Wu summoned the nobles great and small of the royal domain of Yin Shang to meet him outside the settlement of Yin, and delivered an admonition to them, which is the Speech to Shang. The inscription of the Li gui, a Western Zhou bronze unearthed at Lintong in Shaanxi, shows that on the day Xinwei, that is, seven days after the conquest of Shang, King Wu had already left the royal domain of Yin Shang and reached Lanshi; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, Great Capture, King Wu ordered Lü Ta to campaign against the Yuexifang, Hou Lai to attack Miji in the land of Chen, Bai Yan to attack Wei (韦), Chen Ben to attack Li (磿), Bai Wei to attack the Xuanfang and Xin Huang to attack Shu, and all six columns were victorious. After these victories King Wu led his army back to Haojing, and on Gengxu of April held the rite of presenting the captives. On the day Xinhai he sacrificed to Heaven, and with this the war against Zhou (纣) was complete. King Wu's rule after the conquest of Shang was fairly short, three years at the most. In this time King Wu made enfeoffments to the "descendants of the former dynasties" and to his kinsmen and ministers of merit. Among the "descendants of the former dynasties", the descendants of the royal houses of the two dynasties of Xia and Yin, three states in all, were enfeoffed, and are together called the "Three Ke"; of these "Three Ke" the "descendants of Shun" are the state of Chen, the "descendants of Xia" the state of Qi (杞), and as for the "descendants of Yin", they were at first Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, enfeoffed at Bei. Later, when Wu Geng rose in revolt and was put down, the Duke of Zhou ordered Weizi Qi, Di Xin's elder brother by a secondary consort, to "take the place of the descendants of Yin", and the state of Song thus became one of the "Three Ke". Besides these, others too were enfeoffed, such as the descendants of Yandi and the Yellow Emperor, the descendants of Yao and others. Besides Guanshu Xian, sent at the very beginning of the conquest of Shang to assist Wu Geng, King Wu also sent two more of his full brothers, Caishu Du and Huoshu Chu, setting up the "Three Guards" to keep watch over the people of Yin, and divided up the royal domain of Yin Shang; King Wu of Zhou also enfeoffed several of his full brothers at Cao, Gao, Cheng (郕) and other places, and enfeoffed Taigong, Lü Shang, at Yingqiu, who put down the Laiyi and founded the state of Qi (齐), gaining a foothold in the eastern lands. By the beginning of Zhou, people of the Jiang surname had moved in numbers into the middle and upper reaches of Jing River, and lived side by side with Zhou people from the heart of the Western Zhou royal domain in the districts of Lingtai, Chongxin, Ning County, Heshui and Huan County in Gansu, on the main stream of Jing River and its tributary Malian River. After King Wu's death his son King Cheng came to the throne, and Ji Dan, Duke of Zhou, on King Wu's dying charge, "conducted the affairs of the Son of Heaven in his stead", issuing all his orders as "the King's command"; Guanshu and Caishu, who were then in the east overseeing the people of Yin, were greatly displeased, and at once set themselves against him. As for Huoshu, some scholars think he may only have been carried along by his two elder brothers and was not a chief mover of the troubles, which is why the early texts for the most part pass him over; as Guan and Cai openly set themselves against the Duke of Zhou, Wu Geng, Di Xin's son, also raised troops at the settlement of Yin. The traditional accounts for the most part hold that Guan and Cai rose in revolt in league with Wu Geng, but some scholars infer from the record of the Xinian of the Tsinghua slips that Guan and Cai at first perhaps simply opposed the Duke of Zhou and were not in collusion with Wu Geng; the nobles and remnant people of the former royal domain of Yin Shang, seeing the royal house of Zhou at strife within itself, killed the Zhou officers and soldiers left at the settlement of Yin and raised Wu Geng in revolt. According to the Shangshu Dazhuan, the rulers of the state of Yan (奄) and of Pugu also sent men to tell Wu Geng to rise. Guan and Cai gave out that "the Duke will do no good to the young son", so that the other great ministers of the Zhou court, and even King Cheng himself, came to doubt the Duke of Zhou's regency; the Duke of Zhou on the one hand did his utmost to set out the pains he had taken, and on the other made it plain that he would show no indulgence to those who raised revolt. The first year of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign was spent mainly in checking the offensive of Guan, Cai and the old clans of Yin Shang; the Duke of Zhou held the land of Luo in person, while his son Boqin led an army in behind Guanshu's fief, and the other rulers of states and Lords also acted in concert with the Duke of Zhou: the two states of Wen and Tan held the main road running south from the royal domain of Yin Shang to the region of Yi River and Luo River, the two states of Yuan and Yong held the Passes at the southern foot of Taihangshan, and the Ji-surnamed state of Li (黎) guarded the Shangdang Plateau on the western side of Taihangshan; under their blockade the rebel army of the royal domain of Yin Shang could do nothing. Along Ji River, the states that the Zhou army's earlier advance to the east had produced, Qi (齐), Cheng (郕), Cao, Gao and others, moreover pinned down the pro-Shang fang states, of which the state of Yan (奄) and Pugu were the chief, so that they could give no effective support to the royal domain of Yin Shang. In the second year of the eastern campaign the Duke of Zhou utterly defeated Guan and Cai; Guanshu was either put to death or killed himself, and Caishu was either imprisoned or banished together with Huoshu. After the defeat and ruin of Guan and Cai, the Duke of Zhou went on to lead his army against the settlement of Yin and took it, and Wu Geng fled north; from the charred posts and the burnt red earth of the foundations found in the excavations at Xiaotun, Anyang, it can be known that the capital of Yin went through a fire when it was finally abandoned. The royal tombs of Yinxu, and the great majority of the nobles' tombs outside the royal cemetery, were also plundered and wrecked together in the course of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign, and Late Shang Yinxu Phase IV came to a final end. Once King Cheng's misunderstanding of the Duke of Zhou was cleared away, in the third year of the eastern campaign he took part in person in the great campaign of the "trampling of Yan (奄)". On the other side, King Cheng sent the Grand Guardian Shi, Duke of Shao, with an army against Wu Geng, who had fled north; although Wu Geng was overtaken and killed, a part of his following still fled on northwards, and the Duke of Shao pursued them with his army as far as the land of Yan (燕), where he set up strongholds. Afterwards, when the Duke of Shao brought his army home, King Cheng enfeoffed the Duke of Shao's son Ke as Marquis of Yan (匽). Before this there was already in the Beijing region the state of Ji (㠱), founded by Jizi's clan after its move north; to judge from the excavated inscriptions in which the Marquis of Yan (匽) makes gifts to kinsmen of the Marquis of Ji (㠱), this branch of the remnant people of Yin Shang was on fairly good terms with the state of Yan (匽); as for the remnants of Wu Geng's revolt, they perhaps fled to somewhere a little further north, for example the state of Guzhu, and the vessels of Yin Shang type among the remains of western Liaoning at the beginning of the Western Zhou may have to do with them. After the state of Yan (奄) was broken, Feilian, a minister of Di Xin who had taken refuge there, fled on eastwards, and the Zhou army pursued him to the edge of the sea and killed him; King Cheng also moved the remnant people of the state of Yan (奄), Feilian's kinsmen among them, west to Zhuyushan, and ordered them to hold off the "Rong of Nucuo". After destroying the state of Yan (奄), the Duke of Zhou also led his army against the Dongyi state of the Earl of Feng and the state of Pugu; these two states must have been destroyed with Taigong's cooperation, which is why both were afterwards added by King Cheng to the fief of the state of Qi (齐). After this the Duke of Zhou campaigned widely against the southern states. After the fall of the several chief pro-Shang fang states, Ji (纪), Xue and other states of the east also went over to the Zhou people; according to the Yi Zhou Shu, the Duke of Zhou also conquered "seventeen states of the Xiong and Ying clans" of the Dongyi; the great Dongyi state of Xu (徐), however, seems not to have been badly hurt, and later, when the Duke of Zhou's son Boqin was moved to a fief in the east, he still had to fight the state of Xu (徐). After the victory of the eastern campaign, the Duke of Zhou moved a body of the old nobility of Yin Shang who had raised Wu Geng in revolt to Jiubi, that is, near the land of Luo, where a strong force was stationed, so that once the new capital Luoyi was built they could be controlled from close at hand; because they had earlier resisted the rule of the Zhou people, they are also called the "refractory people". In the fifth year of his regency the Duke of Zhou built Chengzhou, Luoyi, after which still more of the old clans of Yin Shang were moved and settled near it. The Duke of Zhou also restated his policy of conciliation, by which men of virtue would be chosen to serve at the royal court, while the other people of Yin moved to Luoyi could also be given fields. Besides Chengzhou, Luoyi, some of the old clans of Yin Shang were also moved and settled in the Zhouyuan and at Feng and Hao; unlike the "refractory people" of Luoyi, these old clans were for the most part the party willing to work with the Zhou people, and as early as the beginning of King Wu's conquest of Shang they were moved one after another to the western lands. As for the royal domain of Yin Shang, many remnant people who had not been moved were still there. The Duke of Zhou had his full brother Kangshu Feng govern the remnant people of Yin Shang who stayed where they were, and after King Cheng took up the government himself he commended Kangshu's services and called him back to court to serve as Minister of Justice. Much as in the royal domain of Yin Shang, in the old land of Shang Yan (商奄), after a body of "refractory people" had later been moved away, many remnant people still stayed where they were, and so Boqin was ordered to move to the east to make fast the fruits of the Duke of Zhou's eastern campaign. Near the capital of the state of Xu (许), however, there still remained Xutian, an "exclave" of the state of Lu, as a lodging for the rulers of Lu when they went to Luo to attend court.
passages.no: 公将不利于孺子: the Metal-bound Coffer of the Documents, after Legge, "the duke would do no good to the (king's) young son". 匽: the form of 燕, Yan, in the bronze inscriptions. 顽民: Legge's rendering in the Charge to the Duke of Bi of the Documents, 毖殷顽民，迁于洛邑, "Cautiously did he deal with the refractory people of Yin, and removed them to the city of Lo". The first years after the conquest of Shang, about 1046 to 1036 BC: King Wu's settlement of the royal domain of Yin Shang and his enfeoffments; the Duke of Zhou's regency, the rising of Guan, Cai and Wu Geng and the three years of the eastern campaign; the founding of Yan (燕) and the fall of Yan (奄) and Pugu; and the moving of the people of Yin to Luoyi, the Zhouyuan and Feng and Hao.

passages.title: c. 1046–1036 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前1046年—公元前1036年 约西周初： 夏家店上层文化承接高台山文化发展；十二台营子文化承接魏营子文化发展。 周代北方的青铜文化逐渐过渡至空白期；保德类型承接石楼类型发展。 寺洼文化进入中期二段，发展形成了栏桥-徐家碾类型。 西团山、宝山、炭河里文化与万发拨子遗存兴起。
passages.en: c. 1046–1036 BC: archaeological appearances c. the beginning of the Western Zhou: The Upper Xiajiadian culture took over from the Gaotaishan culture and carried its development forward; the Shi'ertaiyingzi culture took over from the Weiyingzi culture and carried its development forward. The bronze cultures of the north in the Zhou period passed by degrees into a blank period; the Baode type took over from the Shilou type and carried its development forward. The Siwa culture entered the second stage of its middle period, and as it developed the Lanqiao–Xujianian type took shape within it. The Xituanshan, Baoshan and Tanheli cultures and the Wanfabozi remains arose.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, about the beginning of the Western Zhou: the Upper Xiajiadian and Shi'ertaiyingzi cultures; the Baode type; the Lanqiao–Xujianian type of the Siwa culture; and the Xituanshan, Baoshan and Tanheli cultures and the Wanfabozi remains.

passages.title: c. 1036–1000 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1036年—公元前1000年 周公于摄政的第七年还政成王，死后葬于毕。 成王的胞弟唐叔虞亦受封于昜，叔虞去世后，其子燮父即位，于成王廿八年自唐地迁往晋地。 考古表明，西周初年的燕国在北京地区站稳脚跟后，又尝试向辽西拓展势力；辽宁喀左马厂沟村曾出土一件西周早期的铜盂。 成王去世，太子钊继位。在周王朝的发展中，文王和康王有相当突出的作为，贡献显著；周公东征时曾征伐东夷，但未将东夷消灭，所以周康王时又有征伐反叛的东夷的战争，一直达到了海边，并征伐了东国；不知康王时的楚国有何叛周的举措，但是康王时有“伐楚伯”之战，又有讨伐虎方一事。 司马迁的《史记·周本纪》云：“成康之际，天下安宁，刑错四十馀年不用。”后世皆称成王与康王的统治时期为“成康之治”。
passages.en: c. 1036–1000 BC In the seventh year of his regency the Duke of Zhou gave the government back to King Cheng; after his death he was buried at Bi. King Cheng's full brother Tangshu Yu was likewise enfeoffed, at Yang; after Shuyu's death his son Xiefu succeeded him, and in the twenty-eighth year of King Cheng moved from the land of Tang to the land of Jin. Archaeology shows that the state of Yan of the first years of the Western Zhou, once it had a firm footing in the Beijing region, went on to try to extend its power into western Liaoning; an early Western Zhou bronze yu was once unearthed at Machanggou village, Kazuo, in Liaoning. King Cheng died, and the Heir Apparent Zhao succeeded to the throne. In the growth of the Zhou dynasty King Wen and King Kang did a good deal that stands out, and their contribution was marked; in his eastern campaign the Duke of Zhou had campaigned against the Dongyi but had not destroyed them, and so in the time of King Kang of Zhou there was again a war against the Dongyi, who had risen in revolt, which was carried right to the edge of the sea, and the eastern states were attacked as well; it is not known what the state of Chu did in King Kang's time to turn against Zhou, but in King Kang's time there was the war of the "attack on the Earl of Chu", and also a campaign against the Hufang. Sima Qian's Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says: "In the time of Cheng and Kang all under Heaven was at peace, and the punishments were laid aside, unused for more than forty years." Later ages all call the period of the rule of King Cheng and King Kang the "Good Governance of Cheng and Kang".
passages.no: 昜: so written in a bronze inscription of the early Western Zhou, 王命昜伯侯于晋，唯王廿又八祀; the transmitted texts have Tang 唐. 刑错: 错 is read as 措, to lay aside (Ying Shao, in the Jijie). From the end of the Duke of Zhou's regency to the reign of King Kang, about 1036 to 1000 BC: the Duke of Zhou's death and burial at Bi; the move of Tangshu Yu's house from Tang to Jin; Yan's reach into western Liaoning; King Kang's wars against the Dongyi, the Earl of Chu and the Hufang; and the "Good Governance of Cheng and Kang".

passages.title: c. 1000–950 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前1000年—公元前950年 周康王去世后，其子瑕继位，即为昭王；昭王时的战争主要是南征，传世文献与铭文对比来看，大体吻合，亦有文献所未曾提及者，如伐东夷、桧等。 昭王于十六年伐反荆，考古发现可为佐证；《过伯簋》铭云：“过白从王伐反荆，孚金，用乍宗室宝尊彝。”昭王十九年的伐荆战争相对十六年可能更为惨烈，据古本《竹书纪年》记载，昭王所统的六师也被打得惨败，谓之“丧六师于汉。” 昭王死后，其子满继位，即为穆王；在《史记·周本纪》中言及西周穆王事，比康、昭二王稍详，但也很简略。关于战争，仅征犬戎一事，古本《竹书纪年》所记则较详。 西晋出土的《穆天子传》亦记有周穆王由洛邑出发经历不同部落与国家后见到西王母的故事。 从穆王早期开始，淮夷开始成为了周朝在东南部的大患；穆王时期的出土青铜器铭文开始经常出现抵抗淮夷的记载，汝水、颍水与沙水沿线皆为其侵扰。 穆王时期的出土青铜器铭文中，亦有“戍南夷”的记载；铭中的“戍”为遏止、抵御之义，与戍守之义有别，因此“戍南夷”本身就表明是战争，且是与抵抗淮夷不同的战争。
passages.en: c. 1000–950 BC After King Kang of Zhou's death his son Xia succeeded to the throne; he is King Zhao. The wars of King Zhao's time were mainly the southern campaigns; set side by side, the transmitted texts and the inscriptions agree in the main, and there are also things the texts never mention, such as the attacks on the Dongyi, Kuai and others. In his sixteenth year King Zhao attacked the rebellious Jing, as archaeological finds bear out; the inscription of the Guo Bo gui says: "The Earl of Guo followed the King in attacking the rebellious Jing and took metal; with it he made this treasured sacrificial vessel for the ancestral hall." King Zhao's war against Jing in his nineteenth year was probably more terrible than that of the sixteenth; according to the old-text Bamboo Annals, the six armies under King Zhao's command were also disastrously beaten, which it puts as "the six armies perished in the Han." After King Zhao's death his son Man succeeded to the throne; he is King Mu. What the Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou says of King Mu of the Western Zhou is a little fuller than for the two kings Kang and Zhao, but still very brief. As to war, it has only the campaign against the Quan Rong; the record of the old-text Bamboo Annals is fuller. The Mu Tianzi Zhuan, unearthed under the Western Jin, also tells the story of King Mu of Zhou setting out from Luoyi and, after passing through various tribes and states, meeting the Queen Mother of the West. From the early part of King Mu's reign the Huaiyi began to be a great danger to the Zhou in the south-east; in the inscriptions of the excavated bronzes of King Mu's period records of resisting the Huaiyi begin to appear often, and the lines of Ru River, Ying River and Sha River were all subject to their raids. In the inscriptions of the excavated bronzes of King Mu's period there are also records of "holding off the Nanyi" (戍南夷); the 戍 of the inscriptions has the sense of checking or holding off, which differs from the sense of garrisoning, and so "holding off the Nanyi" in itself shows that this was war, and a war distinct from the resistance to the Huaiyi.
passages.no: 荆: Jing, the name by which the inscriptions and the old texts call Chu. 过伯簋: translated with Robert Eno's version at hand (Inscriptional Records of the Western Zhou, no. 39), which has "Elder of Guo" and "clan shrine". 白 and 乍 are the inscription's forms of 伯 and 作. 丧六师于汉: after Legge's translation of the Bamboo Annals, "The king's six armies perished in the Han". The reigns of King Zhao and King Mu, about 1000 to 950 BC: King Zhao's southern campaigns against Jing and the loss of the six armies in the Han; King Mu in the Shiji, the Bamboo Annals and the Mu Tianzi Zhuan; and the Huaiyi and the Nanyi in the bronze inscriptions of King Mu's time.

passages.title: c. 1000–950 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前1000年—公元前950年 约公元前1000年： 辛店文化进入末期；卡约文化进入第五期。 美松里上层文化承接新岩里二期文化发展。 金滩里青铜文化进入二期。
passages.en: c. 1000–950 BC: archaeological appearances c. 1000 BC: The Xindian culture entered its final period; the Kayue culture entered its Phase V. The Upper Misong-ri culture took over from the Sinam-ri Phase II culture and carried its development forward. The Geumtan-ri Bronze Age culture entered its Phase II.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, about 1000 BC: the final period of the Xindian culture and Phase V of the Kayue culture; and in Korea, the Upper Misong-ri culture and Phase II of the Geumtan-ri Bronze Age culture.

passages.title: c. 950–900 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前950年—公元前900年 穆王晚期伐淮夷与东国，考古发现可为证据；《班簋》其铭云：“三年静东国，亡不成。”另有铭文指出，此时淮夷侵伐内地，穆王命𰒦出征并与其战于胡国。 据出土的大小盂鼎，穆王时亦有盂奉王命两次征伐鬼方的记载；伐鬼方第一次就大有斩获，捉得鬼方的首领三人，割耳四千八百多人，俘一万三千多人，车三十辆，牛三百多头，并回归举行了献俘礼。 穆王去世后，其子繄扈立，即为共王；就目前所知，属于共王世记有战争的器铭者，尚未发现，有一些记有战争的器铭由于不能完全断定究竟属于共、懿还是孝王，只好暂归于“西周中期”。 关于共王时代的征战，传世文献所载的仅有司马迁的《史记·周本纪》中共王灭密一事。 共王去世后，其子囏继位，即为懿王。
passages.en: c. 950–900 BC In his later years King Mu attacked the Huaiyi and the eastern states, as archaeological finds bear witness; the inscription of the Ban gui says: "In three years he brought peace to the eastern states, and none did not submit." Another inscription shows that at this time the Huaiyi invaded the interior, and King Mu ordered Dong to take the field, and he fought them at the state of Hu. According to the excavated Da Yu ding and Xiao Yu ding, in King Mu's time there are also records of Yu twice campaigning against the Guifang at the King's command; the very first campaign against the Guifang brought great gains: three chiefs of the Guifang were captured, the ears of more than four thousand eight hundred men were cut off, more than thirteen thousand men were taken prisoner, with thirty chariots and more than three hundred oxen, and on his return the rite of presenting the captives was held. After King Mu's death his son Yihu was set on the throne; he is King Gong. So far as is known at present, no vessel inscription recording war that belongs to King Gong's reign has yet been found; some vessel inscriptions that record war cannot be assigned with certainty to King Gong, King Yi (懿) or King Xiao, and can only be placed for the time being under the "middle Western Zhou". As to the wars of King Gong's time, all that the transmitted texts record is King Gong's destruction of Mi, in Sima Qian's Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou. After King Gong's death his son Jian succeeded; he is King Yi (懿).
passages.no: 班簋: translated after Robert Eno (Inscriptional Records of the Western Zhou, no. 46), who has "bring peace to the eastern lands" and "none do not submit". 密: the state of Mi, traditionally placed at Lingtai, Gansu, on the land of the former Mixu. The later reign of King Mu and the reign of King Gong, about 950 to 900 BC: King Mu's wars with the Huaiyi and the eastern states in the Ban gui, and Dong's fight at Hu; Yu's campaigns against the Guifang in the Yu ding; the little that is recorded of war under King Gong; and the accession of King Yi (懿).

passages.title: c. 900–860 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前900年—公元前860年 懿王时，王室遂衰，戎狄交侵，暴虐中国。 据懿王时期的出土文物《史密簋》所载，因南夷“广伐东国”，王命师俗、史密率齐国之师加以讨伐。 右扶风槐里，周曰犬丘，懿王都之。 周懿王去世后，共王弟辟方继位，即为孝王。 据《史记·秦本纪》记载，犬丘人秦非子因为善于养马而得到周孝王的赏识，“邑之秦，使复续嬴氏祀，号曰秦嬴。” 周孝王去世后，诸侯复立懿王太子燮，即为夷王。 据《史记·楚世家》所载，楚国在夷王即位后自立为王，至厉王才去王号；《后汉书·西羌传》注引亦有《竹书纪年》所载夷王命虢公率六师伐被穆王所迁于太原之犬戎一事。 据夷王时期的青铜器铭所载，周曾由于南淮夷内伐而出动追击；《敔簋》铭云：“南淮尸迁殳，内伐……令敔追袭于上洛。”《鄂侯驭方鼎》与《史密簋》亦有载录夷王南征与东征之事。 周夷王去世后，其子胡继位，是为厉王。
passages.en: c. 900–860 BC In the time of King Yi (懿) the royal house thereupon declined, and the Rong and Di invaded in turn and ravaged the central states. According to the Shi Mi gui, an excavated object of King Yi (懿)'s period, because the Nanyi "widely attacked the eastern states", the King ordered Shi Su and Shi Mi to lead the army of the state of Qi to punish them. Huaili in Right Fufeng was called Quanqiu under the Zhou; King Yi (懿) made it his capital. After King Yi (懿) of Zhou's death, Pifang, younger brother of King Gong, succeeded; he is King Xiao. According to the Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin, Feizi of Qin, a man of Quanqiu, won the favour of King Xiao of Zhou by his skill in rearing horses, and the King "gave him Qin as his settlement, had him take up again the sacrifices of the Ying clan, and styled him Qin Ying." After King Xiao of Zhou's death the Lords in turn set up Xie, the Heir Apparent of King Yi (懿); he is King Yi (夷). According to the Shiji, Hereditary House of Chu, the state of Chu set itself up as a kingdom after King Yi (夷) came to the throne, and gave up the royal title only in the time of King Li; the commentary to the Hou Hanshu, Account of the Western Qiang also quotes the Bamboo Annals for King Yi (夷) ordering the Duke of Guo to lead the six armies against the Quan Rong whom King Mu had moved to Taiyuan. According to bronze inscriptions of King Yi (夷)'s period, Zhou once sent out a force in pursuit because the Southern Huaiyi attacked inward; the inscription of the Yu gui says: "The Southern Huaiyi moved to Shu and attacked inward … [the King] ordered Yu to pursue and strike them at Shangluo." The E Hou Yufang ding and the Shi Mi gui also record King Yi (夷)'s campaigns to the south and to the east. After King Yi (夷) of Zhou's death his son Hu succeeded; he is King Li.
passages.no: 王室遂衰，戎狄交侵，暴虐中国: the words of the Hanshu, Account of the Xiongnu. 右扶风槐里，周曰犬丘，懿王都之: the entry for Huaili in the Hanshu, Treatise on Geography. 敔簋: translated with Robert Eno's version at hand (Inscriptional Records of the Western Zhou, no. 103), which takes 上洛 as the upper reaches of Luo River and dates the vessel to King Li. 尸 is the inscription's form of 夷. From King Yi (懿) to the accession of King Li, about 900 to 860 BC: the decline of the royal house and the capital at Quanqiu; the Shi Mi gui and the campaign against the Nanyi; King Xiao and Feizi of Qin; and under King Yi (夷), Chu's taking of the royal title, the six armies sent against the Quan Rong of Taiyuan and the pursuit of the Southern Huaiyi.

passages.title: c. 900–860 BC (archaeological appearances)
passages.zh: 约公元前900年—公元前860年 约公元前900年： 辛店文化进入末期晚段；寺洼文化栏桥-徐家碾类型下限。 南京青铜时代二期文化承接了金滩里青铜时代二期文化发展。 虎骨洞四期文化承接虎骨洞三期文化发展。 松菊里文化区形成。
passages.en: c. 900–860 BC: archaeological appearances c. 900 BC: The Xindian culture entered the late stage of its final period; the Lanqiao–Xujianian type of the Siwa culture reached its lower limit. The Namgyeong Bronze Age Phase II culture took over from the Geumtan-ri Bronze Age Phase II culture and carried its development forward. The Beomui-guseok Phase IV culture took over from the Beomui-guseok Phase III culture and carried its development forward. The Songguk-ri culture area took shape.
passages.no: The cultures appearing in the same span, about 900 BC: the last stage of the Xindian culture and the end of the Lanqiao–Xujianian type; and in Korea, the Namgyeong Bronze Age Phase II culture, the Beomui-guseok Phase IV culture and the forming of the Songguk-ri culture area.

passages.title: c. 860–841 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前860年—公元前841年 厉王无道，淮夷入寇，王命虢仲征之，不克；厉王暴虐，熊渠畏其伐楚，亦去其王。 噩侯驭方是这次引导淮夷入侵的首领，噩因而成为周王朝主将武公讨伐的主要目标；《禹鼎》所记这一次战争，由于最终擒获了驭方，对南淮夷、东夷给予了沉重甚或是致命的打击。 据厉王时期的青铜器《宗周钟》铭文所载，在西周厉王后期，噩侯驭方已经消失，代之而起的是服子，而服子所在之都被击溃，不得已之下，服子与南夷、东夷各邦来觐见厉王。由此，西周的东夷、南夷之患，暂时得到安定。 据陕西下泉村出土的《多友鼎》记载，玁狁在厉王时曾入侵镐京周围的地区；周王朝出兵反击，不仅为了击退入侵的戎狄，夺回被俘的人和被劫的财物，更重要的是要戎狄定期献纳贡赋，维持原来“荒服”的制度。
passages.en: c. 860–841 BC King Li was without the Way; the Huaiyi came raiding, and the King ordered Guo Zhong to campaign against them, but he did not prevail. King Li was violent and cruel, and Xiong Qu, fearing that he would attack Chu, likewise gave up his title of king. Yufang, Marquis of E, was the leader who brought the Huaiyi in on this invasion, and E therefore became the chief target of the campaign of Duke Wu, chief commander of the Zhou court; the war recorded in the Yu ding, because it ended in the capture of Yufang, dealt the Southern Huaiyi and the Dongyi a heavy and perhaps even a mortal blow. According to the inscription of the Zongzhou zhong, a bronze of King Li's period, in the later part of the reign of King Li of the Western Zhou, Yufang, Marquis of E, had already disappeared, and Fuzi had risen in his place; the capital where Fuzi was seated was broken, and Fuzi, left with no choice, came with the states of the Nanyi and the Dongyi to have audience of King Li. With this the trouble that the Western Zhou had from the Dongyi and the Nanyi was settled for a time. According to the Duo You ding, unearthed at Xiaquan village in Shaanxi, the Xianyun in King Li's time invaded the region around Haojing; the Zhou court sent out troops to strike back, not only to drive off the invading Rong and Di and to win back the people taken captive and the goods carried off, but, more important, to make the Rong and Di offer tribute at fixed times and to keep up the old system of the "Wild Domain".
passages.no: 厉王无道，淮夷入寇，王命虢仲征之，不克: the words of the Hou Hanshu, Account of the Eastern Yi; 熊渠畏其伐楚，亦去其王 are those of the Shiji, Hereditary House of Chu. 荒服: the outermost of the five domains in the Tribute of Yu of the Documents, in Legge "the Wild domain". The reign of King Li, about 860 to 841 BC: the raids of the Huaiyi and Guo Zhong's failed campaign; Yufang, Marquis of E, and Duke Wu's war in the Yu ding; Fuzi and the audience of the Nanyi and the Dongyi in the Zongzhou zhong; and the Xianyun's invasion in the Duo You ding.

passages.title: c. 841–827 BC
passages.zh: 约公元前841年—公元前827年 王行暴虐侈傲，国人作乱，攻厉王，厉王出奔彘。 所谓“国人”是指居住在国都的“公民”，他们有纳军赋和服兵役的义务，是当时国家政治上和军事上的重要支柱，当国家有危难，有迁都和废立君主等大事，执政者都要征询他们的看法，他们会发表意见，甚至采取行动。这时周厉王暴虐，杀死诽谤的国人，禁止国人言论，因而被国人流放到彘。 于《史记·周本纪》有载：“召公、周公二相行政，号曰共和”，或有不确；当按古本《竹书纪年》所载：“厉王既亡，有共伯和者摄行天子事。” 秦仲立三年，周厉王无道，诸侯或叛之。西戎反王室，灭犬丘大骆之族。 共和十四年，厉王死于彘；太子静长于召公家，二相乃共立之为王，是为宣王。
passages.en: c. 841–827 BC The King's conduct was violent, cruel, extravagant and arrogant; the people of the capital rose in revolt and attacked King Li, and King Li fled to Zhi. The so-called "people of the capital" (国人) are the "citizens" who lived in the capital; they had the duty of paying the military levy and of serving as soldiers, and were an important pillar of the state of the time in both politics and war; when the state was in danger, or there was some great matter such as moving the capital or deposing and setting up a ruler, those in power always had to ask their views, and they would speak their mind and even take action. At this time King Li of Zhou was violent and cruel, killed the people of the capital who spoke ill of him and forbade them to speak, and for this he was banished to Zhi by the people of the capital. The Shiji, Basic Annals of Zhou records: "The Duke of Shao and the Duke of Zhou, the two Chancellors, conducted the government, and it was styled Gonghe", which is perhaps not accurate; the record of the old-text Bamboo Annals should be followed: "When King Li had fled, there was one He, Earl of Gong, who conducted the affairs of the Son of Heaven in his stead." In the third year after Qin Zhong was set up, King Li of Zhou was without the Way, and some of the Lords revolted against him. The Western Rong rose against the royal house and destroyed the clan of Daluo at Quanqiu. In the fourteenth year of Gonghe, King Li died at Zhi; the Heir Apparent Jing had grown up in the house of the Duke of Shao, and the two Chancellors then together set him up as King; he is King Xuan.
passages.no: 厉王既亡，有共伯和者摄行天子事: the Bamboo Annals as the Jinshu, Biography of Shu Xi, reports it, where the received text has 幽王 for 厉王. 秦仲立三年: 842 BC; the paragraph is the text of the Shiji, Basic Annals of Qin. 共和十四年: 828 BC. From King Li's flight to the accession of King Xuan, about 841 to 827 BC: the rising of the people of the capital and King Li's exile at Zhi; the Gonghe years in the Shiji and in the Bamboo Annals; the Western Rong's destruction of the clan of Daluo at Quanqiu; and King Li's death and the setting up of King Xuan.

passages.title: 京城日報 Keijō Nippō
passages.zh: 奉天軍の負傷多數 醫師の不足補充準備中 奉天電報目下もくか城內じゃうないの衛戍病院ゑいじゅびゃうゐんに收容しうようされ居ゐる負傷者ふしゃうしゃは五百六七十名ごひゃくろくしちじふめいで此外このほか二百名にひゃくめいあり輕傷者けいしゃうしゃは尚なほ戰線せんせんにある由よし 今度こんどの戰爭せんさうで最もっとも奮鬪ふんとうしたのは第二だいに、六ろくの兩りゃう旅りょにて彼等かれらは決死隊けっしたいを組織そしきして手てに手榴彈しゅりうだんを携たづさへて悲愴ひさうなる肉彈戰にくだんせんを爲なしたる爲ため最大多數さいだいたすうの負傷者ふしゃうしゃを出いだし城內じゃうない收容者しうようしゃは殆ほとんどその全部ぜんぶが兩旅りゃうりょの兵士へいしである 現在げんざい戰線せんせんに派遣はけんせる支那しな軍醫ぐんいは五百餘名ごひゃくよめいに達たっするも尚なほ不足ふそくにて滿鐵まんてつや赤十字せきじふじ方面はうめんより醫師いし其他そのたの材料ざいれうに就つき補充ほじゅうの準備中じゅんびちうである 奉軍副司令負傷 奉天十二日發電奉天軍ほうてんぐん第三軍だいさんぐん副司令ふくしれい第二だいに旅長りょちゃう郭鐘齡くわくしょうれいの戰死說せんしせつあるが氏しは石門子せきもんしの占領戰せんりゃうせんに奮戰ふんせんして脚部きゃくぶに貫通銃傷くわんつうじうしゃうを受うけ目下もくか錦州きんしうで治療中ちれうちうであると 渤海艦隊出動 青島十二日發電渤海艦隊ぼっかいかんたいの肇永翔てうえいしゃうの二隻にせきは十日とをか青島ちんたうを拔錨ばつべうした一方いっぱう秦皇島しんくわうたうの二艦にかんも出動しゅつどうすべく陸戰隊りくせんたい千五百名せんごひゃくめいの外出ぐわいしゅつを禁きんじ出動命令しゅつどうめいれいを俟まつてゐる 吳佩孚山海關著 天津十二日發電直隸軍ちょくれいぐん總司令そうしれい吳佩孚ごはいふ將軍しゃうぐんは十二日じふににち午前六時ごぜんろくじ山海關さんかいくわんに到着たうちゃくした 列車顛覆計畫 北京十一日發電十一日じふいちにち午前ごぜん吳佩孚ごはいふ氏しの搭乘たふじょうせる列車れっしゃが天津てんしん驛えきを通過つうくわせんとする際さい前方ぜんぱう線路上せんろじゃうに電氣仕掛でんきじかけの爆彈ばくだんが裝置さうちしてあるのを一露西亞人いちろしあじんが發見はっけん急報きふはうしたので辛からくも事ことなきを得えた 側面攻擊 直軍死守激戰 奉天發電十二日じふににち朝あさ著電ちゃくでんに依よれば山海關さんかいくわん第一線だいいっせんは皆みな陷落かんらくしたが所
passages.en: Many wounded in the Hōten army Shortage of doctors; reinforcements in preparation 【Hōten telegram】The wounded now housed in the garrison hospital within the city walls number five hundred and sixty or seventy, and there are two hundred more besides; the lightly wounded are reported to be still at the front. In the present war the hardest fighting fell to the Second and Sixth Brigades: they formed death squads and, grenades in hand, fought a grim battle of human bullets, and so produced the greatest number of wounded; almost all of those housed in the city are soldiers of these two brigades. The Chinese army doctors now sent to the front number more than five hundred but are still too few, and preparations are being made to bring in doctors and other supplies from the South Manchuria Railway and the Red Cross. Hōten deputy commander wounded 【Hōten, the 12th】There is a report that Kaku Shōrei, deputy commander of the Third Army of the Hōten army and commander of its Second Brigade, has been killed in action; but he fought hard in the battle for Sekimonshi, took a bullet through the leg, and is now under treatment at Kinshū. The Bokkai Fleet puts out 【Chintao, the 12th】Two ships of the Bokkai Fleet, the Chōwa and the Eishō, weighed anchor at Chintao on the 10th; the two ships at Shinkōtō are also to put out, and with shore leave stopped for their fifteen hundred marines they await the order to sail. Go Haifu arrives at Sankaikan 【Tenshin, the 12th】General Go Haifu, commander-in-chief of the Chokurei army, arrived at Sankaikan at six in the morning of the 12th. Plot to derail a train 【Pekin, the 11th】On the morning of the 11th, as the train carrying Go Haifu was about to pass through Tenshin Station, a Russian found an electrically fired bomb planted on the line ahead and gave the alarm, and so a disaster was narrowly avoided. Flank attack The Chokurei army fights hard to hold on 【Hōten telegram】By a telegram received on the morning of the 12th, the whole first line at Sankaikan has fallen.
passages.no: Six items from the war page of the Keijō Nippō, the Japanese-language daily of Seoul, of 14 October 1924: telegrams of 11–12 October from the Shanhai Pass front of the Second Zhili–Fengtian War, on the Fengtian wounded, the wounding of Guo Songling, the Zhili fleet, Wu Peifu's arrival at the front and a plot against his train. The transcription keeps the paper's characters and its furigana, in the historical kana spelling of the time. Chinese names are given in the translation in their Japanese readings, as the paper's readers read them; each Persons and Places entry gives the pinyin. The datelines give the place and the day a telegram was sent; the days are of October 1924. Names are given in their Japanese readings, as the paper's readers read them; the pinyin is in the Persons and Places entries. 奉天 Hōten is Fengtian, the Mukden of the Western press of the day and the seat of the Fengtian clique. 城內: inside the walled city, that is Hōten (Fengtian), from which the telegram was sent. 五百六七十名: five hundred and sixty-odd to seventy-odd. 由: the hearsay marker; the sentence reports what is said of the lightly wounded. 肉彈戰: a close assault in which the men themselves are the projectiles, a phrase of the Japanese press since the Russo-Japanese War. 奉天十二日發電: sent from Hōten (Fengtian) on the 12th. 郭鐘齡: the paper's writing of 郭松齡, Kaku Shōrei (Guo Songling in pinyin). 石門子 Sekimonshi: the Shimenzhai 石門寨 of the Chinese accounts, in the hills north-west of Shanhai Pass. 肇永翔: the cruisers Chōwa 肇和 and Eishō 永翔 (Zhaohe and Yongxiang in pinyin), their names run together. 天津驛 Tenshin Station: 驛, here the railway station.

entries.note: A man of Shangcai in Chu, pupil of Xun Qing; came to Qin in 247 BC and entered Lü Buwei's household as a Court Gentleman; later Senior Clerk, Guest Minister, Commandant of Justice and Chancellor of Qin.

entries.name: Lao Ai 嫪毐
entries.note: Lü Buwei's household retainer, passed by him into the Queen Dowager's service as a feigned eunuch; later Marquis Changxin 长信侯.

entries.name: the Queen Dowager 太后 (mother of King Zheng)
entries.alt: 帝太后; 赵姬 Queen Dowager of Qin
entries.note: Mother of King Zheng, the First Emperor; a woman of Zhao, Lü Buwei's concubine given by him to Zichu, the later King Zhuangxiang; later the Imperial Queen Dowager 帝太后, and in later tradition Zhao Ji 赵姬.

entries.name: Zheng Guo 郑国
entries.note: A water engineer of Han, sent into Qin, who built the irrigation canal that bears his name.

entries.name: Duke Mu of Qin 秦穆公
entries.note: Duke of Qin, reigned 659–621 BC, hegemon over the Western Rong; written 缪公 in Li Si's memorial.

entries.name: Duke Xiao of Qin 秦孝公
entries.note: Duke of Qin, reigned 361–338 BC, who employed Shang Yang.

entries.name: You Yu 由余
entries.note: A counsellor of the Rong who went over to Duke Mu of Qin.

entries.name: Baili Xi 百里奚
entries.note: A man of Wan in Chu, minister of Yu, then Grand Master to Duke Mu of Qin; the Xinxu calls him the Grand Master of the Five Rams' Skins 五羖大夫.

entries.name: Jian Shu 蹇叔
entries.note: Friend of Baili Xi, welcomed by Duke Mu of Qin as Senior Grand Master 上大夫.

entries.name: Pi Bao 丕豹
entries.note: A man of Jin who fled to Qin under Duke Mu.

entries.name: Gongsun Zhi 公孙支
entries.alt: 子桑 Grand Master of Qin
entries.note: Zi Sang 子桑, a Grand Master of Duke Mu of Qin.

entries.name: Shang Yang 商鞅
entries.alt: 卫鞅; 公孙鞅 Chancellor of Qin
entries.note: Wei Yang, Lord Shang 商君, minister of Duke Xiao of Qin and author of its laws.

entries.name: Zhang Yi 张仪
entries.note: Chancellor of Qin under King Huiwen, architect of the Horizontal Alliance.

entries.name: Marquis Rang 穰侯
entries.note: Wei Ran 魏冉, maternal uncle of King Zhaoxiang and Chancellor of Qin, deposed in 266 BC.

entries.name: Lord Huayang 华阳君
entries.note: Mi Rong 芈戎, brother of Queen Dowager Xuan, expelled from Qin with Marquis Rang; the Jijie: 华 one text 叶.

entries.name: Lu Zhonglian 鲁仲连
entries.note: A gentleman of Qi, the persuader who refused all reward; the Biography calls him Lu Lian 鲁连.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Tian Dan 田单
entries.alt: 安平君 Lord Anping; General of Qi
entries.note: General of Qi who recovered the state from Yan from his base at Jimo in 279 BC, enfeoffed as Lord Anping 安平君.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Guan Zhong 管仲
entries.alt: 管夷吾; 管子 Chancellor of Qi
entries.note: Guan Yiwu 管夷吾, Chancellor to Duke Huan of Qi; formerly Tutor to Prince Jiu.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Duke Huan of Qi 齐桓公
entries.alt: 桓公; 小白 Duke of Qi
entries.note: Xiaobai 小白, Duke of Qi, reigned 685–643 BC, first of the Five Hegemons.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Prince Jiu of Qi 公子纠
entries.note: Prince of Qi, rival of his brother Xiaobai for the dukedom, killed by Lu in 685 BC; Guan Zhong had been his Tutor.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Cao Mo 曹沫
entries.alt: 曹子; 曹昧 General of Lu
entries.note: General of Lu under Duke Zhuang, who held Duke Huan of Qi at dagger-point at the covenant of Ke (681 BC) and recovered Lu's lost land; the Suoyin writes 曹昧.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Duke Zhuang of Lu 鲁庄公
entries.note: Duke of Lu, reigned 693–662 BC; the lord of Lu of Cao Mo's story.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Mo Di 墨翟
entries.note: Mozi, the philosopher; the Zhengyi recalls his defence of Song against Chu.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Sun Bin 孙膑
entries.note: General and strategist of Qi under King Wei.

pages.label: 247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Pan Geng 盘庚
entries.note: King of Shang, who moved the capital to Yin; elder brother of Xiao Xin and Xiao Yi.

entries.name: Xiao Xin 小辛
entries.note: King of Shang, younger brother and successor of Pan Geng.

entries.name: Xiao Yi 小乙
entries.note: King of Shang, younger brother and successor of Xiao Xin; father of Wu Ding.

entries.name: Wu Ding 武丁
entries.note: King of Shang, son of Xiao Yi, whose reign opens the Yinxu period of the oracle-bone inscriptions.

entries.name: Zi Hua 子画
entries.note: A member of the Shang royal clan in the oracle-bone inscriptions, enfeoffed in the east at Hua in Wu Ding's first years.

entries.name: Que 雀
entries.note: A commander of Wu Ding's campaigns in the west, against the Zhifang, the Peifang and Yue.

entries.name: Zhi Guo 沚馘
entries.note: Chief of the Zhifang after its conquest, Wu Ding's vassal on the western frontier.

entries.name: Fu Zi 妇好
entries.note: Consort of Wu Ding and commander of his campaigns, against the Tufang among others; her tomb at Yinxu was found intact in 1976. The name is also read Fu Hao.

entries.name: Fu Geng 妇耕
entries.note: A consort of Wu Ding who campaigned against the Longfang.

entries.name: Wang Cheng 望乘
entries.note: A commander of Wu Ding, who campaigned with him against the Moufang.

entries.name: Lord Biao 麃公
entries.note: A general of Qin under King Zheng; the Suoyin: the lord of the town of Biao, his surname and name lost; the Zhengyi: Biao is probably a County town of Qin, and a Grand Master is called 公 as in the Chu system.

entries.name: Xiao Ji 孝己
entries.alt: 小王; 小王己 Heir Apparent of Shang
entries.note: Heir Apparent of Wu Ding, who died before his father; called the Junior King 小王 in the oracle-bone inscriptions, and in sacrifice Junior King Ji 小王己.

entries.name: Zu Jia 祖甲
entries.note: King of Shang, youngest son of Wu Ding and successor of his brother Zu Geng.

entries.name: Zu Geng 祖庚
entries.note: King of Shang, son and successor of Wu Ding.

entries.name: Lin Xin 廪辛
entries.note: King of Shang, son and successor of Zu Jia.

entries.name: Kang Ding 康丁
entries.note: King of Shang, son of Zu Jia and successor of his brother Lin Xin.

entries.name: King Tai of Zhou 周太王
entries.note: Gugong Danfu 古公亶父, ancestor of the Zhou kings, who moved the Zhou from Bin to the foot of Mount Qi.

entries.name: Wu Yi 武乙
entries.note: King of Shang, son and successor of Kang Ding.

entries.name: Wen Ding 文丁
entries.note: King of Shang, son and successor of Wu Yi; written Tai Ding 太丁 in the Basic Annals of Yin and the Bamboo Annals, which also has 文丁.

entries.name: Taibo 太伯
entries.note: Eldest son of King Tai of Zhou; by the Shiji the founder, with his brother Zhongyong, of the state of Wu.

entries.name: Zhongyong 仲雍
entries.note: Second son of King Tai of Zhou, brother of Taibo.

entries.name: Jili 季历
entries.note: Youngest son of King Tai of Zhou and father of Chang, King Wen.

entries.name: Tai Jiang 太姜
entries.note: Principal consort of King Tai of Zhou, of the Jiang surname.

entries.name: Tai Ren 太任
entries.note: Wife of Jili and mother of Chang, King Wen.

entries.name: Shi, Duke of Shao 召公奭
entries.note: Shi 奭, Duke of Shao in the first years of the Western Zhou, whose fief was Shao.

entries.name: Di Yi 帝乙
entries.note: King of Shang, son and successor of Wen Ding.

entries.name: Xi, Marquis of You 攸侯喜
entries.note: Xi 喜, Marquis of the state of You, with whom Di Xin campaigned against the Yifang in the oracle-bone inscriptions.

entries.name: Yu 艅
entries.note: A Lesser Minister of the end of Shang, for whom the rhinoceros zun was made.

entries.name: Tai Si 太姒
entries.note: Consort of King Wen of Zhou and mother of Fa, King Wu.

entries.name: King Wu of Zhou 周武王
entries.alt: 发; 太子发; 武王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Wen, born of Tai Si; personal name Fa 发.

entries.name: Hu, Marquis of Chong 崇侯虎
entries.note: Hu 虎, Marquis of the state of Chong.

entries.name: Bigan 比干
entries.note: A prince of the Shang royal house, killed by Di Xin.

entries.name: Jizi 箕子
entries.note: A noble of the Shang royal house, imprisoned by Di Xin.

entries.name: Ci, Grand Preceptor 太师疵
entries.note: Ci 疵, Grand Preceptor of Shang, who went over to Zhou.

entries.name: Qiang, Junior Preceptor 少师彊
entries.note: Qiang 彊, Junior Preceptor of Shang, who went over to Zhou.

entries.name: Taigong 太公
entries.note: Lü Shang 吕尚, called Taigong, commander under King Wu; enfeoffed at Yingqiu, the founder of the state of Qi.

entries.name: Fang Lai 方来
entries.note: A minister of Di Xin who kept up resistance in the royal domain after Muye.

entries.name: Weizi Qi 微子启
entries.note: Qi 启, Weizi, elder brother of Di Xin by a secondary consort, whose fief was Wei 微; made the heir of Yin in Song after Wu Geng's revolt.

entries.name: Wu Geng 武庚
entries.note: Son of Di Xin, enfeoffed by King Wu at Yin.

entries.name: Guanshu Xian 管叔鲜
entries.note: Xian 鲜, Guanshu, brother of King Wu, enfeoffed at Guan; one of the Three Guards.

entries.name: Bishu 毕叔
entries.note: A kinsman of King Wu, sent with Kangshu to free the kinsmen Di Xin had imprisoned.

entries.name: Kangshu Feng 康叔封
entries.note: Feng 封, Kangshu, full brother of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou.

entries.name: Hong Yao 闳夭
entries.note: A minister of King Wu.

entries.name: Lü Ta 吕他
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Hou Lai 侯来
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Bai Yan 百弇
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Chen Ben 陈本
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Bai Wei 百韦
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Xin Huang 新荒
entries.note: A commander of King Wu in the Great Capture chapter of the Yi Zhou Shu.

entries.name: Caishu Du 蔡叔度
entries.note: Du 度, Caishu, full brother of King Wu; one of the Three Guards.

entries.name: Huoshu Chu 霍叔处
entries.note: Chu 处, Huoshu, full brother of King Wu; one of the Three Guards.

entries.name: King Cheng of Zhou 周成王
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Wu.

entries.name: Boqin 伯禽
entries.note: Son of the Duke of Zhou, moved to a fief in the east as ruler of Lu.

entries.name: Ke, Marquis of Yan 匽侯克
entries.note: Ke 克, son of the Duke of Shao, enfeoffed by King Cheng as Marquis of Yan, written 匽 in the bronze inscriptions.

entries.name: Feilian 飞廉
entries.note: A minister of Di Xin who took refuge in the state of Yan 奄.

entries.name: Shun 舜
entries.note: A sage ruler of antiquity, successor of Yao.

entries.name: Yao 尧
entries.note: A sage ruler of antiquity.

entries.name: Tangshu Yu 唐叔虞
entries.note: Yu 虞, Tangshu, full brother of King Cheng, enfeoffed at Tang; the founder of the house of Jin.

entries.name: Xiefu 燮父
entries.note: Son and successor of Tangshu Yu, who moved from Tang to Jin.

entries.name: King Kang of Zhou 周康王
entries.alt: 钊; 太子钊; 康王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Cheng; personal name Zhao 钊.

entries.name: Sima Qian 司马迁
entries.note: The author of the Shiji, Grand Historian under Emperor Wu of Han.

entries.name: King Zhao of Zhou 周昭王
entries.alt: 瑕; 昭王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Kang; personal name Xia 瑕.

entries.name: King Mu of Zhou 周穆王
entries.alt: 满; 穆王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Zhao; personal name Man 满.

entries.name: Earl of Guo 过伯
entries.note: The maker of the Guo Bo gui, who followed King Zhao against Jing; 伯 is written 白 in the inscription.

entries.name: Queen Mother of the West 西王母
entries.note: Xiwangmu, the divine queen of the far west whom King Mu meets in the Mu Tianzi Zhuan.

entries.name: King Gong of Zhou 周共王
entries.alt: 繄扈; 共王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Mu; personal name Yihu 繄扈.

entries.name: King Yi of Zhou 周懿王
entries.alt: 囏; 懿王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Gong; personal name Jian 囏.

entries.name: Dong 𰒦
entries.note: A commander of King Mu, who fought the Huaiyi at Hu; the maker of the Dong gui. The name is also read Zhong.

entries.name: Yu 盂
entries.note: The maker of the Da Yu ding and the Xiao Yu ding, who twice campaigned against the Guifang at the King's command.

entries.name: Shi Su 师俗
entries.note: An officer (师) of the King, sent with Shi Mi against the Nanyi, in the Shi Mi gui.

entries.name: Shi Mi 史密
entries.note: A scribe (史) of the King, the maker of the Shi Mi gui, sent with Shi Su against the Nanyi at the head of the army of Qi.

entries.name: King Xiao of Zhou 周孝王
entries.alt: 辟方; 孝王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, younger brother of King Gong and successor of King Yi 懿; personal name Pifang 辟方.

entries.name: Feizi of Qin 秦非子
entries.note: Feizi, a man of Quanqiu who reared horses for King Xiao of Zhou, was given Qin as his settlement and was styled Qin Ying 秦嬴; the founder of the house of Qin.

entries.name: King Yi of Zhou 周夷王
entries.alt: 燮; 夷王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son of King Yi 懿 and successor of King Xiao; personal name Xie 燮.

entries.name: King Li of Zhou 周厉王
entries.alt: 胡; 厉王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Yi 夷; personal name Hu 胡.

entries.name: Duke of Guo 虢公
entries.note: The Duke of Guo 虢 whom King Yi 夷 ordered to lead the six armies against the Quan Rong of Taiyuan, in the Bamboo Annals.

entries.name: Yu 敔
entries.note: The maker of the Yu gui, ordered to pursue the Southern Huaiyi.

entries.name: Guo Zhong 虢仲
entries.note: Zhong of Guo 虢, the commander King Li sent against the Huaiyi.

entries.name: Xiong Qu 熊渠
entries.note: Ruler of Chu in the time of King Yi 夷 and King Li, who took the title of king and then gave it up.

entries.name: Yufang, Marquis of E 噩侯驭方
entries.alt: 鄂侯驭方; 驭方 Marquis of E
entries.note: Yufang 驭方, Marquis of E, who led the Huaiyi against Zhou under King Li and was taken in Duke Wu's campaign; 噩 is the bronze inscriptions' form of 鄂.

entries.name: Duke Wu 武公
entries.note: The chief commander of the Zhou court under King Li, in the Yu ding.

entries.name: Fuzi 服子
entries.note: The ruler of the southern lands in the Zongzhou zhong, whose capital was broken by King Li.

entries.name: Duke of Shao 召公
entries.note: The Duke of Shao of King Li's time, a descendant of Shi, Duke of Shao; one of the two Chancellors of the Gonghe years, in whose house the Heir Apparent Jing grew up.

entries.name: Duke of Zhou 周公
entries.note: The Duke of Zhou of King Li's time, a descendant of Dan, Duke of Zhou; one of the two Chancellors of the Gonghe years.

entries.name: He, Earl of Gong 共伯和
entries.note: He 和, Earl of Gong, who by the Bamboo Annals conducted the affairs of the Son of Heaven after King Li's flight.

entries.name: Qin Zhong 秦仲
entries.note: Ruler of Qin, reigned 844–822 BC, great-grandson of Feizi.

entries.name: Daluo 大骆
entries.note: Father of Feizi, whose clan held Quanqiu.

entries.name: King Xuan of Zhou 周宣王
entries.alt: 静; 太子静; 宣王 King of Zhou
entries.note: King of Zhou, son and successor of King Li; personal name Jing 静.

entries.name: Qin 秦
entries.note: the state of Qin, with its capital at Xianyang, Shaanxi.

entries.name: Ye 鄴

entries.name: Hao 鄗

entries.name: Xinling 信陵
entries.note: the Prince's fief in Wei; near modern Ningling, Henan.

entries.name: Hewai 河外
entries.note: "beyond the River": the region south of the Yellow River on the Wei–Qin frontier.

entries.name: Hangu Pass 函谷关
entries.note: the pass into Qin from the east; modern Lingbao, Henan.

entries.name: Dong Commandery 东郡
entries.note: a Qin commandery with its seat at Puyang; modern Puyang, Henan.

entries.name: Hejian 河间
entries.note: "between the rivers": the Zhao territory around modern Hejian and Xian County, Hebei.

entries.note: a loess terrace south of Xi'an, in Chang'an District, Shaanxi.

entries.name: Du County 杜县

entries.name: Zhiyang 芷阳

entries.note: the tomb of King Xiaowen of Qin.

entries.name: Ju 莒
entries.note: the former state of Ju, by 255 BC held by Chu; modern Ju County, Shandong.

entries.name: Yuanshi 元氏
entries.note: a Zhao town; modern Yuanshi County, Hebei.

entries.name: Shangyuan 上原
entries.note: a Zhao place near Yuanshi, made a County in 252 BC; the commentaries give no location.

entries.name: Wu 巫
entries.note: Chu's Wu Commandery on the Yangtze gorges; around modern Wushan, Chongqing.

entries.name: Qianzhong 黔中
entries.note: Chu's Qianzhong Commandery; western Hunan, around modern Yuanling.

entries.name: Yan 鄢
entries.note: a Chu city north of Ying; modern Yicheng, Hubei.

entries.name: Ying 郢
entries.note: the capital of Chu; the Jinan city site north of modern Jingzhou, Hubei.

entries.name: Jingling 竟陵
entries.note: modern Qianjiang, Hubei.

entries.name: Chen County 陈县
entries.note: the former capital of the state of Chen, Chu's seat from 278 to 253 BC; modern Huaiyang, Henan.

entries.name: Qi 齐
entries.note: the state of Qi, with its capital at Linzi; modern Zibo, Shandong.

entries.name: Henei 河内
entries.note: Wei's lands north of the Yellow River; around modern Xinxiang, Henan.

entries.name: Yan 燕 (Wei town)
entries.note: the southern Yan, a Wei town; modern Yanjin, Henan.

entries.name: Suanzao 酸枣
entries.note: a Wei town; south-west of modern Yanjin, Henan.

entries.name: Xu 虚
entries.note: a Wei town near Suanzao, in the area of modern Yanjin, Henan.

entries.name: Tao 桃
entries.note: Taocheng in Yan County (Xu Guang); near modern Yanjin, Henan.

entries.name: Xing 邢
entries.note: Xingqiu, twenty li south-east of Wude County in Huaizhou (Zhengyi); modern Wen County, Henan.

entries.name: Pu 蒲
entries.note: Pu Township in Changyuan County (Xu Guang); modern Changyuan, Henan.

entries.name: Yan 衍
entries.note: a Wei town north of modern Zhengzhou, Henan.

entries.name: Shou 首
entries.note: a Wei town in the area of modern Changyuan, Henan.

entries.name: Yuan 垣
entries.note: Changyuan; modern Changyuan, Henan.

entries.name: Ren 仁
entries.note: a Wei town near Pingqiu.

entries.name: Pingqiu 平丘
entries.note: modern Fengqiu, Henan.

entries.name: Huang 黄
entries.note: the old Huang city east of Kaocheng County (Zhengyi); modern Minquan, Henan.

entries.name: Jiyang 济阳
entries.note: the old Jiyang city south-west of Wanju County (Zhengyi); modern Lankao, Henan.

entries.name: Puli 濮磿
entries.note: a place near the Pu River (Suoyin), which flows north into the Ji at Juye (Xu Guang); around modern Puyang, Henan.

entries.name: Yuci 榆次
entries.note: a city of Zhao in the Taiyuan region, south-east of Jinyang; modern Yuci, Jinzhong, Shanxi.
entries.more: where Zhi Bo was defeated (Suoyin); modern Yuci, Jinzhong, Shanxi.

entries.name: Wu 吴
entries.note: the state of Wu and its capital; modern Suzhou, Jiangsu.

entries.name: Gansui 干隧
entries.note: in the Wu country, forty li north-west of Suzhou, where King Fuchai of Wu killed himself (Zhengyi).

entries.name: Yue 越
entries.note: the state of Yue, with its capital at Kuaiji; modern Shaoxing, Zhejiang.

247 BC · Ivar the Boneless' commentary and analysis I

entries.name: Ailing 艾陵
entries.note: Ai Mountain, sixty li south of Bo County in Yanzhou (Zhengyi); modern Tai'an, Shandong.

entries.name: shore of Sanzhu 三渚之浦
entries.note: in the Wu country near Gusu; the Zhanguoce has 三江之浦, the shore of the Three Rivers.

entries.name: Jinyang 晋阳
entries.note: the Zhao stronghold; modern Taiyuan, Shanxi.
